A union subject to a collective bargaining contract providing for negotiation and adoption of modifications at an intermediate date during its term, struck in support of modification demands after the date on which such modifications might, by the terms of the contract, become effective, and more than 60 days after it gave notice of its desire for modification, but prior to the terminal date of the contract. Section 8(d) of the amended National Labor Relations Act provides that a party who wishes to modify or terminate a collective bargaining contract must continue in full force, without resorting to strike or lockout, all the terms and conditions of the contract for a period of 60 days after giving notice of his wish to modify or terminate, or until the "expiration date" of the contract, whichever is later. Because of certain actions of the employer during the strike, the union filed unfair labor practice charges with the National Labor Relations Board, which held the employer guilty of such practices (109 NLRB 680), rejecting the employer's contention that the strike, because it occurred prior to the termination of the collective bargaining contract, was in violation of 8(d). On the employer's petition for review, the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit set aside the Board's order (221 F2d 231).

During a murder trial, in the Jefferson Circuit Court, Criminal Branch, Second Division, Kentucky, the trial judge informed defense counsel on nine different occasions that he was in contempt for his courtroom conduct, affording the attorney, in most instances, an opportunity to respond to the contempt charges at such times. After the jury had returned a guilty verdict in the murder prosecution, the trial judge summarily entered final adjudication of contempt against the attorney, sentencing him to consecutive jail terms on each of the nine contempt counts varying from 30 days to one year, and totaling almost 4 1/2 years. At the time of sentencing the attorney, the trial judge (1) said that the attorney had put on "the worst display" he had seen in many years at the bar, and that "as far as a lawyer is concerned, you're not," and (2) refused to permit the attorney to respond to the charges, even indicating that the attorney might be gagged if he insisted on defending himself. While the attorney's appeal was pending, the trial judge amended the judgment to eliminate one of the counts and to reduce the one year sentences imposed on two counts to 6 months, but did not specify whether the new sentences were to run concurrently or consecutively. The Court of Appeals of Kentucky affirmed, holding, inter alia, that (1) the sentences under the amended judgment ran concurrently for a single 6 months' period, a jury trial thus not being required, (2) the contempt sentences at the end of the trial could not have been a surprise to the attorney because upon each occasion during the trial, he was informed that he was in contempt of court, and (3) the trial judge was not disqualified to sit in judgment on the contempt charges, since he had not been attacked personally and had not bec

An injunction was obtained by the state of Ohio in state court requiring an individual who was the chief executive of a corporation to clean up a hazardous waste site. When the individual failed to comply with his obligation under the injunction, the state obtained the appointment in state court of a receiver who was directed to take possession of all property and other assets of the individual and the corporation and to implement the judgment entry by cleaning up the site. The receiver took possession of the site but had not completed his task when the individual filed a personal bankruptcy petition. The state filed a complaint in the Bankruptcy Court seeking a declaration that the individual's obligation under the judgment order to clean up the site was not dischargeable in bankruptcy because it was not a "debt," or a "liability on a claim," within the meaning of the Bankruptcy Code, and also seeking an injunction against the bankruptcy trustee to restrain him from pursuing any action to recover assets of the individual in the hands of the receiver. The Bankruptcy Court ruled against the state (29 BR 816) as did the District Court. The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed, holding that the state essentially sought from the individual only a monetary payment and that such a required payment was a liability on a claim that was dischargeable under the bankruptcy statute (717 F2d 984).

A Negro woman, discharged from employment on October 25, 1971, filed a charge of race discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission on February 10, 1972, 84 days after her grievance under the procedures of the collective-bargaining agreement in force between her union and her former employer had been denied, but 108 days after her discharge. Upon the Commission's finding that race had not figured in the discharge, the woman brought an action in the United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee under 706 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e-5), but the action was dismissed on the ground that the woman had not filed her charge with the Commission "within ninety days after the alleged unlawful employment practice occurred," 90 days being the time limitation set forth in 706 prior to its amendment on March 24, 1972, when the limitations period was extended to 180 days. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed (525 F2d 124).

A bank brought an action in a Federal District Court against a second bank, alleging that the second bank had failed to comply with its obligations under a certain regulation in respect to a dishonored check, in that the second bank had not properly notified the plaintiff bank that the check was not supported by sufficient funds. The District Court found that the second bank had not exercised ordinary care and entered judgment in favor of the plaintiff bank in the amount of its loss. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit did not reach the merits of the appeal, but (1) instead raised the issue of subject matter jurisdiction; (2) concluded that the civil liability provision of the Expedited Funds Availability Act (12 USCS 4010) provided for federal court jurisdiction only when a person other than a depository institution sues a depository institution, such as when a depositor sues a bank; (3) vacated the District Court's judgment; and (4) remanded with instructions to dismiss the action for lack of jurisdiction (30 F3d 64).

The defendant was tried in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts on charges of having attempted to bribe an internal revenue agent. The evidence showed that the defendant first made an unsolicited offer of money to the agent for the purpose of obtaining his assistance in concealing any cabaret tax liability, and that at a later meeting in defendant's office the latter's improper overtures began almost at the outset of the discussion, which was wire-recorded by a device carried by the agent. Defendant's conviction (on three of the four counts) was affirmed by the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. (305 F2d 825.)

The Federal Communications Commission, in determining its fees for regulation of Community Antenna Television (CATV) systems, set, in addition to filing fees, a 30-cent fee for each subscriber, concluding that this fee would approximate the "value to the recipient" pursuant to the Independent Offices Appropriation Act of 1952 (31 USCS 483a), authorizing the head of each federal agency to prescribe, by regulation, such fee as he shall determine to be fair and equitable taking into consideration "value to the recipient, public policy or interests served and other pertinent facts" (23 FCC2d 880, 28 FCC2d 139). On petitions for review, filed by the representatives of the broadcasting and cable television industries, the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the order of the Commission (464 F2d 1313).

Appellant was convicted in a state court of murder in the first degree. The conviction was affirmed by the state supreme court, 27 Cal. 2d 478, 165 P. 2d 3, which sustained the validity of provisions of the state law challenged as violative of the Federal Constitution.

In a state-law defamation action filed by attorney Johnnie L. Cochran, Jr., a California trial court found that petitioner Tory, assisted by petitioner Craft and others, had, inter alia, falsely claimed that Cochran owed him money, picketed Cochran's office with signs containing insults and obscenities, and pursued Cochran while chanting similar threats and insults, in order to coerce Cochran into paying Tory money to desist from such libelous and slanderous activity. Because Tory indicated that he would continue to engage in the activity absent a court order, the court permanently enjoined petitioners and their agents from, among other things, picketing, displaying signs, and making oral statements about Cochran and his firm in any public forum. The California Court of Appeal affirmed, and this Court granted certiorari. After oral argument, Cochran's counsel informed the Court of Cochran's death, moved to substitute Cochran's widow as respondent, and suggested that the case be dismissed as moot. Petitioners agreed to the substitution, but denied that the case was moot.

While one of appellant's trucks, en route to Brooklyn, New York, passed through the Holland Tunnel, its loan of carbon bisulphide exploded. Appellant was indicted for knowingly violating an Interstate Commerce Commission regulation which required drivers of motor vehicles transporting explosives or inflammable liquids to avoid "so far as practicable, and where feasible," by pre-arrangement of routes, driving through congested thoroughfares, tunnels, etc. The district court dismissed the indictment on the ground that the regulation was invalid for vagueness.

Nike filed this suit, alleging that two of Already's athletic shoes violated Nike's Air Force 1 trademark. Already denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim challenging the validity of Nike's Air Force 1 trademark. While the suit was pending, Nike issued a "Covenant Not to Sue," promising not to raise any trademark or unfair competition claims against Already or any affiliated entity based on Already's existing footwear designs, or any future Already designs that constituted a "colorable imitation" of Already's current products. Nike then moved to dismiss its claims with prejudice, and to dismiss Already's counterclaim without prejudice on the ground that the covenant had extinguished the case or controversy. Already opposed dismissal of its counterclaim, contending that Nike had not established that its covenant had mooted the case. In support, Already presented an affidavit from its president, stating that Already planned to introduce new versions of its lines into the market; affidavits from three potential investors, asserting that they would not consider investing in Already until Nike's trademark was invalidated; and an affidavit from an Already executive, stating that Nike had intimidated retailers into refusing to carry Already's shoes. The District Court dismissed Already's counterclaim, concluding that there was no longer a justiciable controversy. The Second Circuit affirmed. It explained that the covenant was broadly drafted; that the court could not conceive of a shoe that would infringe Nike's trademark yet not fall within the covenant; and that Already had not asserted any intent to market such a shoe.

Following a suspicious vehicle, Sergeant Matt Darisse noticed that only one of the vehicle's brake lights was working and pulled the driver over. While issuing a warning ticket for the broken brake light, Darisse became suspicious of the actions of the two occupants and their answers to his questions. Petitioner Nicholas Brady Heien, the car's owner, gave Darisse consent to search the vehicle. Darisse found cocaine, and Heien was arrested and charged with attempted trafficking. The trial court denied Heien's motion to suppress the seized evidence on Fourth Amendment grounds, concluding that the vehicle's faulty brake light gave Darisse reasonable suspicion to initiate the stop. The North Carolina Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the relevant code provision, which requires that a car be "equipped with a stop lamp," N. C. Gen. Stat. Ann. ¬ß20-129(g), requires only a single lamp-which Heien's vehicle had-and therefore the justification for the stop was objectively unreasonable. Reversing in turn, the State Supreme Court held that, even assuming no violation of the state law had occurred, Darisse's mistaken understanding of the law was reasonable, and thus the stop was valid.

Five years after the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) first approved metoclopramide, a drug commonly used to treat digestive tract problems, under the brand name Reglan, generic manufacturers such as petitioners also began producing the drug. Because of accumulating evidence that long-term metoclopramide use can cause tardive dyskinesia, a severe neurological disorder, warning labels for the drug have been strengthened and clarified several times, most recently in 2009. Respondents were prescribed Reglan in 2001 and 2002, but both received the generic drug from their pharmacists. After taking the drug as prescribed for several years, both developed tardive dyskinesia. In separate state-court tort actions, they sued petitioners, the generic drug manufacturers that produced the metoclopramide they took (Manufacturers). Each respondent alleged, inter alia, that longterm metoclopramide use caused her disorder and that the Manufacturers were liable under state tort law for failing to provide adequate warning labels. In both suits, the Manufacturers urged that federal statutes and FDA regulations pre-empted the state tort claims by requiring the same safety and efficacy labeling for generic metoclopramide as was mandated at the time for Reglan. The Fifth and Eighth Circuits rejected these arguments, holding that respondents‚Äô claims were not pre-empted.

The petitions for writs of certiorari are granted. The judgments are vacated and the cases are remanded to the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York for further proceedings in the light of Shillitani v. United States, ante, P. 364. The two petitioners were found guilty of contempt for failure to testify, after grant of immunity, before a grand jury, and were sentenced to 2 years' imprisonment, with the proviso that they would be released upon answering the questions put to them.

Under the National Labor Relations Act, as originally enacted, which made no provision for enjoining union activities as constituting unfair labor practices, the Supreme Court, in Allen-Bradley Local, U.E.R.M.W. v Wisconsin Employment Relations Board (1942) 315 US 740, 86 L ed 1154, 62 S Ct 820, ruled that the act did not deprive a state of power to enjoin mass picketing, threats to employees desiring to work, physical injury or property damage, obstruction of the entrance to and egress from the place of work, obstructing streets and public roads surrounding such place, and picketing the homes of employees. The issue in the present case was whether state power to enjoin such violent union conduct was eliminated with the passage of the Labor Management Relations Act of 1947, which empowered the National Labor Relations Board to enjoin, among other unfair union labor practices, coercion of employees who wished to refrain from striking.

A defendant was charged with murder and first-degree criminal sexual conduct, and was tried in the Court of General Sessions for Charleston County, South Carolina, on the basis of an incident in which, after he and three other youths had encountered another man, a self-proclaimed preacher, in a wooded section of a park at night and had beaten the man on the head with a bottle, the defendant perforated the man's rectum with an umbrella and stabbed him with a knife. The youths, looking for something to steal, had also rummaged through the victim's belongings, which consisted mainly of some bibles and various other religious tracts and articles, and scattered them on the ground; these items were introduced into evidence without objection at the guilt phase of the trial, but no reference was made at that time to the content of the papers. After the defendant was convicted, a sentencing hearing was held in which the prosecutor, during his closing argument, (1) commented on the fact that the victim had been a religious man, (2) read a prayer that had been printed on one of the victim's cards, (3) noted that the victim had been a vulnerable man with a history of mental problems which prevented him from holding a job, and (4) pointed to a voter registration card which the victim had been carrying as indicating the victim's belief in his community and his country. The defendant was sentenced to death; but the Supreme Court of South Carolina, while affirming the defendant's conviction, reversed the sentence and remanded the case for a new sentencing hearing, as it ruled that the prosecutor's closing argument had violated the rule of Booth v Maryland (1987) 482 US 496, 96 L Ed 2d 440, 107 S Ct 2529, by focusing extensively on the personal characteristics of the victim (295 SC 476,

In a Kentucky trial court an accused's counsel requested that the jury be instructed as to the presumption of the accused's innocence, but the trial judge refused the instruction, giving instead an instruction to the effect that the jury could return a verdict of guilty only if it found beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused had committed the acts charged in the indictment with the requisite criminal intent. The accused was found guilty by the jury, and on appeal in the Supreme Court of Kentucky he argued that he had been denied due process of law in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment by reason of the trial judge's refusal to give the requested instruction. The state Supreme Court reversed the convictions, holding that under the United States Supreme Court's decision in Taylor v Kentucky (1978) 436 US 478, 56 L Ed 2d 468, 98 S Ct 1930,--in which the court reversed a criminal conviction resulting from a trial in which the judge had refused to give a requested jury instruction on the presumption of innocence--an instruction as to the presumption of an accused's innocence is constitutionally required in all criminal trials, and that the failure of a trial judge to give such an instruction could not be harmless error.

The issue was whether attachment of the right to counsel required that a public prosecutor (as distinct from a police officer) be aware of a first appearance or involved in its conduct. Specifically, the question was whether a Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Ann. art. 15.17 hearing marked that point, with the consequent state obligation to appoint counsel within a reasonable time once a request for assistance was made. Prior case law clearly established that the right to counsel attached at the initial appearance before a judicial officer. The article 15.17 hearing was an initial appearance as the accused was taken before a magistrate judge, informed of the formal accusation against him, and sent to jail until he posted bail. The lower court's attachment standard, which depended on whether a prosecutor had a hand in starting the adversarial judicial proceedings, was wrong. Under the federal standard, an accusation filed with a judicial officer was sufficiently formal, and the government's commitment to prosecute it sufficiently concrete, when the accusation prompted arraignment and restrictions on the accused's liberty to facilitate the prosecution.

To stop secondary picketing by a union, an employer sought and obtained a state court injunction and, in addition, filed a charge of unfair labor practice with the National Labor Relations Board. After issuance of an unfair labor practice complaint, the Board's regional director petitioned the District Court for an injunction against the union.

This suit attacking the validity of the Drew Municipal School District's rule against employing parents of illegitimate children was initiated by two such parents, both mothers, against whom the rule militated. Named as defendants were the Drew Municipal School District (the District), George Ferris Pettey, its Superintendent, and the individual members of the District's Board of Trustees (the Board).

In response to subpoenas issued by the Office of Price Administration, the petitioner, after claiming his privilege against self-incrimination, testified before an examiner of this office with respect to matters which were pertinent to his subsequent prosecution for and conviction of intentional misuse of priority ratings in order to purchase textiles, unlawful utilization of the textiles so obtained, and conspiracy to violate the Emergency Price Control Act. His claim of immunity under 202(g) of the Act was, in part, rejected by the court below on the ground that he had answered in the negative a question by the examiner as to whether he claimed immunity with respect to a statement made by him as to the acquisition and disposal of material through the priorities furnished by a manufacturer.

Indians who had executed an oil and gas lease approved by the Department of the Interior for use on allotted lands held by the Indians under trust patents issued by the United States pursuant to the General Allotment Act of 1887 instituted an action against the lessee in the District Court of Oklahoma County, Oklahoma, to recover for an alleged breach of the lease by the lessee. The District Court sustained the lessee's demurrer, dismissing the petition, and the Supreme Court of Oklahoma affirmed on the ground that the petitioners were precluded from suing by the provisions of the lease and by federal regulations promulgated to control oil and gas leases on restricted Indian land.

South Carolina statutes impose a poundage tax on shrimp taken in the three-mile belt of its coast, require a license fee for each shrimp boat owned by a nonresident one hundred times the fee for boats owned by residents, condition the issuance of licenses to nonresidents on submission of proof that the applicants have paid South Carolina income taxes on all profits from operations in that state during the preceding year, and that all boats licensed to trawl for shrimp in the state's waters dock at a South Carolina port and unload, pack, and stamp their catch with a tax stamp before shipping or transporting it to another state or the waters thereof.

While jury selection was underway, after a defendant's Arizona trial for first-degree murder of a newspaper reporter had begun, the defendant and the state prosecutor reached an agreement--accepted by the state trial court--whereby, in return for a specified prison sentence and specified actual incarceration time, the defendant would (1) plead guilty to a charge of second-degree murder, and (2) testify against two other suspects who were allegedly involved in the reporter's murder. The agreement added that should the defendant refuse to testify or at any time testify untruthfully, then the entire agreement was "null and void" and the original charge would automatically be reinstated. The defendant then testified at a trial of the two suspects, and, while appeals from their convictions were pending, the trial court imposed sentence on the defendant, but, after the suspects' convictions were reversed on appeal, (1) the defendant said he would not testify at the suspects' retrials unless certain conditions were met, (2) the state informed the defendant that he was in breach of the plea agreement, (3) the defendant refused to testify at certain pretrial proceedings in connection with the retrials, and (4) the state filed a new information charging the defendant with first-degree murder. The defendant's motion to quash the new information was denied by the trial court, but the Arizona Supreme Court, in 1980, vacated the defendant's second-degree murder conviction, dismissed the new information, and reinstated the original first-degree murder charge. The Arizona Supreme Court expressed the view that (1) contrary to the defendant's restrictive interpretation of the plea agreement, the agreement contemplated the availability of the defendant's testimony whether at trial or retr

An illiterate man, convicted by a Florida state court of the noncapital offenses of incest and assault in a lewd, lascivious, and indecent manner upon a female child under the age of 14, who was not afforded the assistance of counsel for his defense, obtained a provisional writ of habeas corpus from the Florida Supreme Court on a petition asserting that the failure to provide counsel for his defense deprived him of rights guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment. On the petition, the return, and the accused's reply, but without a hearing, the Florida Supreme Court denied the writ. (123 So 2d 249.)

An individual sought leave to proceed in forma pauperis in the United States Supreme Court with respect to a petition for certiorari to review a United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit decision that affirmed a Federal District Court's dismissal with prejudice of the individual's complaint for failure to amend his complaints pursuant to the District Court's instructions. The individual had filed in the Supreme Court 20 petitions, including 16 within two terms, and the Supreme Court had (1) denied all the petitions without recorded dissent, and (2) in one instance, denied the individual leave to proceed in forma pauperis by invoking Supreme Court Rule 39.8, which authorizes the Supreme Court to deny such leave with respect to frivolous petitions.

The United States brought suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California against a labor union, the union's business agent, and four grease peddlers who were members of the union, seeking to restrain a continuing violation of 1 of the Sherman Act (15 USC 1). The parties stipulated that the grease peddlers purchased grease from restaurants and sold it to processors of yellow grease; that the grease peddlers joined the union at the business agent's instigation, for the purpose of increasing the margin between the prices they paid for the grease and the prices at which they sold the grease; that to accomplish this, fixed purchase and sale prices were agreed upon and enforced by union agents by threatening strikes and boycotts against processors who dealt with nonunion grease peddlers; and that the business agent allocated accounts and territories for both purchases and sales among the various grease peddlers. It was further stipulated that the grease peddlers were independent businessmen and not employees of the processors, and that the defendants had unlawfully combined and conspired in unreasonable restraint of foreign trade and commerce in yellow grease. The district court enjoined the practices found to be illegal, and in addition ordered the union to terminate the union membership of all self-employed grease peddlers. (196 F Supp 12.)

California residents, who suffered injuries in an automobile collision on a California highway with a Nevada-owned vehicle driven by an employee of the University of Nevada while engaged in official business, filed a suit for damages in the Superior Court for the City of San Francisco, naming the administrator of the driver's estate, the University, and the state of Nevada as defendants. The trial court granted a motion to quash service on the state of Nevada, but its order was reversed on appeal, the Supreme Court of California holding, as a matter of California law, that the state of Nevada was amenable to suit in California courts (8 Cal 3d 522, 105 Cal Rptr 355, 503 P2d 1363). On remand, Nevada filed a pretrial motion to limit the amount of damages that might be recovered, arguing that the full faith and credit clause of the United States Constitution (Art IV, 1) required the California courts to enforce a Nevada statute placing a limit of $ 25,000 on any award in a tort action against Nevada pursuant to its statutory waiver of sovereign immunity. After the motion was denied, a jury found the Nevada driver was negligent and awarded damages of $ 1,150,000. The trial court entered judgment on the verdict, the California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District affirmed (74 Cal App 3d 280, 141 Cal Rptr 439), and the Supreme Court of California denied review.

A union whose members include persons employed in casino hotels, and the union's president, filed a complaint in the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey seeking declaratory and injunctive relief on the grounds that provisions of the New Jersey Casino Control Act, which provide for the comprehensive regulation of casino gambling, including the regulation of unions representing industry employees, were pre-empted by federal law and were unconstitutional. The District Court denied the motion for a preliminary injunction (536 F Supp 317). The New Jersey Casino Control Commission then ordered, pursuant to the Casino Control Act, that certain individuals be removed as officers, agents, or principal employees of the union. The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed the District Court's ruling, holding that a provision of the Casino Control Act was pre-empted by federal law (709 F2d 815).

In the Court of Common Pleas of Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, an accused was convicted of violating a Pennnsylvania statute which prohibited the operation of a hazardous waste facility without a permit, as the state (1) conceded that the accused in fact had a permit, but (2) argued that the accused had deviated so dramatically from the permit's terms that he nonetheless had violated the statute. The accused's conviction became final after the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania, in 1990, declined to review his case. However, in a 1993 decision, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed the conviction of a codefendant who had been convicted at the same time as the accused for the same crime, as the court (1) interpreted the state statute for the first time, and (2) said that a person who deviated from a permit's terms (a) was not a person without a permit, and (b) hence, did not violate the statute (535 Pa 273, 634 A2d 1109). The accused then sought collateral relief in the Pennsylvania state courts. When he was again unsuccessful, he brought a habeas corpus action in the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania, which granted the writ. However, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed, as that court expressed the view that (1) the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's 1993 decision announced a new rule of law, and (2) state courts were under no federal constitutional obligation to apply their own decisions retroactively (149 F3d 221). The United States Supreme Court then (1) granted certiorari to determine whether the accused's conviction was inconsistent with the due process clause of the Federal Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment (526 US 1038, 143 L Ed 2d 497, 119 S Ct 1332), and (2) certified to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court t

After petitioners fell behind schedule in developing a stealth aircraft (A‚Äì12) for the Navy, the contracting officer terminated their $4.8 billion fixed-price contract for default and ordered petitioners to repay approximately $1.35 billion in progress payments for work the Government never accepted. Petitioners filed suit in the Court of Federal Claims (CFC), challenging the termination decision under the Contract Disputes Act of 1978. They argued that Federal Circuit precedent permitted their default to be excused because the Government had failed to share its ‚Äúsuperior knowledge‚Äù about how to design and manufacture stealth aircraft. Uncovering the extent of such knowledge proved difficult because the design, materials, and manufacturing process for prior stealth aircraft, operated by the Air Force, are closely guarded military secrets. After military secrets were disclosed during discovery, the Acting Secretary of the Air Force warned the CFC that further discovery into the extent of the Government‚Äôs superior knowledge would risk disclosing classified information. The CFC terminated such discovery and found the superior-knowledge question nonjusticiable. The CFC subsequently converted the termination into a less-Government-friendly termination for convenience and awarded petitioners $1.2 billion. The Federal Circuit reversed. On remand, the CFC sustained the default termination and reaffirmed that petitioners‚Äô superior-knowledge affirmative defense could not be litigated. The Federal Circuit again reversed, but it found that the state-secrets privilege prevented adjudicating petitioners‚Äô superior-knowledge defense. On remand, the CFC again found petitioners had defaulted, and the Federal Circuit affirmed.

A nonresident of Delaware, who owned stock in a corporation which was incorporated in Delaware but which maintained its principal office in Arizona, brought a shareholder's derivative action in the Court of Chancery for New Castle County, Delaware, naming as defendants the corporation, a wholly owned subsidiary of the corporation, and 28 present or former officers of one or both corporations. Pursuant to the plaintiff's motion under 10 Del C 366, the court sequestered certain property, primarily stock, of a number of the nonresident individual defendants. The defendants contended, inter alia, that they did not have sufficient contacts with Delaware to sustain the jurisdiction of that state's courts, but the Court of Chancery ruled that the situs of the stock, which was by Delaware statute considered to be within that state, provided a sufficient basis for the exercise of quasi in rem jurisdiction by a Delaware Court. On appeal, the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the minimum contacts rule was not applicable since the jurisdiction in the instant case was quasi in rem and founded on the presence of stock in the state (361 A2d 225).

A government employee occupying a nonsensitive position in the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, who was charged with sympathetic association with Communists, was summarily dismissed by the head of that agency, who exercised the powers accorded her by the Summary Suspension Act of 1950, which authorizes heads of specified agencies to summarily dismiss employees when necessary in the interest of national security. Because the Summary Suspension Act provides that an agency head's determination of the necessity of a discharge is conclusive and final, the discharge of the employee operated to deprive him of the right to appeal to the Civil Service Commission which would otherwise have been available to him under the Veterans' Preference Act. The employee thereupon brought an action in a Federal District Court seeking a declaratory judgment that his discharge was invalid as violating the Veterans' Preference Act.

During a joint trial of Evans and Bruton in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri on a federal charge of armed postal robbery, at which Evans did not testify, a postal inspector testified to Evans' oral confession that Evans and Bruton had committed the robbery. The court instructed the jury that although Evans' confession was competent evidence against Evans, it was inadmissible hearsay against Bruton and must be disregarded in determining Bruton's guilt or innocence. Both were convicted. The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit set aside Evans' conviction on the grounds that his admissions to the postal inspector were tainted by the poison of his prior unconstitutional confession, but affirmed Bruton's conviction because of the trial court's limiting instructions. (375 F2d 355.)

Defendants who had been charged with violating a New York statute which prohibits loitering in a public place for the purpose of engaging or soliciting another person to engage in deviate sexual intercourse or other sexual behavior of a deviate nature, challenged the constitutionality of the statute and the New York Court of Appeals sustained their claim.

An accused was arrested when, during a routine traffic stop, a check on the police computer indicated an outstanding misdemeanor warrant for the accused's arrest. A subsequent search of the accused's vehicle revealed a bag of marijuana, and the accused was charged with possession of the drug. It was later discovered that the misdemeanor warrant had been quashed prior to the arrest. The accused sought suppression of the marijuana as the fruit of an unlawful arrest. An Arizona trial court granted the motion to suppress, and the Arizona Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the purpose of the exclusionary rule would not be served by excluding evidence which was seized as a result of an error by employees not directly associated with the arresting officers or their police department (172 Ariz 314, 836 P2d 1024). The Arizona Supreme Court reversed, (1) rejecting the distinction between clerical errors committed by law enforcement personnel and similar mistakes by court employees, and (2) opining that application of the exclusionary rule would serve to improve the efficiency of those who keep records in the criminal justice system (177 Ariz 201, 866 P2d 869).

The Interstate Commerce Commission "has power," under _ 204 of the Motor Carrier Act, 1935, to establish qualifications and maximum hours of service with respect to a "checker" or "terminal foreman," a substantial part of whose activities consists of doing, or immediately directing, the work of one or more "loaders" of freight for an interstate motor carrier, as such class of work has been defined by the Commission and found by it to affect the safety of operation; and such an employee is expressly excluded by _ 13 (b) (1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act from the overtime compensation requirements of _ 7, although the Commission has not exercised its power affirmatively by establishing qualifications and maximum hours of service with respect to "loaders."

A group comprised of licensed physicians and one physician-assistant practicing in Montana brought against the attorney general of Montana an action challenging, under the Federal Constitution, a Montana statute that restricted the performance of abortions to licensed physicians. The United States District Court for the District of Montana, expressing the view that the practitioners had not established any likelihood of prevailing on their claim that the law imposed an undue burden concerning abortion rights, denied the practitioners' motion for a preliminary injunction (906 F Supp 961). The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, expressing the view that the practitioners had shown a fair chance of success on the merits of their claim and thus had met the threshold requirement for injunctive relief, vacated the District Court judgment and remanded with instructions to determine whether entry of a preliminary injunction was ultimately warranted (94 F3d 566). On remand, the District Court (1) entered an injunction pending appeal pursuant to Rule 62(c) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, and (2) postponed a hearing on the preliminary injunction motion until the United States Supreme Court's disposition of the state attorney general's certiorari petition.

After the evidence was all in, a defendant in a wrongful death action moved for a directed verdict in its favor. Reserving decision on the motion, the trial court submitted the case to the jury, which returned a verdict for the plaintiff. Judgment was entered on the verdict. Within ten days after reception of the verdict the defendant moved to have it set aside on the ground that it was excessive and contrary to the evidence. This motion was denied, together with the pre-verdict motion for a directed verdict. Holding that the motion for a directed verdict should have been granted, the Court of Appeals reversed. Both parties agreed that this reversal required the trial court to enter judgment for the defendant notwithstanding the verdict. The issue was whether the Court of Appeals could direct such a judgment consistently with Rule 50(b) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, under which, within ten days after reception of a verdict, a party who has moved for a directed verdict "may move to have the verdict and any judgment entered thereon set aside and to have judgment entered in accordance with his motion for a directed verdict."

The county argued that a state policy caused any deprivation. The Ninth Circuit found for the parents on their claim for declaratory relief because Monell did not apply to prospective relief claims. The Supreme Court found Monell's policy or custom requirement applied to ¬¨√ü 1983 irrespective of the relief sought. A person who met ¬¨√ü 1983's elements was liable in an action at law, suit in equity, or other proper proceeding for redress. Thus, a county could be sued directly under ¬¨√ü 1983 for monetary, declaratory, or injunctive relief where the alleged unconstitutional action implemented or executed a policy or custom. The Monell Court thought Congress intended potential ¬¨√ü 1983 liability where a municipality's own violations were at issue, not where only the violations of others were at issue. The policy or custom requirement rested upon that distinction. Whether an action or omission was a county's "own" had to do with the nature of the action or omission, not the nature of the relief later sought. The rejection of respondeat superior liability rested not on a county's economic needs, but on the fact that liability in such a case was not based on the county's own wrongful conduct.

In a suit by a seller against a buyer on notes given for the accumulated balance remaining on a running account of sales and credits over a period of years, it is no defense that the seller had engaged in price discriminations against the buyer in violation of the Robinson-Patman Act, which prescribes criminal penalties and entitles injured persons to triple damages, but does not expressly make the contract of sale illegal or the purchase price uncollectible.

In a proceeding before the Federal Labor Relations Authority, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms was held to have committed an unfair labor practice by refusing to pay the travel expenses and a per diem allowance of a union negotiator (4 FLRA No. 40). The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit enforced the Authority's order (672 F2d 732).

The United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio dismissed an injured longshoreman's negligence claim for lack of in personam jurisdiction. After concluding that personal jurisdiction could properly be asserted over the corporate defendant, the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed on the ground that the longshoreman's acceptance of compensation payments, in the absence of a formal compensation order or award by the Secretary of Labor, did not operate as an assignment of his third-party claim to his employer pursuant to 33 USCS 933(b) (684 F2d 352).

The California legislature amended the state's Medicaid plan to increase the amount of income which a medically needy couple could keep for nonmedical needs and still be eligible to receive Medicaid, and submitted that amendment for approval by the United States Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The Secretary of HHS disapproved the amendment, and state officials filed a petition with the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit seeking review of the Secretary's decision. Holding that the Secretary's decision violated binding HHS regulations and was therefore arbitrary and capricious, and that approval of the amendment was required by 2373(c) of the Deficit Reduction Act of 1984 (see Note following 42 USCS 1396a), the Court of Appeals reversed the Secretary's decision (781 F2d 1421). After the Secretary of HHS had petitioned the United States Supreme Court for a writ of certiorari and the case had been briefed and argued, (1) Congress enacted 4106 of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1987 (PL 100-203, 101 Stat 1330), which required the Secretary to approve the California amendment retroactively to the date of the amendment's proposal; and (2) the Secretary complied with that requirement.

Teachers who were dismissed by the School Board of a Wisconsin school district because of their participation in a strike prohibited by state law and their persistent refusal to return to their duties brought a class action, in the Circuit Court, Outagamie County, Wisconsin, against members of the Board and other school officials to invalidate the Board's action and for their reinstatement, alleging noncompliance by the Board with federal due process requirements. The Circuit Court granted the Board's motion for summary judgment on the teachers' due process claim. On appeal, the Wisconsin Supreme Court reversed (66 Wis 2d 469, 225 NW2d 658).

An American union petitioned the National Labor Relations Board for certification as the representative of the unlicensed seamen employed on certain Honduran flag vessels owned by a Honduran corporation, the entire stock of which was owned by an American corporation. The crew members were all aliens, claiming Honduras as their residence and home port, were required to sign Honduran shipping articles, and were represented by a Honduran union which had a collective bargaining agreement with the Honduran corporation. The American corporation integrated the vessels into its fleet organization, determining the ports of call of the vessels, their cargoes, and their sailings, which were for the most part between Central and South American ports and ports of the United States. The Board ordered an election (134 NLRB 287), and thereafter the Honduran corporation, in No. 91, brought suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York for an injunction against the holding of the election, which relief was denied. (200 F Supp 484.) The American union intervened (No. 93), and the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed, holding that the Act did not apply to the maritime operations in question. (300 F2d 222.) Meanwhile, in No. 107, on the application of the Honduran union, the United States District Court for the District of Columbia enjoined the Board members from holding the election. (201 F Supp 82).

In a patent infringement suit by a research company in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, the defendant, a radio and television set manufacturer, counterclaimed for treble damages and injunctive relief, alleging antitrust violations consisting of both misuse of the research company's patents and a conspiracy in restraint of trade by the research company, its parent corporation, and Canadian, English, and Australian patent pools. Holding that the research company had misused its patents, the District Court awarded the manufacturer treble damages and injunctive relief against the research company; and further holding that the research company and its parent corporation had conspired in restraint of trade, the District Court, relying upon a pretrial stipulation that the research company and its parent corporation were to be considered as an entity for purposes of the litigation, awarded the manufacturer treble damages and injunctive relief against both the research company and its parent corporation (239 F Supp 51). On appeal, the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, affirming the treble damage award for patent misuse, but otherwise reversing the judgment of the District Court, (1) held that the District Court lacked jurisdiction over the research company's parent corporation, and that the stipulation relied upon by the District Court was an insufficient basis for entering judgment against the parent corporation, (2) modified in certain respects the District Court's injunction against patent misuse, (3) held that the manufacturer had failed to prove that it had sustained damage as a result of the conspiracy in restraint of trade, and (4) struck the injunction against the research company's participation in conspiracies restricting

A union fined 10 of its members who resigned during a strike and returned to work, for violation of the provision of the union's constitution that resignations from the union are not permitted during a strike. An employer representative filed charges with the National Labor Relations Board, claiming that levying fines against the employees was an unfair labor practice under 8(b)(1)(A) of the National Labor Relations Act (29 USCS 158(b)(1)(A)), which makes it an unfair labor practice for a union to restrain or coerce employees in the exercise of their rights under 7 of the Act (29 USCS 157). The Board agreed that 8(b)(1)(A) prohibited the union from imposing sanctions on the 10 employees, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit enforced the Board's order (724 F2d 57).

One indicted for murder by a Vanderburgh County, Indiana, grand jury was granted a change of venue to adjoining Gibson County, but was denied a second change of venue and a continuance, sought on the ground of local prejudice. He was convicted and sentenced to death in the Circuit Court of Gibson County, and the conviction was affirmed by the Indiana Supreme Court. (236 Ind 384, 139 NE2d 898.) The prisoner sought a writ of habeas corpus in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana, claiming that his conviction had been obtained in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment in that he did not receive a fair trial. The District Court dismissed the proceeding on the ground that the petitioner had failed to exhaust his state remedies (153 F Supp 531), and the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed. (251 F2d 548.) The United States Supreme Court granted certiorari and remanded the case to the Court of Appeals for decision on the merits or remand to the District Court for reconsideration. (359 US 394, 2 L ed 2d 900, 79 S Ct 825.) The Court of Appeals retained jurisdiction and decided the claim adversely to the prisoner. (271 F2d 552.)

Defendant's convictions on four counts of an indictment charging offenses under the narcotics laws were affirmed by the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. (274 F2d 352.) Petitioner was convicted on four counts of a five-count indictment charging offenses under the narcotics laws. The Solicitor General suggested to this Court that the combination of circumstances in the case, beginning with one judge's clearly expressed intention to impose a five-year sentence and ending with another judge's imposition of a twenty-year sentence, was not consistent with the orderly administration of criminal justice in the federal courts. Held: A due regard for the fair administration of justice requires that the convictions under Counts 3, 4 and 5 be set aside; but the conviction under Count 2, to which petitioner originally pleaded guilty, is affirmed. Pp. 646-647.

Petitioner Michael Currier was indicted for burglary, grand larceny, and unlawful possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. Because the prosecution could introduce **2146 evidence of Mr. Currier's prior burglary and larceny convictions to prove the felon-in-possession charge, and worried that evidence might prejudice the jury's consideration of the other charges, Mr. Currier and the government agreed to a severance and asked the court to try the burglary and larceny charges first, followed by a second trial on the felon-in-possession charge. At the first trial, Mr. Currier was acquitted. He then sought to stop the second trial, arguing that it would amount to double jeopardy. Alternatively, he asked the court to prohibit the state from relitigating at the second trial any issue resolved in his favor at the first. The trial court denied his requests and allowed the second trial to proceed unfettered. The jury convicted him on the felon-in-possession charge. The Virginia Court of Appeals rejected his double jeopardy arguments, and the Virginia Supreme Court summarily affirmed.

A witness before a federal grand jury who invoked his privilege against compulsory self-incrimination during his questioning complied with an order to testify after being granted immunity in accordance with the federal immunity statute (18 USCS 6002), providing that when a witness is compelled to testify over his claim of a Fifth Amendment privilege, no testimony or other information compelled under the order to testify may be used against the witness in any criminal case, "except a prosecution for perjury, giving a false statement, or otherwise failing to comply with the order." The witness was subsequently prosecuted in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania for having made false statements before the grand jury in violation of 18 USCS 1623(a). Overruling the defendant's objection to the admission of portions of his immunized grand jury testimony other than those portions charged in the indictment against him as being false, the District Court admitted testimony of such nature into evidence on the ground that it was relevant to prove that the defendant had knowingly made the charged false statements. The defendant was found guilty in the District Court, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed the defendant's conviction, holding that because the immunized testimony which had been admitted in the District Court did not constitute the "corpus delicti" or "core" of the defendant's false-swearing indictment, it should not have been admitted (584 F2d 1264).

In an action brought on behalf of all persons involuntarily confined in the forensic unit of a state hospital, which action challenged the constitutionality of treatment at the hospital, the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri, after a trial, found constitutional violations in five of the six general areas of treatment. Subsequent to the trial, the representatives of the certified plaintiff class of involuntarily confined inmates filed a request for attorneys' fees under the Civil Rights Attorney's Fees Awards Act of 1976 (42 USCS 1988), which provides that in federal civil rights actions, "the court, in its discretion, may allow the prevailing party, other than the United States, a reasonable attorney's fee as part of the costs." After determining that the plaintiff class was the prevailing party under 42 USCS 1988, even though they had not succeeded on every claim, the District Court refused to eliminate from the fee award compensation for hours spent on unsuccessful claims. The District Court found that the significant extent of the relief obtained clearly justified the award of a reasonable attorney's fee. The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed (664 F2d 294).

Petitioner, a Swiss corporation, sued in the District Court for the return of certain of its property vested in 1942 by the Alien Property Custodian under the Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917, as amended by the First War Powers Act of 1941. Petitioner was largely owned and controlled by a national of Germany, through a son with whom he had a usufruct agreement. Petitioner had been acquired with usufruct property for the purpose of enabling the father to control and use his property as he saw fit. The father had and used the substance, while the son had the bare legal title except for a 20% interest in the income of the usufruct property. Such right as the son had he exercised or failed to exercise in complete subordination to the will of the father.

Seven individuals who had been arrested following the execution of a warrant for the search of an apartment in Chicago, Illinois, along with the legal representatives of two other persons who had been killed in the course of the search, brought an action for damages under federal civil rights laws in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois against Cook County, Illinois, the City of Chicago, various state and local officials, three FBI agents, and an FBI informant, alleging that their constitutional rights had been violated by the defendants. Following trial, the District Court directed verdicts for all of the defendants, but subsequently the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed and remanded the case to the District Court for a new trial as to all of the defendants and awarded the plaintiffs their costs on appeal, including attorney's fees which the Court of Appeals believed were authorized by the Civil Rights Attorney's Fees Awards Act of 1976 (42 USCS 1988), the court concluding that the plaintiffs were "prevailing" parties within the meaning of the Act, and thus authorized to receive attorney's fees, because they had prevailed in obtaining rulings which (1) reversed the directed verdicts, (2) reversed the District Court's denial of a motion to discover the identity of the FBI informant, and (3) directed the District Court on remand to consider allowing further discovery (600 F2d 600).

Two common carrier motor carriers brought suit before a three-judge United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts to set aside orders of the Interstate Commerce Commission disapproving a proposed merger of the carriers and requiring the owner of all the stock in one of the carriers to divest himself of such stock. The ICC's order was based on a finding that the carriers had violated 5(4) of the Interstate Commerce Act (49 USC 5(4)), which makes unlawful "the control or management in a common interest of any two or more carriers." The District Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the orders were reasonable and supported by substantial evidence. (196 F Supp 351.)

The Patent Office rejected a patent application involving claims as to a method for programming any type of general purpose digital computer to convert binary-coded-decimal numerals into pure binary numerals, such claims not being limited to any particular art or technology, to any particular apparatus or machinery, or to any particular end use. The United States Court of Customs and Patent Appeals reversed (441 F2d 682).

The California statute prohibited several classes of employers that received state funds from using the funds to assist, promote, or deter union organizing. The district court found that Cal. Gov't Code __ 16645.2 and 16645.7were preempted by the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), 29 U.S.C.S. _ 151 et seq., because they regulated employer speech about union organizing. The court of appeals concluded that Congress did not intend to preclude states from imposing such restrictions on use of state funds. The Supreme Court held that Machinists preemption applied because __ 16645.2 and 16645.7 regulated within a zone protected and reserved for market freedom. The addition of 29 U.S.C.S. _ 158(c) to the NLRA manifested congressional intent to encourage free debate on labor-management issues; _ 158(c) expressly precluded regulation of noncoercive speech about unionization. The fact that the California statute restricted use rather than receipt of state funds did not significantly lessen the inherent potential for conflict with the NLRA. Certain federal statutory restrictions on union-related advocacy did not contract the NLRA's preemptive scope.

During the trial of a federal prosecution for drug offenses in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida, the trial court, over defense counsel's objection, entered an order preventing the defendant from consulting with counsel during a 17-hour overnight recess between the defendant's direct and cross-examination, the trial judge concluding that such order was necessary to avoid possible improper influencing of the defendant's testimony. The trial resulted in a conviction, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding that the defendant's failure to claim any prejudice resulting from his inability to consult with counsel during the recess was fatal to his appeal (502 F2d 1).

The Patent Remedy Act (35 USCS 271h), 296(a)) expressly provides in 271(h) that the entities subject to a patent infringement suit under 35 USCS 271(a) include states, state instrumentalities, and state officers and employees. In 296(a), the Act expressly abrogates the immunity, under the Federal Constitution's Eleventh Amendment, of states, state instrumentalities, and state officers and employees from patent infringement suits under 35 USCS 271. A New Jersey chartered bank brought, in the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey, an action under 271(a) alleging that a Florida state agency had willfully infringed the bank's patent on the financing methodology used in the bank's annuity contracts for financing future college expenses, as well contributed to and induced infringement. The state agency moved to dismiss the action on the grounds that the Act was an unconstitutional attempt by Congress to use its powers under the Constitution's Article I to abrogate state sovereign immunity, but the bank responded that Congress had properly exercised its power pursuant to 5 of the Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment to enforce the guarantees of the due process clause in the Fourteenth Amendment's 1. After the United States intervened to defend the constitutionality of the statute, the District Court denied the motion to dismiss (948 F Supp 400). The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, in affirming, expressed the view that Congress had clearly expressed its intent to abrogate the states' immunity from suit in federal court for patent infringement, and that Congress had the power under 5 to do so (148 F3d 1343).

Teachers who were nonmembers of a teachers union brought suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois against the teachers union and its officials, as well as against a city board of education and its members, and contended that a procedure instituted pursuant to an agency shop agreement between the union and the board of education, whereby fees amounting to 95 percent of union dues were deducted from the paychecks of nonmembers of the union, violated nonmembers' First Amendment rights to freedom of expression and association and Fourteenth Amendment due process rights, and permitted the use of their proportionate shares for impermissible purposes. Under the procedure, no protest was permitted prior to deduction of the fees, and subsequent protests were permitted to various bodies of the union, and ultimately to an arbitrator chosen by the union president from a list maintained by the state board of education. The union informed nonmembers that the amount of their proportionate share fee was based on calculations indicating that approximately 5 percent of union expenditures were unrelated to collective bargaining and contract administration. The District Court rejected all of the challenges, holding that the union's procedure was the least restrictive means to protect the nonmembers' First Amendment rights while also protecting the union's legitimate interest in promptly obtaining service fees from nonmembers (573 F Supp 1505). The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed, holding that the Federal Constitution required the union to follow a procedure that protected the nonmembers from being compelled to subsidize political or ideological activities not germane to the collective bargaining process, that the union's

Section 81 of the National Bank Act (12 USCS 81) limits the general business of a national bank to its headquarters and any branches permitted by 36 of the Act (12 USCS 36). Under 36(c) of the Act, a national bank is permitted to branch only in its home state and only to the extent a bank of the same state is permitted to branch under state law. Under 36(f) of the Act, "branch" includes any branch bank, branch office, branch agency, additional office, or any branch place of business at which deposits are received, or checks paid, or money lent. Two national banks applied to the Comptroller of the Currency for permission to open offices that would offer discount brokerage services to the public, one bank to acquire an existing discount brokerage operation and the other to establish an affiliate. Both banks proposed to offer discount brokerage services not only at their branch offices, but also at other locations inside and outside of their home states. Concluding that nonchartered offices at which an affiliate will offer its services would not constitute a branch under the National Bank Act because none of the statutory branching functions would be performed there, the Comptroller approved the applications. A trade association representing securities brokers, underwriters, and investment bankers sued in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, contending that bank brokerage offices are branches within the meaning of 36(f) of the Act and thus subject to the geographical restrictions imposed by 36(c). The District Court held that the trade association had standing to maintain the action, and rejected the Comptroller's submission that national banks may offer discount brokerage services at nonbranch locations (577 F Supp 252). The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) was created by Congress as part of the 1974 amendments to the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) (7 USCS 1 et seq.). Pursuant to the CEA as amended, the CFTC generally was authorized to regulate the market in futures contracts in fungible commodities. However, Congress also enacted an exemption that came to be known as the "Treasury Amendment" (7 USCS 2(ii)), which provided that nothing in the CEA would be deemed to govern or in any way be applicable to "transactions in foreign currency" unless such transactions involved a sale for future delivery conducted on a board of trade. In 1994, the CFTC brought an action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and alleged that the named defendants had solicited investments and operated a fraudulent scheme which involved "off-exchange" trading in options to purchase or sell various foreign currencies. The District Court granted the CFTC's ex parte application for a restraining order which froze the defendants' assets. Thereafter, the CFTC requested the appointment of a temporary receiver to take control of the defendants' property for the benefit of their customers. The defendants argued that the District Court lacked subject matter jurisdiction, because, according to the defendants, options in foreign currency were exempt from the CEA. However, the District Court appointed a temporary receiver. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed (58 F.3d 50).

In 1994, the Missouri legislature enacted a statute to restrict the permissible amounts of monetary contributions to candidates for state office. The statute took effect in 1995, after a ballot initiative with even stricter contribution limits--although approved by 74 percent of Missouri voters--had been invalidated as violative of the Federal Constitution's First Amendment by the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, which had nevertheless noted alleged improprieties with respect to contributions to Missouri political figures (72 F3d 633, cert den 518 US 1033, 135 L Ed 2d 1094, 116 S Ct 2579). The statute provided, among other matters, that (1) with respect to elections for statewide offices, including state auditor, the amount of contributions made by or accepted from any person other than the candidate was not to exceed 1,000; (2) contributions to candidates for some other state offices were to be limited to as little as 250; and (3) the statutory dollar amounts were to be adjusted each even-numbered year by taking into account the consumer price index. Thus, as of 1998, the limit was adjusted to 1,075 for contributions to candidates for statewide office, while the limit on contributions to candidates for some other state offices was adjusted to 275. A political action committee (PAC) gave a candidate for state auditor 1,025 in 1997 and another 50 in 1998. The PAC, alleging that it would have contributed more to the candidate's campaign but for the limitation--and the candidate, alleging that he could campaign effectively only with more generous contributions than those allowed by the statute--brought suit in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri against various Missouri officials to enjoin enforcement of the statute a

As authorized by statute, a state corporation commission issued orders, generally fixing the minimum wellhead price on all gas taken from one field and specifically directing a producer in this field, which also operated an interstate gas pipeline system, to take gas ratably from another producer in the same field at such price.

A defendant's failure to appeal from a judgment of denaturalization under the circumstances set forth in Headnote 3 was held by five of the Justices of the Supreme Court, in an opinion by Minton, J., not to be justified so as to entitle him to be relieved from the judgment under Rule 60(b)(6) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
The judgment of the Supreme Court of Alabama is reversed. Thompson v. City of Louisville, 362 U.S. 199; Garner v. Louisiana, 368 U.S. 157.

An inmate in a New York state maximum security correctional facility was transferred to another maximum security facility in New York after prison officials had seized a document addressed to a federal judge which the inmate had circulated among other prisoners, such document containing the alleged complaint of 82 prisoners that the inmate's removal from his assignment as a prison law library clerk had deprived them of legal assistance. Seeking relief against a prison official at the facility from which he had been transferred, the inmate filed a petition with the United States District Court for the Western District of New York, alleging that the seizure of the document had infringed his federally guaranteed right to petition for judicial redress of grievances, and that his transfer had been made to prevent him from pursuing his remedies and in reprisal for his actions. The District Court dismissed the action, holding that a prison rule against giving legal assistance without official consent, which the inmate allegedly disregarded in circulating the document, was reasonable, that the seizure of the document did not violate the United States Constitution, and that the inmate's transfer did not violate his rights. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed and remanded, ruling that the District Court's judgment was erroneous because of the unresolved issues of material fact whether the inmate's transfer was punishment for his disobedience of prison rules, and, if so, was whether the effects of the transfer were sufficiently burdensome to require a hearing under the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment (505 F2d 977).

That Court held that the Postal Service must comply with an arbitration award that orders to reinstate to a letter carrier position an individual who has been criminally convicted of failing to deliver over 3500 pieces of mail, [*2] and who an arbitrator found posed a risk of again delaying the mail in the future.

A union representing insurance agents, while negotiating collective bargaining agreements with the employer, sought to bring economic pressure upon the employer by having its agent-members engage in certain planned, concerted on-the-job activities designed to harass the employer. The employer thereupon brought unfair labor practice proceedings before the National Labor Relations Board, charging the union with refusing to bargain collectively. The board entered a cease-and-desist order against the union (119 NLRB 768), and the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit set aside this order (104 App DC 218, 260 F2d 736).

A shipper by air of 714 pounds of numismatic materials, for transportation from Philadelphia to London, and which had made no special declaration of value at the time of delivery, sued the air carrier for their loss, seeking damages of $ 250,000. The United States District Court ruled that under the Warsaw Convention the air carrier's liability was limited to $ 9.07 per pound, or $ 6,475.98. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed (690 F2d 303) but ruled that 60 days from the issuance of the mandate the Convention's liability limit would be unenforceable in the United States.

The respondent, a producer of evaporated milk sold under its name as a nationally advertised brand, also marketed evaporated milk under various private brands owned by its customers. Although this milk was physically and chemically identical with the milk distributed under respondent's own brand, it was sold at prices regularly below those obtained for the brand milk. The Federal Trade Commission found that the milk sold as respondent's own brand and that sold under private brands was of "like grade and quality" as required for the applicability of 2(a) of the Clayton Act as amended by the Robinson-Patman Act, held the price differential to be discriminatory, and issued a cease and desist order. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit set aside the order on the sole ground that, as a matter of law, the customer label milk was not of the same grade and quality as the milk sold under respondent's brand. (339 F2d 133.)

A state prisoner whose opportunity to reduce the length of his prison term through the accumulation of "gain time" for good conduct had been restricted by a state statute enacted after his crime was committed sought a writ of habeas corpus from the Supreme Court of Florida on the ground that the new statute as applied to him was an ex post facto law prohibited by the United States and the Florida Constitutions. The Supreme Court of Florida summarily denied the petition, relying on its earlier decision in which it reasoned that gain time allowance is an act of grace rather than a vested right and may be withdrawn, modified, or denied.
