A driver's license was revoked under an Illinois statute (and implementing regulations) authorizing the Secretary of State of Illinois to suspend or revoke a driver's license, without a preliminary hearing, upon a showing by official records or other sufficient evidence that the driver has been repeatedly convicted of traffic offenses to a degree indicating lack of ability to exercise ordinary and reasonable care in the safe operation of a motor vehicle or disrespect for the traffic laws and safety of other persons upon the highway. The Illinois statutes also provide that a full evidentiary, administrative hearing is to be held after the suspension or revocation if timely requested by the licensee, and that a person whose license has been suspended or revoked may obtain a restricted driving permit for commercial use or in case of hardship. The driver whose license had been revoked made no request for an administrative hearing, but instead filed suit against the Secretary of State of Illinois in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, challenging the constitutionality of the statute under which his license had been revoked. A three-judge District Court granted judgment for the driver, holding that a license could not constitutionally be suspended or revoked under the challenged statute until after a hearing was held to determine whether the licensee met the statutory criteria for suspension or revocation.

Petitioner Menachem Binyamin Zivotofsky was born in Jerusalem. His mother requested that Zivotofsky's place of birth be listed as "Israel" on a consular report of birth abroad and on his passport, pursuant to ¬ß214(d) of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Year 2003. That provision states: "For purposes of the registration of birth, certification of nationality, or issuance of a passport of a United States citizen born in the city of Jerusalem, the Secretary shall, upon the request of the citizen or the citizen's legal guardian, record the place of birth as Israel." U. S. officials refused the request, citing a State Department policy that prohibits recording "Israel" as the place of birth for those born in Jerusalem. Zivotofsky's parents filed a suit on his behalf against the Secretary of State. The District Court dismissed the case, holding that it presented a nonjusticiable political question regarding Jerusalem's political status. The D. C. Circuit affirmed, reasoning that the Constitution gives the Executive the exclusive power to recognize foreign sovereigns, and that the exercise of that power cannot be reviewed by the courts.

One indicted on a charge of "buying, receiving, concealing and withholding property knowing the same to have been stolen or appropriated wrongfully in such manner as to constitute larceny," upon agreement with the district attorney was permitted to plead guilty to the reduced charge of attempted second degree grand larceny, received a suspended sentence, and ultimately was discharged from probation. About seven years thereafter, having been convicted of another crime, he sought to avoid punishment as a second offender by seeking vacation of the former conviction as being one for a crime for which he was not indicted, contrary to his right under the state constitution to be prosecuted only by grand jury indictment, and as involving a denial of due process.

At his trial in a Florida state court on sexual battery charges, the accused moved to suppress evidence seized in a second search of his automobile, after it had been impounded in a locked, secure area. The motion was denied and the accused was convicted. The Florida District Court of Appeal for the Fourth District reversed, holding that even though the accused conceded that the initial search of the automobile was valid, the second search violated the Fourth Amendment. The court also ruled that the accused's cross-examination of the victim had been unduly restricted by the trial court. The Florida Supreme Court denied the state's petition for discretionary review.

About 8 months after a fire largely destroyed an Ohio corporation's plant, manufacturing equipment and machinery, and business offices, the corporation's shareholders adopted a plan of dissolution and complete liquidation pursuant to Ohio law. Within 12 months after the fire, the corporation settled its fire insurance claims in an amount exceeding its adjusted income tax basis in the insured property, thereby realizing a gain. The corporation did not report the gain, relying on the provision of 26 USCS 337(a) for the nonrecognition of gain or loss from a corporation's "sale or exchange" of property which takes place during the 12-month period following the corporation's adoption of a plan of complete liquidation effectuated within that period. The Internal Revenue Service asserted deficiencies which the corporation paid. The corporation then brought a refund suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio, which entered judgment for the corporation (339 F Supp 1134). The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed (481 F2d 954).

An export association having a membership of several fertilizer-producing companies, made 11 sales of concentrated phosphate, supplied by its members, to the Republic of Korea, under the United States foreign aid program. The government filed a civil antitrust complaint for injunctive relief in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, contending that the concerted activities of the association and its members in regard to such sales violated 1 of the Sherman Act (15 USC 1). The association and its members defended on the ground, inter alia, that their activities were exempted from antitrust liability by 2 of the Webb-Pomerene Act (15 USC 62) as "acts done in the course of export trade." The District Court held that the Webb-Pomerene Act did immunize the defendants' conduct, and dismissed the complaint. (273 F Supp 263.)

In 1961, when petitioner was on active duty in the United States Army, he was tried and convicted by a general court-martial of kidnapping and raping two women. Each of the women, one of whom was the sister of a serviceman and the other of whom was a serviceman's wife, was raped on military reservation property. Petitioner's death sentence was later reduced to hard labor for 30 years, total forfeitures of all pay and allowances, and a dishonorable discharge, and the Court of Military Appeals denied a petition for review in 1963. In 1967, petitioner filed an application for a writ of habeas corpus with the United States District Court for the District of Kansas, alleging inadequate representation by counsel in the court-martial, which application was denied. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reviewed the petitioner's inadequate representation claim, and other claims raised for the first time as well, but affirmed the District Court's denial of relief (409 F2d 824). Several weeks thereafter, the United States Supreme Court decided O'Callahan v Parker (395 US 258, 23 L Ed 2d 291, 89 S Ct 1683), in which case the court held that a court-martial could not try a member of the Armed Forces charged with attempted rape of a civilian, with housebreaking, and with assault with intent to commit rape, when the alleged offenses were committed off-post on American territory, when the soldier was on leave, and when the charges could have been prosecuted in a civilian court, since the alleged crimes were not sufficiently "service-connected."

An officer in the United States Army filed a petition in the Superior Court of California in and for the City and County of San Francisco requesting dissolution of his marriage. Upon dissolution of a marriage under California law, each spouse has an equal and absolute right to a half-interest in all community and quasi-community property, while retaining his or her separate property. The officer requested, in his petition, that all military retirement benefits be confirmed to him as his separate property. In dissolving the marriage, the Superior Court held that the officer's military pension and retirement rights were subject to division as quasi-community property, and ordered him to pay to his ex-spouse a specified portion of his military retired pay upon retirement. Subsequently, the officer retired, and began receiving retired pay, of which his ex-spouse was entitled to receive 45 percent under the decree of dissolution. The officer sought review in the California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, of that portion of the Superior Court's decree that awarded his ex-spouse an interest in his retired pay. The Court of Appeal affirmed the award, declining to accept his contention that because the federal scheme of military retirement benefits preempts state community property laws, the supremacy clause of the United States Constitution (Art VI, cl 2) precluded the trial court from awarding his ex-spouse a portion of his retired pay. The California Supreme Court denied the officer's petition for hearing.

The core judicial inquiry on an Eighth Amendment excessive force claim was whether force was applied in a good-faith effort to maintain or restore discipline, or maliciously and sadistically to cause harm. When prison officials maliciously and sadistically used force to cause harm, contemporary standards of decency were always violated, whether or not significant injury was evident. Otherwise, the Eighth Amendment would permit any physical punishment, no matter how diabolic or inhuman, inflicting less than some arbitrary quantity of injury. The prisoner alleged that he was punched, kicked, kneed, choked, and body slammed "maliciously and sadistically" and "without any provocation." To conclude, as the district court did, that the absence of some arbitrary quantity of injury required automatic dismissal of an excessive force claim improperly bypassed the core inquiry. To prevail, the prisoner would ultimately have to prove not only that the assault actually occurred but also that it was carried out "maliciously and sadistically" rather than as part of a good-faith effort to maintain or restore discipline. But, dismissal was error.

The Federal Kidnapping Act (28 USC 1201) provides for the death penalty if the kidnapped person has not been liberated unharmed. The main issue in the present case was whether a charge of kidnapping omitting a statement that the victim has not been liberated unharmed is the charge of a capital offense, which can be made only by way of indictment, and not by way of information. In an information filed in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama defendant was charged with transporting a kidnapping victim across state lines, in violation of the act. He waived indictment, counsel, and venue, and upon his plea of guilty he was convicted and sentenced. Prior to his waivers and plea the trial judge, at the instance of an Assistant United States Attorney, had an interview with a special agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation in the judge's chambers, dealing with defendant's background and his connection with the kidnapping, neither the defendant nor anyone representing him being present at the interview. Defendant sought relief in the District Court under 28 USC 2255 from his conviction and sentence, alleging the invalidity. After protracted litigation the District Court resentenced petitioner, but refused him permission to withdraw his waivers and plea of guilty. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed, one of the judges dissenting. (250 F2d 842.)

This case requires this Court for the first time in the history of the nation to determine the extent of the personal immunity of the President of the United Stales and his closest advisors for money damages arising from the claimed violation of constitutional rights resulting from the performance of his official duties.

The Comprehensive Crime Control Act of 1984, 18 USCS 3147, provides that anyone who commits a felony while on release pending judicial proceedings must be sentenced to at least two years' imprisonment in addition to the sentence imposed for the underlying felony. The accused was arrested for selling cocaine, and while released on a personal recognizance bond, she was arrested again, for selling heroin. In the United States Court for the Southern District of New York, the accused pled guilty to both charges, and although the sentencing judge recognized the applicability of 3147's provision for a sentence of at least two years' imprisonment in addition to the sentence for the underlying drug offenses, the sentencing judge, relying on the Probation Act, 18 USCS 3651, suspended execution of the additional two-year sentence and instead placed the accused on probation for two years. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed, holding that 3147 required imposition of a two-year minimum term of imprisonment for the commission of a felony while on release pending judicial proceedings, and that 3651 had been superseded by 3147 (794 F2d 24).

The plaintiff was an independent distributor who had purchased a home delivery route for the morning newspaper published by the defendant. After the plaintiff began charging his customers higher prices than those suggested by the defendant, the defendant, who had reserved the right to compete with the plaintiff if he overcharged, hired a circulation sales company to solicit customers from the plaintiff's route, about 300 of the plaintiff's 1,200 former customers were assigned to a new route, and the new route was made available without cost to another distributor, with the understanding that the route might have to be returned if the plaintiff conformed to the suggested prices. The defendant subsequently informed the plaintiff that he could have his customers back if he charged the suggested prices. A few days later, the plaintiff brought a treble-damage suit in the District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, charging a combination in restraint of trade in violation of 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act. Pending litigation, the plaintiff's distributorship was terminated by the defendant, and the plaintiff sold his route for less than he would have received if he had been able to turn over 1,200 customers instead of 900. Following a jury trial, there were a verdict and judgment in favor of the defendant, and the plaintiff's motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict was denied. The Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed, holding that the defendant's conduct was wholly unilateral and that there was no restraint of trade. (367 F2d 517.)

Decedent to whom life insurance policies had been issued on the condition that she also purchase annuity policies, irrevocably assigned all of her rights and interests in the insurance policies prior to her death, but retained the annuity payments until death. Following her death, the proceeds of the assigned policies were not included in her estate in the federal estate tax return, and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, determining that these proceeds should have been included, assessed a deficiency. The decedent's executors paid the adjusted tax and when their claim for refund was denied, instituted the present action in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. The District Court granted the refund (142 F Supp 561) but the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed (241 F2d 690).

Section 205 (e) of the Emergency Price Control Act, 56 Stat. 34, as amended, provides that a buyer of goods at above the ceiling price may sue the seller "in any court of competent jurisdiction" for three times the amount of the overcharge plus costs and a reasonable attorney's fee; and _ 205 (c) provides that the federal district courts shall have jurisdiction of such suits "concurrently with" state courts. Having purchased an automobile at above the ceiling price, the purchaser sued the seller under _ 205 (e) and obtained judgment for damages and costs in a state court having adequate general jurisdiction to enforce similar claims arising under state law. On appeal, the State Supreme Court reversed the judgment on the ground that the suit was for a penalty based on a statute of a foreign sovereign and could not be maintained in the state courts.

The defendant, an officer in the United States Air Force, was a resident and domiciliary of Washington, but was stationed in California. While on temporary duty in Alabama, he purchased and registered a car there and obtained Alabama license plates. After driving the car back to California and while using it in California, he was stopped by a highway patrol officer and advised to register the car in California. Since Washington required registration only for vehicles driven on its highways and the defendant had not driven his car in Washington, he had not registered it there. When he attempted to register the car in California, he was informed that his payment of about $ 100 in fees and penalties, based on a "license fee" measured by 2 percent of the market value of the car and imposed by the California Revenue and Taxation Code, was a prerequisite to registration. He refused to pay such fees and was subsequently arrested and convicted for violating a California statute prohibiting a person from driving a motor vehicle upon a highway unless it is registered and the appropriate fees have been paid under the California Vehicle Code. The Supreme Court of California reversed the conviction, holding that California's right to exact the fees from the defendant was precluded by 514 of the Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act, which exempts nonresident servicemen from personal property taxes and also exempts them from having to pay a state's "licenses, fees, or excises imposed in respect to motor vehicles or the use thereof: Provided, That the license, fee, or excise required by the State ... of which the person is a resident or in which he is domiciled has been paid." (61 Cal 2d 833, 40 Cal Rptr 681, 395 P2d 593.)

In Bruton v United States (1968) 391 US 123, 20 L Ed 2d 476, 88 S Ct 1620, the United States Supreme Court held that a defendant's rights under the confrontation clause of the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution were violated by the introduction, at a joint criminal trial, of a nontestifying codefendant's confession which named and incriminated the defendant. However, the scope of Bruton v United States was limited by Richardson v Marsh (1987) 481 US 200, 95 L Ed 2d 176, 107 S Ct 1702, in which the Supreme Court held that the confrontation clause was not violated by the admission, at a joint criminal trial, of a nontestifying codefendant's confession, when (1) a proper limiting instruction was given to the jury, and (2) the confession was redacted to eliminate not only the nonconfessing defendant's name, but also any reference to his or her existence. In the case at hand, at a joint Maryland trial of two defendants for murder, the trial judge (1) permitted the state to introduce a redacted version of a nontestifying codefendant's confession, with the nonconfessing defendant's name substituted with a blank space or the word "deleted"; and (2) gave a limiting instruction that the confession be used only against the codefendant. The jury convicted both defendants. Maryland's Court of Special Appeals held that Bruton v United States prohibited use of the confession and set aside the nonconfessing defendant's conviction. The Court of Appeals of Maryland disagreed and reinstated the conviction (344 Md 417, 687 A2d 660). On certiorari, the Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings.

South Carolina prison inmates who claimed that they had been unnecessarily beaten by prison guards during a prison uprising sought criminal arrest warrants against the guards from a state court magistrate. After the magistrate expressed his intent to issue the warrants, the state solicitor--as a result of a meeting with the legal advisor to the state's department of corrections, the prison warden, the county sheriff, and deputy attorney--wrote the magistrate a letter which requested that the warrants not be issued and stated that the solicitor intended to ask state officials to conduct an investigation concerning the charges made against the officers involved. The magistrate did not issue the warrants, and no investigation was conducted. The inmates subsequentely filed suit in the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina contending, among other claims, that the state correctional officials had conspired in bad faith to block the issuance of the arrest warrants and thereby violated 42 USCS 1983 and 1985(3). The District Court ultimately concluded that the state correctional officials denied the inmates their right to a meaningful ability to set in motion the governmental machinery, because the officials' activity stopped the machinery unlawfully, not in a proper way, as for example, upon a valid determination of lack of probable cause, and the court awarded the inmates compensatory and punitive damages. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed, concluding that even though a private citizen lacks a judicially cognizable interest in the prosecution or nonprosecution of another, that did not foreclose the inmates' right to seek an arrest warrant.

After earlier proceedings in a private antitrust action, wherein the United States Supreme Court entered a mandate directing entry of judgment for the plaintiff (395 US 642, 23 L Ed 2d 599, 89 S Ct 1871), the plaintiff filed an application in the United States District Court for the District of Oregon for allowance of attorneys' fees for services performed during the appellate stages of the litigation, both in the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and in the Supreme Court. The District Court denied the application, ruling that the allowance of such attorneys' fees was not authorized under 4 of the Clayton Act, which provides for recovery of treble damages "and the cost of suit, including a reasonable attorney's fee." The Court of Appeals on the plaintiff's appeal and on his simultaneously filed applications for such attorneys' fees, concluded that the Supreme Court's mandate, by not mentioning attorneys' fees, precluded an award of such fees.

The Department of Pensions and Security of Alabama--a state participating in the Federal Government's Aid to Families With Dependent Children Program (AFDC)--issued a so-called "substitute father" regulation which denied AFDC payments to children of a mother who "cohabits" in or outside her home with any single or married man. The present class action, instituted in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama, sought declaratory and injunctive relief against enforcement of this regulation. A three-judge District Court granted relief, finding the regulation to be inconsistent with the Social Security Act and the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. (277 F Supp 31.)

To circumvent Georgia law which, as then in force, restricted city banks from opening branches in suburban areas, a Georgia national bank (C&S National) formed a holding company (C&S Holding), and the latter company embarked upon a program of forming de facto branch banks in the suburbs of Atlanta. This program involved, among other features, ownership by C&S Holding of 5 percent of the stock of each of the suburban banks (the maximum allowed by state law), and ownership of much of the remaining stock by parties friendly to the C&S system of banking entities (C&S), this system including C&S National and its majority owned affiliates and C&S Holding, but excluding the 5-percent banks. After Georgia amended its banking statutes to allow de jure branching on a countywide basis, C&S applied to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) under the Bank Merger Act of 1966 (12 USCS 1828(c)) for permission to acquire all of the stock of six of the 5-percent banks operated by C&S as de facto branches. The FDIC authorized all but one of the proposed acquisitions. The government immediately commenced the instant litigation in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia for injunctive relief, alleging that the five acquisitions authorized by the FDIC would lessen competition in relevant banking markets, thus violating 7 of the Clayton Act (15 USCS 18), and that the historic "de facto branch" relations between C&S and the six 5-percent banks constituted unreasonable restraints of trade in violation of 1 of the Sherman Act (15 USCS 1). The District Court rendered judgment for C&S on all the issues (372 F Supp 616).

On April 4, 1996, a federal grand jury indicted a defendant on multiple charges in connection with some allegedly counterfeit bonds. After granting some continuances, the United States District Court for the Eastern Court of New York, during a November 8, 1996, status conference, (1) requested a defense waiver of Speedy Trial Act rights "for all time"; and (2) produced a waiver form, which the defendant and his counsel signed. The court then agreed to schedule a further status conference on January 31, 1997. At the January 31 conference, (1) the defense sought another continuance to gather evidence of the supposed authenticity of the bonds in question; (2) the ‚àö¬∂[**750]‚àö¬∂ defense and the Federal Government expressed the view that this request raised no issue under the Act because of the defendant's earlier waiver; and (3) the District Court, in granting the continuance, made no mention of the Act and did not make any findings to support exclusion of the (eventual) 91 days between January 31 and the defendant's next court appearance on May 2, 1997.

In an action brought under the Federal Employers' Liability Act in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York the defendant offered, for the purpose of impeaching the plaintiff's testimony as to his motive for not returning to work and as to the permanency of his injuries, evidence that he was receiving disability pension payments under the Railroad Retirement Act. Upon objection the trial court excluded the evidence. The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed, holding it prejudicial error to exclude the evidence of the disability pension. (319 F2d 12.)

At a pretrial suppression hearing, a Massachusetts Superior Court judge refused to suppress evidence obtained in a warrant search of a suspect's residence although the warrant authorized a search for controlled substances rather than evidence of murder, which was indicated in the affidavit underlying the warrant application and which was found in the search. The Superior Court judge ruled that the murder evidence was admissible notwithstanding the defect in the warrant because the police had acted in good faith in executing what they reasonably thought was a valid warrant. At a subsequent trial, the suspect was convicted. The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts reversed (387 Mass 488, 441 NE2d 725).

Jane Cummings, who is deaf and legally blind, sought physical therapy services from Premier Rehab Keller and asked Premier Rehab to provide an American Sign Language interpreter at her sessions. Premier Rehab declined to do so, telling Cummings that the therapist could communicate with her through other means. Cummings later filed a lawsuit seeking damages and other relief against Premier Rehab, alleging that its failure to provide an ASL interpreter constituted discrimination on the basis of disability in violation of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and the Affordable Care Act. Premier Rehab is subject to these statutes, which apply to entities that receive federal financial assistance, because it receives reimbursement through Medicare and Medicaid for the provision of some of its services. The District Court determined that the only compensable injuries allegedly caused by Premier Rehab were emotional in nature. It held that damages for emotional harm are not recoverable in private actions brought to enforce either statute. The District Court thus dismissed the complaint, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed.

Petitioners, Comcast Corporation and its subsidiaries, allegedly "cluster" their cable television operations within a particular region by swapping their systems outside the region for competitor systems inside the region. Respondents, named plaintiffs in this class-action antitrust suit, claim that they and other Comcast subscribers in the Philadelphia "cluster" are harmed because Comcast's strategy lessens competition and leads to supra-competitive prices. They sought class certification under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(b)(3), which requires that "questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members." The District Court required them to show (1) that the "antitrust impact" of the violation could be proved at trial through evidence common to the class and (2) that the damages were measurable on a classwide basis through a "common methodology." The court accepted only one of respondents' four proposed theories of antitrust impact: that Comcast's actions lessened competition from "overbuilders," i.e., companies that build competing networks in areas where an incumbent cable company already operates. It then certified the class, finding that the damages from overbuilder deterrence could be calculated on a classwide basis, even though respondents' expert acknowledged that his regression model did not isolate damages resulting from any one of respondents' theories. In affirming, the Third Circuit refused to consider petitioners' argument that the model failed to attribute damages to overbuilder deterrence because doing so would require reaching the merits of respondents' claims at the class certification stage.

Pre-1988 Medicaid eligibility rules for married applicants often required both spouses to deplete their combined resources before a spouse who was institutionalized, as in a nursing home, became eligible for benefits. In order to prevent the pauperization of the "community spouse"--that is, the spouse remaining at home--the Medicare Catastrophic Coverage Act of 1988 (MCCA) (42 USCS 1396r-5 et seq.) (1) directed that, in any month in which one spouse was institutionalized, no income of the community spouse was to be deemed available to the institutionalized spouse ( 1396r-5(b)(1)); (2) required states to set a "minimum monthly maintenance needs allowance" (MMMNA) for the community spouse ( 1396r-5(d)(3)); and (3) prescribed that, if the community spouse's posteligibility income was insufficient to yield income equal to or above the MMMNA, the shortfall--called the "community spouse monthly income allowance" (CSMIA)--could be deducted from the institutionalized spouse's income and paid to the community spouse ( 1396r-5(d)(1)(B)). In determining the institutionalized spouse's Medicaid eligibility, a portion of the couple's resources--called the "community spouse resource allowance" (CSRA)--was to be reserved for the benefit of the community spouse ( 1396r-5(c)(2)). Under 1396r-5(e)(2)(C), a couple could obtain a higher CSRA by establishing that the standard CSRA was inadequate to raise "the community spouse's income" to the MMMNA. An administrative hearing for such a purpose was authorized by 1396r-5(e)(2)(A)(v). An Illinois state trooper stopped a driver for speeding on a highway. When the trooper radioed the police dispatcher to report the stop, a second trooper overheard the transmission. Although the second trooper presumably had no information about the driver except that the driver had been stopped for speeding, the second trooper headed for the scene with a narcotics-detection dog. While the first trooper was writing a warning ticket, the second trooper walked the dog around the car, and the dog alerted at the trunk. On the basis of the alert, the troopers searched the trunk, found marijuana, and arrested the driver. The entire incident lasted less than 10 minutes.

An importer brought suit against the United States in the United States Court of Claims under the Tucker Act (28 USCS 1491), alleging breach of an implied contract of bailment arising from the loss of goods which the United States Customs Service had seized for customs violations but later had agreed to return. The Court of Claims granted the United States' motion for summary judgment on the ground that the importer had failed to state a claim upon which relief could be granted, ruling that the importer's action was barred because of the provision of the Federal Tort Claims Act (28 USCS 2680(c)) which sets forth an exception to the Act's general waiver of the United States' immunity from tort liability as to claims against the United States "arising in respect of ... the detention of any goods or merchandise" by customs officers (579 F2d 617).

During a 1969 investigation by the Internal Revenue Service of a restaurateur's tax returns, an IRS special agent issued a summons to the restaurateur's outside accountant to produce records which the restaurateur had given him regularly since 1955 for tax preparation purposes and remained in his continuous possession. Notwithstanding the restaurateur's invocation of her Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination, the United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia issued a production order to the restaurateur's attorney, to whom the accountant had surrendered the records after being served with the summons. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed (449 F2d 141).

Upon a plea of guilty in a criminal prosecution in a state court, petitioner was sentenced as a second offender, the length of the sentence being based partly on a previous conviction. Upon sentence as a second offender, petitioner had full opportunity, so far as appears, to contest any infirmity in the previous sentence. While serving the second sentence, petitioner applied to the court which had imposed the earlier sentence to vacate the judgment there rendered against him, on the ground of denial of his right to counsel under the Federal Constitution. The state court denied the motion, and its judgment is here affirmed.

Three lawfully admitted permanent resident aliens, after unsuccessfully applying for positions as deputy probation officers in Los Angeles County, California, filed suit in the United States District Court for the Central District of California challenging the constitutionality of a provision in the California statutes that required "peace officers," including probation officers, to be United States citizens under, inter alia, the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. A three-judge panel of the District Court held the provision unconstitutional both on its face and as applied to the aliens (427 F Supp 158), and reaffirmed this position after reconsidering it on remand from the United States Supreme Court (490 F Supp 984).

An employee who was denied access to his employer's plant by a striking union which engaged in mass picketing and threats of violence brought an action against the union in the Circuit Court, Morgan County, Alabama, claiming compensatory damages for loss of earnings and mental anguish, plus punitive damages. The union filed a plea to the jurisdiction, alleging that the National Labor Relations Board had exclusive jurisdiction of the controversy, and the trial court overruled the employee's demurrer to the plea. The Supreme Court of Alabama reversed the trial court (258 Ala 615, 64 So2d 384), and, on remand, the trial court, after sustaining the employee's demurrer to the union's jurisdictional plea, entered judgment on a verdict for the employee which included punitive damages. The Supreme Court of Alabama reaffirmed the trial court's jurisdiction and also affirmed on the merits (264 Ala 456, 88 So2d 175, 62 ALR2d 669).

A nonprofit, unincorporated medical association formed a political action committee which was registered with the Federal Election Commission and became subject to the provisions of the Federal Election Campaign Act (2 USCS 431 et seq.) relating to multicandidate political committees. One such provision (2 USCS 441a(a)(1)(C)) prohibits individuals and unincorporated associations from contributing more than $ 5,000 per calendar year to any multicandidate political committee, and a related provision (2 USCS 441a(f)) makes it unlawful for political committees, such as the medical association's political action committee, knowingly to accept contributions exceeding this limit. After receiving formal notification that the Commission intended to institute a civil enforcement action against the medical association and political action committee to secure compliance with the contribution limitations of the Act, both the association and political action committee, together with two individual members of the organizations, filed a declaratory judgment action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California challenging the constitutionality of the statutory contribution limitations. Subsequently, the Commission filed an enforcement action in the same District Court, and, in the second suit, the medical association and the political action committee pleaded as affirmative defenses the same constitutional claims raised in their declaratory judgment action. Pursuant to the special expedited review provisions of the Act set forth in 2 USCS 437h, the District Court certified the constitutional questions raised in the declaratory judgment action to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. Exemption 2 used "personnel" in the exact same way as Exemption 6,¬¨√ü 552(b)(6). Exemption 2 did not reach the information at issue. These data and maps calculated and visually portrayed the magnitude of hypothetical detonations. By no stretch of imagination did they relate to "personnel rules and practices." They concerned the physical rules governing explosives, not the workplace rules governing sailors; they addressed the handling of dangerous materials, not the treatment of employees. Exemption 2's plain meaning covered human resources matters. The court rejected the "Low 2, High 2" distinction. Exemption 2 covered all of what had been referred to as "Low 2" and the use of a "High 2" exemption was rejected: "High 2" was better labeled "Non 2." That the records requested assisted Navy personnel in storing munitions did not mean the data and maps related to "personnel rules and practices." Exemption 2, consistent with the plain meaning of the term "personnel rules and practices," encompassed only records relating to issues of employee relations and human resources. The explosives maps and data requested did not qualify for withholding under Exemption 2.

The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed a judgment of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, holding a witness before a grand jury in contempt, and the District Court's denial of the witness' motion to vacate the contempt judgment. (370 F2d 1019.)

Two cases presented the question of the proper mode of calculating the depreciation allowance, provided for by 23(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939, with respect to automobiles used in auto rental and allied services. In No. 141, the taxpayer, an automobile dealer, assigned certain cars to company personnel and rented others, selling these cars upon the receipt of new models, if not sooner; the taxpayer claimed a depreciation allowance calculated on the basis of an estimated 4-year useful life for the cars, with no residual salvage value, and, when he sold the cars, he deducted this depreciation allowance from their initial cost, added the sale price to the figure so arrived at, and paid a capital gains tax on the difference between this total and the initial cost. In No. 143, the taxpayer, engaged in leasing new cars to a U-drive agency, followed a similar practice with respect to cars which he sold when they were 15 months old. In both cases the Commissioner of Internal Revenue denied the taxpayers' depreciation claims, on the theory that the useful life of the automobiles was not their total economic life, but only the period they were actually used by the taxpayers in their business, and that the salvage value of the automobiles was not junk value but the resale value at the time of disposal. In No. 141, the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, in a suit initiated by the taxpayer in order to obtain a refund of the tax that he had paid, decided against the Commissioner (156 F Supp 516), but the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed. (264 F2d 552.) In No. 143, in a tax deficiency proceeding, the Tax Court accepted the Commissioner's theories, but the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed. (264 F2d 502.)

In the first of two consolidated cases, a security guard employed by a board of education was dismissed on grounds that he had failed to disclose a prior felony conviction on his job application. In the second case, a school bus mechanic was discharged because he failed an eye examination. Both employees were classified civil servants who could be terminated only for cause and both were entitled to posttermination administrative review of the decisions. However, neither employee was afforded a pretermination opportunity to respond to the charges. Subsequent complaints in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio were dismissed, the District Courts concluding that the statutory procedures for dismissal satisfied due process. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed, finding that the discharged employees were entitled to a pretermination hearing and thus had been deprived of due process (721 F2d 550).

An Indian tribe's industrial development commission agreed to purchase certain stock from a corporation, and the chairman of the tribe's business committee signed a promissory note in the name of the tribe. Although the note recited on its face that it had been signed in an Oklahoma community where the tribe had a complex on land held for it in trust for the tribe by the United States, the corporation subsequently claimed that the note had been executed and delivered to it in Oklahoma City, beyond the tribe's lands. When the tribe defaulted, the corporation brought an action on the note in the Oklahoma state courts. The tribe's motion to dismiss the action for lack of jurisdiction, based partly on its asserted sovereign immunity from suit, was denied by an Oklahoma trial court, which rendered judgment in favor of the corporation. The Oklahoma Court of Appeals, affirming, held that Indian tribes were subject to suit in state court for breaches of contract involving off-reservation commercial conduct. The Supreme Court of Oklahoma declined to review the judgment.

In a proceeding for the reorganization of a railroad under _ 77 of the Bankruptcy Act, the reorganization court confirmed a report of a special master finding that (1) certain proofs of claim of New Jersey for taxes were properly filed by state officers acting in pursuance of their statutory authority, (2) _ 77 confers on the reorganization court jurisdiction over the kind of claims asserted by the State in the proceeding, and such construction of the Act is not unconstitutional, and (3) the entire property of the debtor is in custodia legis, subject to the rights of lienholders, and the reorganization court is the proper court to determine the validity and amount of the tax claims, subject to certain limitations.

During an organizational campaign among store employees, the union filed unfair labor practice charges with the NLRB, and after securing a favorable ruling by the trial examiner, the union picketed the employer's stores. Before the NLRB reviewed the trial examiner's findings and recommended order, the employer secured an injunction against the picketing from the District Court of Hall County, Nebraska. The NLRB then brought the instant suit in the United States District Court for the District of Nebraska to restrain enforcement of the state court injunction. The District Court denied relief (320 F Supp 858), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed (434 F2d 971).

An Indian tribe entered into a contract for the installation of a roof on a commercial building owned by the tribe on off-reservation, nontrust land. The standard form construction contract, which was proposed by the tribe, contained (1) an arbitration clause providing that disputes between the parties would be decided by arbitration, that an award rendered by the arbitrator would be final, and that judgment could be entered upon an arbitral award in accordance with applicable law in any court having requisite jurisdiction, and (2) a choice-of-law clause providing that the contract would be governed by the law of the place where the project was located. Before commencement of the work, the tribe decided to change the roofing material, whereupon it solicited new bids and retained another company to install the roof. The original contractor, claiming the tribe had dishonored the contract, initiated an arbitration proceeding in which the tribe declined to participate, asserting sovereign immunity, and the arbitrator rendered an award in favor of the contractor. The contractor then filed suit to enforce the arbitral award in the District Court of Oklahoma County, a state court of general, first instance, jurisdiction. The tribe appeared specially for the limited purpose of moving to dismiss the action on the ground that the tribe was immune from suit, but the District Court denied the motion and entered a judgment confirming the award. The Oklahoma Court of Civil Appeals affirmed, the Oklahoma Supreme Court denied review, and the tribe petitioned for certiorari in the United States Supreme Court. Under 57(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (26 USCS 57(a)), the excess of the income tax deduction allowable for depletion over the adjusted basis of the taxpayer's property is an item of tax preference that is subject to a minimum tax for the tax year in question, and 57(a) refers to 614 of the Code (26 USCS 614), which defines "property" to include interests in mineral deposits. On their federal income tax returns for the years 1981 and 1982, taxpayers who were in the oil and gas exploration and production business claimed deductions for depletion with respect to their interests in oil and gas deposits. In calculating their minimum tax for each year, the taxpayers determined the adjusted bases of their deposit interests by including, in addition to the unrecovered portions of the amounts they paid to purchase the interests, the unrecovered costs of tangible items--including machinery, tools, and pipes--used to exploit the deposits; such tangible items are identified in a Treasury Regulation, 26 CFR 1.612-4(c)(1), as depreciable capital items. After the Commissioner of Internal Revenue assessed a larger minimum tax, based on the exclusion of the tangible costs from the deposits' adjusted bases, the taxpayers paid the resulting deficiencies for the 2 years and filed a refund claim, which the Commissioner denied. The taxpayers then sued the United States for a refund in the United States Claims Court, which granted summary judgment in favor of the taxpayers (21 Cl Ct 713). The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit affirmed the Claims Court judgment (945 F2d 1529).

The president of a bankrupt corporation, having failed to comply with a turnover order, was found by the referee in bankruptcy guilty of a civil contempt notwithstanding his denial that the property was in his possession. This finding was affirmed by a district court and circuit court of appeals.

A jury of the Superior Court of Orange County, California, returned a verdict of death for a defendant convicted of robbery, attempted murder, and first degree murder after being instructed by the trial judge that the sentence of life imprisonment without the possibility of parole may be commuted by the governor to a sentence that includes the possibility of parole. This instruction was mandated by California law. On appeal, the Supreme Court of California affirmed the defendant's conviction but reversed the death sentence, concluding that the instruction violated the Federal Constitution (30 Cal 3d 553, 639 P2d 908).

Petitioner used a vehicle to flee after an officer ordered him to stop, which was, as Ind. Code ¬¨√ü 35-44-3-3 provided, a class D felony. The Court determined that petitioner was properly sentenced under the ACCA because the vehicle flight that ¬¨√ü 35-44-3-3 proscribed was a violent felony. Indiana's prohibition on flight from an officer by driving a vehicle fell within the residual clause of 18 U.S.C.S. ¬¨√ü 924(e)(2)(B)(ii) because (1) as a categorical matter, it presented a serious potential risk of physical injury to another, (2) petitioner's argument that the Court's Begay and Chambers decisions required ACCA predicates to be purposeful, violent, and aggressive in ways that vehicle flight was not, was rejected, and the felony at issue was not a strict liability, negligence, or recklessness crime, (3) Indiana treated violations of ¬¨√ü 35-44-3-3(b)(1)(A) and (b)(1)(B) as crimes of the same magnitude, and the similarity in punishment for these related, overlapping offenses suggested that subsection (b)(1)(A) was the rough equivalent of one type of subsection (b)(1)(B) violation, and (4) Congress chose to frame ACCA in general and qualitative, rather than encyclopedic, terms.

The plaintiff, an alien against whom a final order of deportation had been outstanding for more than six months, brought in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri an action against an officer of the Immigration and Naturalization Service to enjoin an order of supervision issued under 242(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, charging that the order was unconstitutional. A three-judge court was convened and entered the judgment described in the headnote below (145 F Supp 569).

Under 18 USCS 3142(e), a provision of the Bail Reform Act of 1984, pretrial detention of an accused in a federal criminal case is required if, "after a hearing pursuant to" 18 USCS 3142(f), the accused is found to pose a risk of flight and a danger to others or to the community and if no condition or combination of conditions of release can give reasonable assurances against these contingencies. Section 3142(f) provides that the hearing "shall" be held immediately upon the accused's first appearance before a judicial officer, unless a continuance is granted pursuant to the statute. An accused arrested by federal agents in New Mexico for possession of cocaine admitted his intent to deliver the cocaine to purchasers in Chicago, Illinois, and agreed to co-operate with federal agents in making a controlled delivery under surveillance. The accused was transported to Chicago, but the anticipated purchasers did not appear. The accused was subsequently brought before a magistrate in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois for a hearing on his transfer back to New Mexico, where a federal criminal complaint had been filed against him. The instant cases presented the question of the extent of the right to counsel at the time of sentencing in a state criminal case in which the sentencing has been deferred subject to probation. In No. 16, the petitioner was convicted, upon his plea of guilty entered with the advice of court-appointed counsel, in the Superior Court of Spokane County, Washington, of the offense of "joyriding." He was then placed on probation for 2 years, and the imposition of sentence was deferred pursuant to a Washington statute. Subsequently, at a hearing in which petitioner was not represented by counsel, the court revoked his probation and sentenced him to the maximum sentence of 10 years, as required by Washington law, but with a recommendation to the parole board that he be required to serve only a year. His petition for habeas corpus, based on deprivation of his right to counsel, was denied by the Supreme Court of Washington. (68 Wash 2d 882, 416 P2d 104.) In No. 22, the petitioner was convicted, upon his plea of guilty entered with the advice of his retained counsel, in the Superior Court for Thurston County, Washington, of burglary in the second degree. He was placed on probation for 3 years and the imposition of sentence was deferred. Subsequently, at a hearing conducted in the absence of his retained counsel, the court revoked his probation and imposed a maximum sentence of 15 years. His petition for habeas corpus, claiming denial of his right to counsel at the combined probation-revocation and sentencing proceeding, was denied by the Supreme Court of Washington.

The issue in the present case was whether the Federal Power Commission has authority, under the Natural Gas Act, to tender a certificate of public convenience and necessity without time limitation to an independent producer, disregarding his request that the certificate be limited in time to the duration of a contract for the sale of gas which the producer had made. The Commission tendered a certificate without time limitation. (19 FPC 618, reh den 19 FPC 1107.) Rejecting the producer's objections, the Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed the order of the Commission. (267 F2d 471.)

A witness called to testify before a grand jury investigating a wide range of federal offenses, including violations of the narcotics laws and conspiracy to commit such offenses, refused, under a claim of privilege of self-incrimination, to answer questions as to his business and as to his last meeting and conversations with, and the whereabouts of, a fugitive witness. He was adjudged in criminal contempt on the ground that there was no real danger of incrimination. On his appeal the Court of Appeals refused to take into consideration data in a supplemental record consisting of his application to the trial court for reconsideration of allowance of bail and vacation of his sentence on constitutional grounds. These data showed that he had been publicly labeled as a racketeer and gangster at various occasions and that he had a twenty-year police record, including a sentence on a narcotics charge.

Petitioner, injured while on board defendant's vessel on navigable waters in New York State for the purpose of visiting a member of the crew, sought recovery in an action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleging unseaworthiness of the vessel and negligence on the part of its crew. The District Court held that New York substantive law was applicable, and accordingly eliminated the unseaworthiness claim and instructed the jury that petitioner was a licensee who could recover only if the shipowner had failed to warn him of a dangerous condition within his actual knowledge and only if he himself were entirely free from contributory negligence. A jury's verdict in plaintiff's favor was set aside, and the complaint was dismissed, on the ground that there was no proof that the shipowner had actually known of the dangerous conditions causing petitioner's injury. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed, but its opinion failed to indicate whether the affirmance was based upon agreement that New York law was applicable, or upon the determination that the controlling legal principles would be no different under maritime law. (245 F2d 175.)

Petitioner, employed as a pile driver in connection with the installation of a radar tower located at sea, was injured when a Navy life ring, used to carry him from a tug to the tower, collided with the pilot house on the tug; immediately prior to his injury petitioner had been working for some six hours on an unmanned barge to prepare for transfer of construction material to the radar tower. In an action in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, petitioner sought damages for his injuries under the Jones Act. The District Court denied relief, holding that petitioner's exclusive remedy was under the Defense Bases Act, providing for compensation for disability or death of persons employed in military bases outside the United States; the District Court indicated, however, that the evidence created a fact question on the issue as to whether or not petitioner was a crew member. The Court of Appeals for the First Circuit held that the Defense Bases Act did not provide the exclusive remedy for a crew member, in view of its provision that it should not apply in respect to the injury of a master or member of a crew of any vessel, but affirmed the District Court's judgment on the ground that the evidence was not sufficient to create a fact question as to whether petitioner was a crew member (245 F2d 437).

After being convicted of a federal crime upon trial in a United States District Court, the defendant appealed to the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, but the appeal was dismissed for want of timely prosecution for failure to pay the requisite filing fee. The defendant contended that he thought payment of the fee was unnecessary since he had been granted leave to appeal in forma pauperis by the District Court judge.

A longshoreman who sustained injuries in the course of his employment elected to accept compensation under the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act. Without a hearing, a compensation award was entered in his favor. Under the pertinent provisions of the act, his acceptance of the award had the effect of assigning his rights of action against third parties to his employer, and his employer's insurer, which made the payments under the award, was in turn subrogated to all the employer's rights. Subsequently, the longshoreman filed an action in admiralty against third parties to recover for his injuries. The employer's insurer was also the insurer of one of these third parties. The question before the Supreme Court was whether the plaintiff was entitled to maintain his action.

Before a criminal case was set for trial, the defendants obtained two orders for the production by the government of documentary evidence and other materials, one under Rule 16 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure for the inspection of materials belonging to the defendants and obtained from others by seizure or process, and one under Rule 17 (c) for inspection of materials obtained by the government by means other than seizure or process. The government moved to quash the latter order, contending that the access of a defendant in a criminal proceeding to materials in custody of government attorneys is limited to the rights granted by Rule 16. The motion was denied and the government attorney in possession of the materials was held in contempt.

In a government civil antitrust suit to enjoin the nation's fourth largest brewer from acquiring a brewer which was the largest seller of beer in New England, the United States District Court for the District of Rhode Island entered judgment for the defendant and dismissed the complaint on the ground that the acquiring company had no intent to enter the New England market except through acquisition and that it therefore could not be considered a potential competitor in that market (332 F Supp 970).

This case, a companion case to Green v County School Board of New Kent County, supra, p. 716, similarly presents the question whether a board of education's "freedom-of-choice" plan, which allows a pupil to choose his own public school, adequately complies with the board's responsibility to achieve a system of determining admission to the public schools on a nonracial basis. The school system in question consisted of two combination elementary and high schools, one of which was almost all white and the other of which was all Negro. The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas dismissed a complaint by Negro children arising out of the operation of such "freedom-of-choice" plan, and approved the adequacy of the plan. The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed the dismissal. (381 F2d 252.)

An oil corporation contracted with another company for the latter to perform certain completion operations on oil drilling platforms offshore of Louisiana, the drilling company promising, as part of the agreement, to indemnify the oil company for all claims resulting directly or indirectly from the work. During a storm occurring while work was in progress, an employee of the drilling company working on an oil drilling platform above the seabed of the outer continental shelf was taken safely aboard a boat chartered by the oil company, but was subsequently injured while assisting crewmen of the boat to evacuate workers from other platforms. The employee brought a suit for damages in the District Court of Harris County, Texas, alleging negligence by the oil company and the boat owner. The oil company filed a third-party complaint for indemnification against the drilling company, but in its third-party answer, the drilling company denied that the state court had subject-matter jurisdiction over the third-party complaint, arguing that the oil company's cause of action arose under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (43 USCS 1331 et seq.) and that the Act invested exclusive subject-matter jurisdiction in a United States District Court. The Texas trial court rejected this contention, and the case went to trial before a jury. In submitting the case to the jury, the trial court denied a request by the drilling company to instruct the jury that personal injury damage awards are not subject to federal income taxation and that they should not increase or decrease an award in contemplation of tax consequences. The jury found the oil company negligent and awarded the employee damages for his injuries, and it also found that the employee sustained his injuries while performing work

The constitutionality of a California statute prohibiting carriers from transporting government property at rates other than those approved by the California Public Utilities Commission was challenged by the United States in a suit under the Federal Declaratory Judgment Act in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California. The District Court rendered judgment for the United States (141 F Supp 168).

A Texas school district employed, at a high school, a white individual who was a teacher, athletic director, and head football coach. The school's black principal recommended that the teacher be relieved of his duties as athletic director and head football coach, on the alleged grounds of (1) poor leadership and planning skills, and (2) improper comportment before and after a particular football game. Eventually, the district's superintendent affirmed the recommendation, the district made or attempted to make several reassignments of the teacher to positions which did not include any athletic director or head football coach duties, and the teacher sent a formal letter of resignation to the district. The teacher also filed an action against the school district and the principal in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, under 42 USCS 1981 and 1983, and alleged various statutory and constitutional violations, including an equal protection and 1981 claim that (1) the teacher's removal from the athletic director and head coaching positions was motivated by the fact that he was white, and (2) the principal and, through him, the district were responsible for the racially discriminatory diminution in the teacher's employment status. Under the District Court's jury instructions that the school district was liable for the actions of its delegated administrative officials--including the superintendent and school principals--with regard to wrongful or unconstitutional action taken against or concerning school district personnel, the jury found for the teacher on all counts. Petitioner Atlantic Coast Pipeline, LLC (Atlantic), sought to construct an approximately 604-mile natural gas pipeline from West Virginia to North Carolina along a route that traversed 16 miles of land within the George Washington National Forest. As relevant here, Atlantic secured a special use permit from the United States Forest Service, obtaining a right-of-way for a 0.1-mile segment of pipe some 600 feet below a portion of the Appalachian National Scenic Trail (Appalachian Trail or Trail), which also crosses the National Forest. Respondents filed a petition for review in the Fourth Circuit, contending, inter alia, that the issuance of the special use permit for the right-of-way under the Trail violated the Mineral Leasing Act (Leasing Act). Atlantic in- tervened. The Fourth Circuit vacated the permit, holding that the Leasing Act did not empower the Forest Service to grant the right-of- way because the Trail became part of the National Park System when the Secretary of the Interior delegated its authority over the Trail’s administration to the National Park Service, and that the Leasing Act prohibits pipeline rights-of-way through lands in the National Park System.

One convicted in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana of assault with intent to murder was committed to the Attorney General's custody for 20 years pursuant to 18 USC 4208(b), which provides that such commitment is for the purpose of securing more detailed information "as a basis for determining the sentence to be imposed," and "shall be deemed to be for the maximum sentence." After having received the information in question, the court, in the absence of the prisoner and his counsel, modified the original order by reducing the period of imprisonment to 5 years. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed on the ground that it was error to impose final sentence under 4208(b) in the absence of the prisoner and his counsel. (312 F2d 223.)

Acting within the provisions of a Texas venue statute, a receiver for a Texas insurance company in liquidation in the Ninety-eighth District Court of Travis County, Texas, brought suit in that court against two national banks and 143 other parties, alleging a conspiracy to defraud the insurance company. Each national bank filed a plea of privilege asserting that it was located in Dallas County, Texas, and therefore was immune from suit in Travis County by virtue of Revised Statutes 5198, which is now incorporated in 12 USC 94, and provides that suits against a national bank may be had in any state or county court in the county in which the bank is located having jurisdiction in similar cases. The pleas were overruled, but the Austin Court of Civil Appeals of the Third Supreme Judicial District reversed. (331 SW2d 349.) The Supreme Court of Texas reversed the judgment of the Court of Civil Appeals and affirmed the judgment of the trial court on the grounds that (1) 94, being permissive and not mandatory, does not prohibit a suit against a national bank when a state venue statute expressly permits it, and (2) 94 has been repealed. (161 Tex 349, 341 SW2d 161.)

The owner of a patent for fluxes used in electric welding and the process of welding by using them, brought suits for infringement in which both the District Court and the Court of Appeals found that the composition of the fluxes involved invention in view of the fact that their use eliminated glare, open arc, splatter, and to a great extent, smoke, permitted the welding of thicker plates, increased welding speeds, and produced welds of superior quality.

Under 42 USCS 418(a), states may voluntarily obtain coverage under the Social Security System for their employees and employees of their political subdivisions by executing federal-state agreements (" 418 Agreements") with the Secretary of Health and Human Services. Formerly, 42 USCS 418(g) permitted a state to terminate any 418 Agreement by giving at least 2 years' advance notice. In 1983, however, Congress amended 418(g) to provide that no 418 Agreement might be terminated, either in its entirety, or with respect to any particular coverage group of employees, on or after April 20, 1983; the amendment expressly prevented withdrawal even if a termination notice had been filed prior to enactment of the amendment (Social Security Amendments Act of 1983, PL 98-21, 97 Stat 71, 103). Previously, in 1951, the state of California had entered into a 418 Agreement which (1) extended Social Security coverage to employees of the state and its subdivisions; (2) recited that the provisions of the Agreement were in conformity with 418; and (3) mirroring 418(g), permitted the state to terminate the agreement either in its entirety or with respect to particular coverage groups. When the 1983 amendment, however, prevented pending California termination notices for 71 political subdivisions from taking effect, two lawsuits challenging the amendment were filed in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of California: one by the state, the other by various plaintiffs including several state public agencies, their employees, taxpayers, and an organization opposed to the amendment. In an opinion governing both suits (613 F Supp 558), the District Court held that (1) the 418 Agreement created a contractual right to withdraw, so that the amendment to 418(g) effected a taking

The Supreme Court of California reversed a lower court decision that had reversed petitioner's conviction. The United States Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Supreme Court of California's interpretation of the Batson rule. Petitioner argued that the Supreme Court had jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C.S. _ 1257 because the Batson issue had been finally decided in the state courts. However, petitioner had made no convincing claim of erosion of federal policy that was not common to all decisions rejecting a defendant's Batson claim. Thus, the fourth category of cases to be regarded as "final" on the federal issue despite the ordering of further proceedings in the lower state courts did not apply. Petitioner's case also did not fit within the third category of cases to be regarded as final because if the lower state court on remand affirmed the judgment of conviction, petitioner could have again sought review of the Batson claim in the Supreme Court of California, albeit unsuccessfully, and then sought certiorari on the claim from the Supreme Court. Since the decision at issue was not final, the case was subject to dismissal for want of jurisdiction.

After protracted proceedings in the Interstate Commerce Commission, in which the nation's railroads, including the plaintiffs, sought a general revenue increase in their proposed tariffs, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, in a suit filed by the plaintiffs against the Commission, permanently enjoined the Commission from enforcing, against the plaintiffs, an order requiring the application of increased revenues to deferred capital improvements and deferred maintenance as a condition for the nonsuspension of the rate increases (392 F Supp 358).

When petitioner was tried in a Massachusetts trial court, the courtroom could not accommodate all the potential jurors. As a result, for two days of jury selection, an officer of the court excluded from the courtroom any member of the public who was not a potential juror, including petitioner's mother and her minister. Defense counsel neither objected to the closure at trial nor raised the issue on direct review. Petitioner was convicted of murder and a related charge. Five years later, he filed a motion for a new trial in state court, arguing, as relevant here, that his attorney had provided ineffective assistance by failing to object to the courtroom closure. The trial court ruled that he was not entitled to relief. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court affirmed in relevant part. Although it recognized that the violation of the right to public trial was a structural error, it rejected petitioner's ineffective-assistance claim because he had not shown prejudice.

Petitioner, convicted of crime in a state court, applied for habeas corpus, alleging that the highest state court, in hearing his appeal, had before it a transcript of the trial proceedings which had been fraudulently prepared by the prosecuting attorney and the court reporter.

After being called to assist local authorities in controlling civil disorders, the Army instituted an intelligence system for surveillance of civilian political activity to secure information relating to potential or actual civil disturbances, the principal sources of such information being the news media and publications in general circulation. The plaintiffs instituted a class action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, claiming that the mere existence and operation of the Army's surveillance system imposed a chilling effect on the exercise of First Amendment rights of the plaintiffs, who alleged no specific action of the Army against them, but based their claims of chilling effect on the contention that the surveillance system was not appropriate to the proper role of the Army, which might misuse the information in the future, causing direct harm to the plaintiffs. The District Court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that there was no justiciable claim for relief, but the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reversed (444 F2d 947).

Defendant was convicted in a New York state court for selling "girlie" magazines to a minor in violation of a New York statute, in the meantime repealed, which prohibited the sale of magazines which would appeal to the lust of minors or their curiosity as to sex or to the anatomical differences between the sexes. His conviction was affirmed by the Appellate Term of the New York Supreme Court, First Judicial Department.

Several members of a civil rights organization who participated in a peaceful demonstration on the public sidewalk in front of the home of the Mayor of Chicago, Illinois, protesting the mayor's alleged failure to support the busing of school children to achieve racial integration, were arrested and later convicted of misdemeanor offenses in a state court for violating an Illinois statute barring all picketing of residences or dwellings, while excepting from its prohibition "the peaceful picketing of a place of employment involved in a labor dispute." The members later commenced a lawsuit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, seeking a declaratory judgment that the statute was unconstitutional on its face and as applied, and an injunction prohibiting various state, county, and city officials from enforcing the statute. The District Court, ruling on cross-motions for summary judgment, denied all relief (462 F Supp 518). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed, holding that the statute's differential treatment of labor and nonlabor picketing could not be justified either by the state's interest in protecting the peace and privacy of the home or by the special character of a residence that is also used as a "place of employment," and therefore held that the statute, both on its face and as it had been applied, violated the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment (602 F2d 791).

A general contractor purchased a comprehensive "wrap-up" policy under which the insurer agreed to make compensation payments for any injuries suffered by workers employed in the construction of a rapid transit system for the District of Columbia, including employees of the general contractor's subcontractors. Five employees of various subcontractors, none of which had obtained its own workers' compensation insurance, collected lump sum compensation awards for work-related injuries under the general contractor's wrap-up policy. These employees subsequently attempted to supplement their workers' compensation awards by bringing tort actions against the general contractor in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia. The five different judges before whom these tort actions were brought each granted summary judgment for the general contractor on the ground that it was immune from tort liability for such claims under 5(a) of the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act (LHWCA) (33 USCS 905(a)) which immunizes employers who comply with the Act from tort liability to employees. In a consolidated appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia reversed, reasoning that 5(a) of the LHWCA grants a general contractor immunity from tort actions by subcontractor employees only if the general contractor has secured compensation insurance in satisfaction of a statutory duty and in this case the general contractor had not acted under such a duty because the subcontractors had not actually refused to secure the worker's compensation insurance, but rather, the general contractor had pre-empted its subcontractors through its unilateral decision to purchase a "wrap-up" policy covering all subcontractor employees (717 F2d 574).

A company headquartered in California filed, with the Commission's DG-Competition, an antitrust complaint against a second company, also headquarted in California. This complaint alleged that the second company had violated EU competition law with respect to the European market. While the complaint apparently was still in the investigative stage, the first company requested, from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, a discovery order under _ 1782(a), allegedly in connection with the complaint, to direct the second company to produce some documents that had been produced in previous antitrust litigation involving the second company. However, the District Court denied the request, as assertedly unsupported by applicable authority.

In the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey, the appellants alleged that New Jersey legislation providing for "Assistance to Families of the Working Poor" violated the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by discriminating against illegitimate children in the provision of benefits. The legislation limited benefits to only those families which consisted of a household composed of two adults of the opposite sex ceremonially married to each other who had at least one minor child of both, the natural child of one and adopted by the other, or a child adopted by both. A three-judge District Court upheld this legislation on the ground that it was designed to preserve and strengthen family life (349 F Supp 491).
