A husband and wife, who were the foster parents of the wife's brother and sister, instituted a class action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois challenging the validity, on equal protection grounds, of Illinois' welfare program under which foster parents who are related to the foster child do not qualify for "foster care" payments made to unrelated foster parents as part of the federal Aid to Families with Dependent Children program (42 USCS 601 et seq.)--related foster parents, such as the plaintiffs, being eligible to receive smaller regular Aid to Families with Dependent Children payments and upon an adequate showing of financial need, to receive supplemental payments for child care bringing the total payments to approximately the same amount as "foster care" payments made to unrelated foster parents. A three-judge District Court held that the Illinois scheme did not violate equal protection requirements (374 F Supp 1204), and the plaintiffs filed a jurisdictional statement in the United States Supreme Court challenging the Illinois scheme on both equal protection grounds and on the ground of conflict with the Social Security Act in violation of the supremacy clause of the Federal Constitution (Art VI, cl 2).
A seaman, injured as a consequence of an assault by a drunken fellow crew member, sought recovery from the shipowner on the grounds of negligence and breach of the warranty of seaworthiness.

The plaintiff, a stockholder in a corporation, brought the present action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York on behalf of the corporation under 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 to recover from the defendant partnership and the defendant partner with interest "short swing" profits earned by the partnership from dealings in stock of the corporation, of which the defendant partner was a director. The District Court refused to render a judgment, either against the partnership or against the partner individually, for the full amount of the profits realized by the partnership, but rendered judgment against the individual partner for his proportionate share of the profits; interest on that recovery was denied. (173 F Supp 590.) On appeal, taken by both the plaintiff and the defendants, the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed. (286 F2d 786.)

An accused was convicted of theft in an Illinois state court after the court, at an earlier trial for the same offense, declared a mistrial on the state's motion, and over the accused's objection, because the indictment was fatally deficient under Illinois law. On the accused's petition for habeas corpus, the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois dismissed the petition, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed (447 F2d 733).

The Pittsburgh Commission on Human Relations found that the Pittsburgh Press violated the city's Human Relations Ordinance by placing help-wanted advertisements in columns captioned "Jobs--Male Interest," "Jobs--Female Interest," and "Male-Female." The Commission ordered the newspaper to cease such violations and to utilize a classification system with no reference to sex. The Court of Common Pleas, Allegheny County, affirmed, and the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania affirmed the order as modified to except employment exempt from the ordinance (4 Pa Commw 448, 287 A2d 161). The Pennsylvania Supreme Court denied review.

Kansas imposed a tax on the receipt of motor fuel by fuel distributors within the state's boundaries. An Indian tribe, the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation (Nation), owned and operated, on its reservation in Kansas, a casino and a gasoline station, at which station the Nation imposed its own tax on fuel sales, of which 73 percent were made to casino patrons and 11 percent were made to persons who lived or worked on the reservation. The fuel sold at the station was purchased by the Nation from off-reservation, non-Indian distributors who paid the state fuel tax and passed the cost of that tax to their customers, including the Nation. In the United States District Court for the District of Kansas, the Nation brought an action for declaratory judgment and injunctive relief from the state's collection of its tax from distributors who delivered fuel to the reservation. The District Court (1) applied the interest-balancing test set forth in White Mountain Apache Tribe v. Bracker (1980) 448 U.S. 136, 100 S. Ct. 2578, 65 L. Ed. 2d 665, for determining a state's authority over non-Indians' conduct on a reservation; (2) decided that the balance of state, federal, and tribal interests favored the state; and (3) granted the state summary judgment ( 241 F. Supp. 2d 1295).

The plaintiffs are packers of frozen stuffed turkeys. Each package of turkey has a label indicating the net weight of the package, including stuffing, in conformity with a federal statute and Department of Agriculture regulations. Under a New York statute, as interpreted administratively, such packages must indicate the weight of the turkey, excluding stuffing, as well as the weight of the entire package. The plaintiffs, requesting a three- judge District Court under 28 USC 2281, sought to enjoin the enforcement of the New York law on the ground that it would violate the commerce clause and Fourteenth Amendment of the Federal Constitution and also, because of overriding requirements of federal law, would violate the supremacy clause of the Constitution. The District Court for the Southern District of New York, acting both in a three-judge and single-judge capacity because of uncertainty as to its jurisdiction, dismissed the suit on its merits. (230 F Supp 398.) The single-judge determination was appealed to the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, and the three-judge decision was appealed to the United States Supreme Court under 28 USC 1253.

The Federal Trade Commission held that a trading stamp company violated 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act by attempting to suppress the operation of trading stamp exchanges and other "free and open" redemption of stamps, because the company's practices restrained trade and injured competition. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed on the ground that the FTC had not demonstrated that the company's conduct violated either the letter or the spirit of the antitrust laws (432 F2d 146).

Workers who had been injured in a mine accident in Arizona brought, against the United States on the basis of federal mine inspectors' alleged negligence, a suit under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) (28 U.S.C.S. __ 1346, 2671 et seq.), which in 28 U.S.C.S. _ 1346(b)(1), authorized private tort actions against the United States "under circumstances where the United States, if a private person, would be liable to the claimant in accordance with the law of the place where the act or omission occurred."

After the plaintiff collection agency obtained money judgments against participants in an "employee welfare benefit plan" as defined in 3(1) of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) (29 USCS 1002(1)), a Georgia state trial court granted the collection agency's request to garnish the debtor participants' plan benefits. The Georgia Court of Appeals reversed, holding that a Georgia statute barring the garnishment of funds or benefits of an employee benefit plan or program subject to ERISA exempted plan benefits from garnishment (178 Ga App 467, 343 SE2d 492). The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed, concluding that the state antigarnishment statute was pre-empted by ERISA and that the plan was therefore subject to garnishment under the general Georgia garnishment statute (256 Ga 499, 350 SE2d 439).

A federally licensed Indian trader who operated a general store on an Indian reservation brought suit seeking a declaratory judgment that she did not need a California license for retail sale of distilled spirits for off-premises consumption. The United States District Court for the Southern District of California dismissed the action, ruling that the trader was required to have a state license under 18 USCS 1161, which provides that liquor transactions in Indian country are not subject to prohibition under federal law if such transactions are in conformity with state laws and tribal ordinances. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that 1161 pre-empted state licensing and distribution jurisdiction over tribal liquor sales in Indian country (678 F2d 1340).

The 1994 version of the Hyde Amendment (107 Stat 1113, later re-enacted unchanged for fiscal year 1995), which was a federal appropriations provision, limited funding for abortions to situations in which abortion was necessary save the mother's life or the pregnancy was the result of rape or incest. Medicaid providers and physicians who performed abortions in Arkansas filed against state officials a suit, seeking injunctive and declaratory relief, alleging that the constitutional amendment was inconsistent with a requirement in Title XIX of the Social Security Act, as amended (the Medicaid Act) (42 USCS 1396 et seq.), as affected by the 1994 version of the Hyde Amendment, that states fund medically necessary abortions when the pregnancy resulted from an act of rape or incest. The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas granted summary judgment for the Medicaid providers and the physicians and enjoined enforcement of the constitutional amendment (860 F Supp 609). The driver of a stolen automobile was killed at the end of a high-speed nighttime chase when his vehicle collided with a truck which county police officers had positioned across the road to serve as a roadblock. Members of the driver's family subsequently brought an action under 42 USCS 1983 in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of California, which action alleged that the county, the individual officers involved, and various other parties, acting under color of law, had violated the driver's constitutional rights in that, among other things, they had used excessive force in establishing the roadblock--particularly since they had allegedly concealed the roadblock by placing it behind a curve, leaving it unilluminated, and positioning a police car so that its headlights would shine in the face of an oncoming driver--and had thus effected an unreasonable seizure of the driver in violation of the Federal Constitution's Fourth Amendment. The District Court granted a motion to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a claim, on the ground--with regard to the Fourth Amendment claim--that establishing a roadblock was not unreasonable under the circumstances. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed with respect to the Fourth Amendment claim, as it held that the use of the roadblock to stop the driver did not constitute a "seizure" for Fourth Amendment purposes (817 F2d 540).

In a class action in the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina, black voters residing in Edgefield County, South Carolina, challenged a South Carolina statute enacted in 1966 which altered Edgefield County's election practices, on the ground that the 1966 statute had never been submitted to federal officials as required by 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. A three-judge District Court concluded that the United States Attorney General's approval of a 1971 statute amending the 1966 statute and re-enacting its remaining provisions rendered moot any objection to the superseded 1966 provisions.

An employee of a Florida electric company, who belonged to an electrical workers' union, was assigned to a job that required her to perform tasks allegedly beyond the scope of her training and experience. Shortly after commencing her new assignment, she was injured on the job. Two years later, the employee sued the union in state court in Broward County, Florida, alleging that the union had breached a duty, arising under (1) the collective bargaining and ancillary agreements between the union and the company, and (2) her relationship with the union, to provide her with a safe workplace. The union removed the lawsuit to the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida on the grounds that the alleged duty arose solely from the collective bargaining agreement and that any breach of this duty was actionable only under 301 of the Labor Management Relations Act (29 USCS 185(a)), which provides for federal court jurisdiction of suits for violation of contracts between employers and labor organizations, and which has been construed by the United States Supreme Court to require the application of federal law in such suits. The employee raised no objection to the removal when it occurred. In the District Court, the union moved to dismiss the complaint on the ground that it was untimely under the applicable federal statute of limitations. The employee argued that her action was a state-law suit in tort for negligence, and sought to have the case remanded to state court. The District Court granted the union's motion to dismiss, holding that (1) the claim was pre-empted by federal labor law, and (2) the suit was untimely because it was governed by the same 6-month statute of limitations that was applicable to unfair labor practice claims. Petitioners are six individuals whose applications for disability benefits were denied by the Social Security Administration (SSA). They each unsuccessfully challenged their respective adverse benefit determination in a hearing before an SSA administrative law judge (ALJ). The SSA Appeals Council denied discretionary review in each case. Thereafter, this Court decided Lucia v. SEC, 585 U. S. ___, which held that the appointment of Securities and Exchange Commission ALJs by lower level staff violated the Constitution‚Äôs Appointments Clause. Because the SSA ALJs who denied petitioners‚Äô claims were also appointed by lower level staff, petitioners argued in federal court that they were entitled to a fresh administrative review by constitutionally appointed ALJs. In each case, the Court of Appeals held that petitioners could not obtain judicial review of their Appointments Clause claims because they failed to raise those challenges in their administrative proceedings.

The shareholders contended that their allegations were sufficient to establish a strong inference that the officer acted with the intent to deceive, manipulate, or defraud, as required by _ 78u-4(b)(2). The officer argued that the shareholders failed to allege any financial motive of the officer to support scienter and offered vague and ambiguous allegations. The U.S. Supreme Court held that, while the shareholders' allegations plausibly permitted an inference of the requisite scienter, further analysis was required to determine whether the inference of fraudulent intent was a powerful or cogent inference which was at least as compelling as any opposing inference of nonfraudulent intent. The strong inference of scienter required by _ 78u-4(b)(2) was not required to be irrefutable or even the most plausible inference, but the strength of the inference could not be evaluated in a vacuum and consideration of plausible, nonculpable explanations for the officer's conduct was required. Further, any lack of pecuniary motive on the part of the officer did not by itself preclude a finding of scienter, and any ambiguities in the shareholders' allegations were relevant but not determinative.

A truck owner-driver, engaged in leasing his truck and services to motor carriers, brought an action in the Court of Common Pleas, Summit County, Ohio, for an injunction restraining the union of which he was a member and the motor carriers which employed him from carrying out a provision of the collective bargaining contract between the union and the motor carriers prescribing terms and conditions governing the minimum rental and other terms of lease when a motor vehicle was leased to a carrier by an owner who drove his vehicle in the carrier's service. The Court of Common Pleas held that the contract provision in question was not concerned with a subject of mandatory collective bargaining under the amended National Labor Relations Act; and that the provision was in violation of the state anti-trust law in that it precluded a truck owner from reasonable freedom of action in leasing his truck. The Ninth Judicial District Court of Appeals of Ohio affirmed, and the Ohio Supreme Court dismissed an appeal from that affirmance. (167 Ohio St 299, 4 Ohio Ops2d 344, 147 NE2d 856.)

Joanne Siragusa and Tom Grimmett, the bankruptcy trustee of Joanne's ex-husband Vincent's estate, appeal the district court's dismissal of their civil RICO suit. In their November 1994 suit, Joanne and Grimmett alleged that defendant Patricia Brown masterminded the reorganization of Vincent's medical practices so as to cheat Joanne out of her post-divorce community property [**2] interest in those practices. The district court found their suit barred by RICO's four-year statute of limitations. The question in the present case is whether an American trust--a trust established in the United States, governed by the laws of one of the states, and administered in that state by an American trustee--was exempted from payment of the United States tax on capital gains retained by the trust and realized in the United States, by virtue of Article 14 of the Income Tax Convention between the United States and the United Kingdom of April 16, 1945--which exempts from United States taxation capital gains of a "resident of the United Kingdom"--although all of the beneficiaries of the trust were citizens and residents of the United Kingdom. After having paid the appropriate amount of tax on its capital gains, the trust, represented by its successor trustee, filed an action for refund in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York. The District Court entered summary judgment for the plaintiff. The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed, denying the plaintiff's claim of exemption under the Convention. (299 F2d 565.)

Alleging that she had been discharged solely because of her race in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e et seq.), an airline flight attendant sued her former employer in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, seeking reinstatement, backpay, and attorney's fees and costs. A few months after the complaint was filed, the airline made a formal offer of judgment in the amount of $ 450. The offer was refused, the case was tried, and the flight attendant lost. The District Court entered judgment in favor of the airline, and directed that each party bear its own costs. The airline then moved for modification of the judgment, contending that under Rule 68 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure--which provides that if a plaintiff rejects a defendant's formal settlement offer, and if "the judgment finally obtained by the offeree is not more favorable than the offer," the plaintiff "must pay the costs incurred after the making of the offer"--the plaintiff should be required to pay the airline's costs incurred after the offer of judgment had been refused. The District Court denied the motion on the ground that the $ 450 offer had not been made in a good-faith attempt to settle the case and therefore did not trigger the cost-shifting provisions of Rule 68. The Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed, holding that Rule 68 applied only if the defendant's settlement offer was sufficient to justify serious consideration by the plaintiff (600 F2d 699).

The Communist Party of Michigan and its Executive Secretary brought an action in the District Court for a declaration that the Michigan Communist Control Bill, requiring the registration of Communists, the Communist Party, and Communist front organizations, was unconstitutional on the ground of vagueness of statutory definitions. The District Court found the statute constitutional, and plaintiffs appealed. The action in the District Court had been commenced five days after the statute had become law, and, at the time of the appeal from that court's decision, a bill contesting the statute's constitutionality on federal and state grounds was pending in a state court.

In a suit in the Superior Court of Fulton County, Georgia, a railway worker sought damages from a railroad for "wrongful discharge," alleging that he was an employee of the railroad before his automobile accident and that following the accident he fully recovered and was physically able to resume his work for the railroad, but that the railroad refused to allow him to return to work. The railroad removed the case to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, which dismissed the complaint for the plaintiff's failure to exhaust his remedy before the National Railroad Adjustment Board (65 LC 11,903). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed (441 F2d 1222).

The natural mother of three sons voluntarily placed them in the legal custody of a county agency, which then placed the children in foster homes. Subsequently, the agency initiated parental termination proceedings, and a state court declared that the mother's parental rights respecting the three sons were terminated. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed the termination order (497 Pa 322, 383 A2d 1228), and the United States Supreme Court denied a petition for certiorari (58 L Ed 2d 192). The mother then sought a writ of habeas corpus under 28 USCS 2254(a)--which requires federal courts to entertain an application for a writ of habeas corpus in behalf of the person in custody pursuant to the judgment of a state court--in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. The District Court dismissed the petition, concluding that the custody maintained by the mother over her three children is not the type of custody to which the federal habeas corpus remedy may be addressed, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed (648 F2d 135).

An indictment charging an attorney with violating the federal perjury statute (18 USC 1621) by making a wilfully false statement of a material fact in a hearing under oath, held pursuant to a local rule of a Federal District Court in which it was sought to determine the attorney's fitness to practice before the court, was dismissed by the United States District Court for the Northern District of Iowa, Central Division. The dismissal was based upon the District Court's holding that the local rule under which the attorney took his oath was not a law of the United States for purposes of the perjury statute's provision that perjury is committed by one who, having taken an oath before a competent tribunal, officer, or person, in any case in which a law of the United States authorizes an oath to be administered, that he will testify truly, wilfully and contrary to such oath states any material matter which he does not believe to be true.

The Court considers for the second time the Ninth Circuit's determination that respondent stockholders' complaint states a claim against petitioner fiduciaries for breach of the duty of prudence. The first time, the Court vacated and remanded in light of Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer, 573 U. 5. __(2014), a case which set forth the standards for stating a claim for breach of the duty of prudence against fiduciaries who manage employee stock ownership plans (ESOPs). On remand, the Ninth Circuit reiterated its conclusion that the complaint states such a claim. The Court now reverses and remands. The stockholders are former employees of Amgen Inc. and its subsidiary Amgen Manufacturing, Limited, who participated in plans that qualified under 29 U. S. C. ¬ß 1 107(d)(3)(A) as eligible individual account plans. Like ESOPs, these plans offer ownership in employer stock as an option to employees. The parties agree that the decision in Fifth Third is fully applicable to the plans at issue here.

The lower court concluded that the error in failing to update the computer database to reflect the recall of the arrest warrant was negligent, not reckless or deliberate. That negligent error was not enough, by itself to require the extreme sanction of exclusion under the Fourth Amendment. Assuming that a Fourth Amendment violation occurred when defendant was arrested on the recalled arrest warrant, the exclusionary rule did not apply as the error that occurred arose from nonrecurring and attenuated negligence. It was far removed from the core concerns that led to the exclusionary rule's adoption. To trigger the exclusionary rule, police conduct had to be sufficiently deliberate such that exclusion could meaningfully deter it, and sufficiently culpable that such deterrence was worth the price paid by the justice system. In this case, the miscommunications were not routine or widespread; they were not so objectively culpable as to require exclusion.

After a union had terminated a collective bargaining agreement with an employer while negotiating contract changes, the union threatened a strike. The employer then closed its plant and refused the union's demand that severance pay be paid to qualified employees under the terminated bargaining agreement. The employer also refused to arbitrate the severance pay claim pursuant to a clause in the terminated bargaining agreement requiring submission of all disputes to arbitration. The union then instituted an action in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, seeking to compel the employer to arbitrate the severance pay issue or, in the alternative, a judgment for the severance pay due. The District Court granted the employer's motion for summary judgment on both issues, holding as to the arbitration question that the duty to arbitrate terminated with the contract that had created it (382 F Supp 1354). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed, holding that the duty to arbitrate survived the contract's termination with respect to claims that arose by reason of the collective bargaining agreement (530 F2d 548).

Under a New York statute which generally regulated hospital rates for in-patient care, patients were to be charged at a standard rate for the average cost of treating their medical problem rather than for the cost of their individual treatment. Patients covered by nonprofit health service corporations, such as Blue Cross/Blue Shield, were billed at the standard rate. However, the statute imposed a 24 percent surcharge on patients served by commercial insurers and up to a 9 percent surcharge on health maintenance organizations (HMOs) based on the monthly charges paid by HMOs for their members' care. In separate actions filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York against state officials, several commercial insurers acting as fiduciaries of plans which they administered under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) (29 USCS 1001 et seq.), joined by insurance industry trade associations, alleged that the surcharge provisions were invalid because they were pre-empted by 514(a) of ERISA (29 USCS 1144(a)), which provides that ERISA supersedes state laws insofar as they "relate to" any employee benefit plan covered by ERISA. Two Blue Cross/Blue Shield entities and a state hospital association intervened as defendants, and a state HMO conference and several HMOs intervened as plaintiffs. Consolidating the actions, the District Court granted summary judgment to the plaintiffs and enjoined enforcement of the surcharges (813 F Supp 996). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, affirming, expressed the view that the surcharge provisions were pre-empted because they related to employee benefit plans covered by ERISA, in that the surcharges imposed a significant economic burden on commercial insurers

Certain provisions of the Social Security Act (42 USCS 301 et seq.) in effect between 1979 and 1983 authorized payment of survivor's benefits to a wage earner's widowed spouse who remarried after age 60 but not to a similarly situated surviving spouse who had been divorced from the decedent. A divorced widow applied for such benefits, but her claim was denied because of her remarriage. She then brought a class action in the United States District Court for the Central District of California, challenging the constitutionality of the provisions, and the District Court held the challenged provisions unconstitutional, stating that because Congress in 1977 had treated surviving divorced spouses and widowed spouses in the same manner upon the wage earner's death, there was no logical basis for distinguishing between the two classes of individuals upon their subsequent remarriage.

A defendant was convicted of attempted murder, kidnapping, robbery, and sexual assault in a jury trial in a Connecticut Superior Court. The court had instructed the jury regarding intent that "every person is conclusively presumed to intend the natural and necessary consequences of his act." The Supreme Court of Connecticut affirmed the defendant's convictions for kidnapping and sexual assault but reversed the convictions for attempted murder and robbery on the basis of the instructions regarding intent, which were held to violate due process (440 A2d 858).

Respondents Yassir Fazaga, Ali Malik, and Yasser Abdel Rahim, members of Muslim communities in California, filed a putative class action against the Federal Bureau of Investigation and certain Government officials, claiming that the Government subjected them and other Muslims to illegal surveillance under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 (FISA). FISA provides special procedures for use when the Government wishes to conduct foreign intelligence surveillance. Relevant here, FISA provides a procedure under which a trial-level court or other authority may consider the legality of electronic surveillance conducted under FISA and order specified forms of relief. See 50 U. S. C. ¬ß1806(f). The Government moved to dismiss most of respondents‚Äô claims under the ‚Äústate secrets‚Äù privilege. See, e.g., General Dynamics Corp. v. United States, 563 U. S. 478. After reviewing both public and classified filings, the District Court held that the state secrets privilege required dismissal of all respondents‚Äô claims against the Government, except for one claim under ¬ß1810, which it dismissed on other grounds. The District Court determined dismissal appropriate because litigation of the dismissed claims ‚Äúwould require or unjustifiably risk disclosure of secret and classified information.‚Äù 884 F. Supp. 2d 1022, 1028‚Äì1029. The Ninth Circuit reversed in relevant part, holding that ‚ÄúCongress intended FISA to displace the state secrets privilege and its dismissal remedy with respect to electronic surveillance.‚Äù 965 F. 3d 1015, 1052.

Under the Alien Enemy Act, the power of the Attorney General to remove to Germany a German citizen residing in this country ended when Congress, by the Joint Resolution of October 19, 1951, terminated the state of war which had existed between the United States and Germany. Petitioner, a German citizen residing in this country, who had been interned in 1942 and ordered removed to Germany in 1946 and who had applied for a writ of habeas corpus before the passage of the Joint Resolution of October 19, 1951, terminating the state of war between the United States and Germany, is no longer removable under the Alien Enemy Act and is entitled to his release.

An individual who had been terminated from her employment as a liquor store clerk in Idaho brought an action in an Idaho state trial court against officials of the Idaho liquor dispensary. The individual, alleging that her termination had deprived her of property without due process of law in violation of the Federal Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment, sought damages under 42 USCS 1983. The officials moved to dismiss the individual's complaint on the ground that the officials were entitled to qualified immunity. However, the trial court, treating the motion as a motion for summary judgment because affidavits had been filed in support, denied the motion. The Supreme Court of Idaho, dismissing the officials' timely filed appeal, rejected the officials' arguments that (1) the order denying the officials' motion for summary judgment was final within the meaning of an Idaho appellate rule, and (2) the officials had a right to appeal as a matter of federal law.

Petitioner prison inmate was convicted in state court of felony murder and sentenced to death, but asserted that the prosecution failed to disclose that a key witness was a paid informant and knowingly allowed the witness to testify falsely. Upon the grant of a writ of certiorari, the inmate appealed the judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit which reversed a grant of the inmate's habeas corpus petition. It was conceded that the prosecution failed to disclose the informant's status and did not correct the informant's false testimony that he did not talk to police until shortly before trial. The lower appellate court found, however, that the issue of suppression of impeachment evidence concerning the informant was procedurally barred since the inmate failed to pursue the issue in state court proceedings, despite indications of the prosecutorial misconduct. The United States Supreme Court held the inmate's claim was not barred since the inmate showed cause for failing to develop the claim in state court and the impeachment evidence was clearly material, at least with regard to the penalty proceedings. The inmate's failure to investigate the informant's status resulted from the prosecution's persistent misrepresentations and omissions concerning such status, and the inmate was entitled to credit the prosecution's statements. Further, the inmate was prejudiced from the lack of the evidence since the prosecution relied heavily on the informant's penalty phase testimony about the inmate's propensity to commit further crimes without disclosing the informant's active role in the case.

A New York statute which permits trust companies to pool small trust estates into one common fund for investment administration also provides for notice, to interested beneficiaries, of a petition of such trust company for judicial settlement of its accounts by publication in a local newspaper, setting forth merely the name and address of the trust company, the name and the date of establishment of the common trust fund, and a list of all participating estates, trusts, or funds.

The petitioner, then president of the Miami branch of the NAACP, was ordered to appear before a committee of the Florida state legislature investigating infiltration of Communists into organizations operating in the field of race relations, and to bring with him membership records of the association which were in his possession or custody. However, he refused to produce these records for the purpose of answering questions concerning membership in the NAACP; his refusal was based on the ground that to bring the lists to the hearing and to utilize them as a basis of his testimony would interfere with the free exercise of the Fourteenth Amendment associational rights of members and prospective members of the NAACP. A Florida state court adjudged him in contempt and the Florida Supreme Court affirmed the judgment below. (126 So 2d 129.)

A special grand jury investigated certain commodity futures transactions, and a defendant who was never indicted eventually pleaded guilty to two misdemeanor counts of violating the Commodities Exchange Act (7 USCS 6c(a)(A)). Eight months after the plea, the government filed a motion under Rule 6(e)(3)(C)(i) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure for disclosure of grand jury transcripts and documents to the Internal Revenue Service for its use in an audit to determine the defendant's civil income tax liability. Rule 6(e)(3)(C)(i) provides that disclosure of grand jury materials may be made when so directed by a court preliminarily to or in connection with a judicial proceeding. The United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois granted disclosure. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed (662 F2d 1232).

An accused, having been held in custody upon being unable to post bond, wore clothing distinctly marked as prison issue during his criminal trial before a jury in the 177th Judicial District Court of Harris County, Texas. The accused had asked an officer at the jail for his civilian clothes when he learned that he was going to trial, but the request was denied, and during the trial the accused's attorney expressly referred to the accused's wearing of jail clothing at voir dire, but neither the accused nor his counsel objected concerning the jail attire to the trial judge, whose practice was to permit any accused who so desired to change into civilian clothing. The accused was found guilty of assault with intent to commit murder with malice and, upon affirmance of his conviction by the Court of Criminal Appeals of Texas, sought habeas corpus relief in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas. Although holding that the trial of the defendant in jail clothing was inherently unfair, the District Court denied relief on the ground of harmless error (364 F Supp 335). Disagreeing with the District Court on the issue of harmless error, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed (500 F2d 206).

The Secretary of the Interior denied an application for a patent to certain public lands based on the applicant's discovery there of quartzite stone, one of the most common of all solid matters. The Secretary held that the quartzite deposits did not qualify as "valuable mineral deposits" under 30 USC 22, which provides that persons finding such deposits on public land may obtain title to the land by application to the Department of the Interior, since the quartzite deposits did not meet the "marketability test," that is, the stone could not be marketed at a profit. The Secretary also rejected the contention that the quartzite deposits made the land "chiefly valuable for building stone" under 30 USC 161, which authorizes entry on such lands under the provision of the mining laws in relation to placer mineral claims, the Secretary holding that the quartzite was a common variety of stone under 30 USC 611, which provides that a deposit of common varieties of stone shall not be deemed a valuable mineral deposit within the meaning of the mining laws so as to give effective validity to any mining claim. Upon the applicant's remaining in possession of the land, the government instituted an ejectment action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California, Central Division, against the applicant and his lessee, who filed a counterclaim seeking the issuance of a patent. The District Court rendered summary judgment for the government, but the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed (363 F2d 190; 379 F2d 555).

This case involves a Selective Service registrant whose local board denied him a conscientious objector exemption. In order to secure aid for his appeal, the registrant met with a Government appeals agent. The agent made out a report which was placed in the registrant's file, and which was before the appeal board when it considered petitioner's claim. The report was unfavorable, and the Solicitor General so concedes. The Solicitor General also concedes that because of the appeal agent's special position in the Selective Service System, his views probably carried substantial weight with the appeal board. Yet, this crucial report was not shown to the registrant, so that he might have attempted to rebut the unfavorable statements contained therein.

In defendants' trial, in the Chancery Court of McMinn County, Tennessee, on a charge of criminal contempt committed by violating an injunction issued in connection with a labor dispute and barring the inflicting of harm or damage upon the persons or property of the employees or any other person, defendants' request for trial by jury was denied. Over their timely objection, the court admitted in evidence an air rifle found by police officers in defendants' automobile as a result of a warrantless search--after their arrest for a traffic offense--conducted while defendants were in custody inside the courthouse and their automobile was parked on the street outside. Defendants were found guilty and were given the maximum sentence authorized by statute, 10 days in jail and a $ 50 fine. The Supreme Court of Tennessee affirmed. (219 Tenn 472, 410 SW2d 881.)

A lessee holding an oil and gas lease for a tract of land in Karnes County, Texas, after contracting in 1953 to sell to a pipeline company for a 10-year period all merchantable natural gas now or hereafter produced from the tract, obtained a certificate of public convenience and necessity as required under 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act (15 USCS 717f(c)), since the pipeline company was one which would resell in interstate commerce the gas sold to it by the lessee. In 1966, the lease was again assigned, and shortly thereafter, when the only successful well on the tract stopped producing, the pipeline company was informed that existing wells were depleted and that no other gas would be available. A newspaper reporter who had obtained information regarding alleged improper conduct by local public officials was called to testify before a special Florida grand jury investigating those allegations. At the time he testified, the reporter was warned that a state statute prohibited grand jury witnesses, among others, from disclosing testimony given before the grand jury, and that any such disclosure could result in a criminal prosecution. The reporter, wishing to publish a news story about the subject matter of the grand jury investigation and to include in such story his own testimony and experience before the grand jury, filed an action against the state in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida, which action sought (1) a declaration that the statute in question was an unconstitutional abridgment of the reporter's freedom of speech, and (2) an injunction preventing the state from prosecuting the reporter for disclosing his testimony. The District Court granted summary judgment in favor of the state, as it held that (1) the state was entitled to make the judgment that a permanent and total ban on the disclosure of witness testimony was necessary to the proper functioning of the grand jury, and (2) this was the exceptional case where a severe infringement on rights under the Federal Constitution's First Amendment was permissible (678 F Supp 1552). The United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit reversed and remand, as it held that the statute was unconstitutional to the extent that the statute applied to witnesses who speak about their testimony after the grand jury investigation is completed (866 F2d 1318).

The Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC) brought suit in the United States District Court for the Central District of California against a person who was alleged to be one of several conspirators in a stock manipulation scheme that disabled two broker-dealers from meeting obligations to customers. It was alleged that the scheme had triggered SIPC's authority, pursuant to a provision of the Securities Investor Protection Act (SIPA) (15 USCS 78fff-3(b)(2)), to advance funds to the broker-dealers' trustees in order to reimburse the customers. SIPC claimed that the alleged conspirators had violated 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 USCS 78j(b)), the Securities and Exchange Commission's Rule 10b-5 ( 17 CFR 240.10b-5), and various provisions of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) (18 USCS 1961-1968), and that SIPC was thus entitled to recover treble damages under a provision of RICO (18 USCS 1964(c)). The District Court, entering summary judgment for the defendant on the RICO claims, held that (1) SIPC did not meet the purchaser-seller requirements for standing to assert RICO claims that were predicated on 10(b) and Rule 10b-5, given that SIPC was not a purchaser or seller of securities, and (2) SIPC had not shown that the defendant's alleged acts were the proximate cause of SIPC's losses. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded on the grounds that (1) the RICO cause of action under 1964(c) does not impose a purchaser-seller requirement for standing, and (2) the District Court had erred in finding no proximate cause (908 F2d 1461).

Defendant having been convicted of a criminal offense, the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida withheld imposition of sentence of confinement and placed him on probation. Subsequently the court revoked the probation and orally sentenced defendant to one year imprisonment, and thereafter, in the defendant's absence, entered a formal written judgment which enlarged the penalty by one day. On appeal, the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the order without mentioning the propriety of the enlargement of the sentence. (317 F2d 608.)

In a prosecution in the Municipal Court of Tulsa, Oklahoma, for an alleged violation of a municipal ordinance, the defendant, during cross- examination, referred to his alleged assailant as "chicken shit," whereupon the defendant was prosecuted and convicted under an information that charged him with criminal contempt by using such expletive in the presence of the trial judge. The Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed the contempt conviction, holding that the conviction rested not only on the use of the expletive, but also on the defendant's discourteous responses to the trial judge.

Suits were brought against the government under the Tort Claims Act for the death of civilians killed in the crash of a military airplane. The civilians were aboard the plane as observers in the testing of secret electronic equipment. The plaintiffs moved, under Rule 34 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, for the production by the government of the official accident report and other documents containing statements taken in connection with the official investigation of the crash. A formal claim of privilege was filed by the Secretary of the Air Force objecting to production of the documents on the ground that the plane had been engaged in a highly secret mission. An affidavit to the same effect was filed by the Judge Advocate General. This affidavit offered to produce the three surviving crew members for examination by the plaintiffs, allowing them to refresh their memories and testify as to all matters except those of a classified nature. The District Court ordered production of the documents, for examination by the judge so that he could determine the existence of the privilege, and, on the government's refusal, entered an order, in accordance with Rule 37(b) (2) (i), that the facts on the issue of negligence would be taken as established in the plaintiffs' favor. Judgment was accordingly entered for the plaintiffs and affirmed on appeal.

The next morning, she was unable to reach her husband by phone, so she called the police to request a welfare check. The responding officers accompanied Caniglia‚Äôs wife to the home, where they encountered Caniglia on the porch. The officers called an ambulance based on the belief that Caniglia posed a risk to himself or others. Caniglia agreed to go to the hospital for a psychiatric evaluation on the condition that the officers not confiscate his firearms. But once Caniglia left, the officers located and seized his weapons. Caniglia sued, claiming that the officers had entered his home and seized him and his firearms without a warrant in violation of the Fourth Amendment. The District Court granted summary judgment to the officers. The First Circuit affirmed, extrapolating from the Court‚Äôs decision in Cady v. Dombrowski, 413 U. S. 433, a theory that the officers‚Äô removal of Caniglia and his firearms from his home was justified by a ‚Äúcommunity caretaking exception‚Äù to the warrant requirement.

The petitioner, a captain in the Air Force, was convicted by a court- martial on March 8, 1968, of wilfully disobeying a lawful order, and was sentenced to one year's confinement at hard labor. He was then ordered confined to his quarters at Cannon Air Force Base, New Mexico, and the court- martial's judgment was forwarded for review by the convening authority, which approved the sentence, ordering that pending completion of appellate review, the petitioner be confined in the United States Disciplinary Barracks, Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. The petitioner's attorneys appealed the merits of the conviction to the Air Force Board of Review, and also sought habeas corpus relief from the United States District Court for the District of New Mexico, arguing that (1) both his confinement at the Cannon Air Force Base and his proposed transfer to Fort Leavenworth constituted an attempt to "execute" his sentence in violation of Article 71(c) of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, and (2) since no finding had been made that restraint was necessary to prevent his flight from the jurisdiction, as was required by Article 13 of the Code, the civilian court should require his complete release. In separate cases, two individuals pleaded guilty in Illinois state court to a charge of burglarly, an offense punishable by imprisonment for an indeterminate term of years and a mandatory three-year parole term. The defendant in neither case was informed during the plea acceptance hearing that the negotiated sentence included the mandatory parole term. In each case, the defendant was discharged from prison and released on parole, but later returned to prison as a parole violator. While in custody, they each filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, alleging that they were not informed that a mandatory parole term had attached to their sentence until after their discharge from prison and that their incarceration as a result of a violation of that parole term violated the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The cases were consolidated, and the District Court ordered their release through "specific performance" of the plea bargain, rather than nullification of the guilty pleas (447 F Supp 95). The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed on the ground that the defendants had failed to exhaust an available state remedy (594 F2d 614). On remand, the District Court reentered judgment for the defendants, but since both had been released from the custody of Illinois corrections officials, the court simply entered an order declaring void the mandatory parole terms (483 F Supp 775), and the Court of Appeals affirmed (633 F2d 71).

During World War II holders of claims against enemy banks caused state court attachment warrants to be levied on accounts maintained by the debtors in a New York bank. The attachments were followed by default judgments, which remained unsatisfied because the attached funds were blocked under executive orders issued under the Trading With the Enemy Act. The Alien Property Custodian issued orders vesting in himself the debts owing to the foreign banks, but did not issue a directive requiring the New York bank to turn over to him the funds for administration. Due to the outstanding attachment levies the New York bank refused to release the accounts. The Custodian sued for a declaratory judgment that the creditors obtained no lien or other interest in the attached accounts and that he was entitled to take the entire balances.

An inmate in a state prison brought an action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California under federal civil rights laws, asserting, among other claims, a claim under 42 USCS 1983 that prison officials negligently and inadvertently interfered with his outgoing mail and that supervisory prison personnel negligently failed to provide proper training to their subordinates. The District Court granted summary judgment for the prison officials as to such claim, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed (536 F2d 277).

The latest chapter in the battle over the 2019 rule, which expanded the definition of ‚Äúpublic charge‚Äù ‚Äì a term in immigration law for people who are ineligible for a green card if the government believes that they are likely to rely too heavily on certain forms of government aid, such as Medicaid or food stamps. Because the Biden administration decided to stop defending the rule, it dismissed a challenge to the rule that had been pending in the Supreme Court in 2021. It then rescinded the rule without seeking public comments on its decision to do so.

A railroad, claiming that as applied to it the rates prescribed by the Interstate Commerce Commission for the transportation of mail did not afford the fair and reasonable compensation to which it was entitled under the Railway Mail Pay Act, brought an action against the United States in the Court of Claims for the difference between what it had received and the amount to which it claimed to be entitled.

After hearing evidence at public hearings relating to sexually explicit entertainment in "topless" and "bottomless" bars and nightclubs, which evidence indicated that sexual conduct had taken place between customers and entertainers, and that prostitution, rape, indecent exposure, and assaults on police officers had taken place on or immediately adjacent to licensed premises, the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control promulgated regulations prohibiting certain sexually explicit live entertainment or films in licensed bars and nightclubs--such regulations prohibiting the performance of specified acts, or simulated acts, including sexual intercourse, masturbation, sexual acts prohibited by law, touching or fondling of breast or genitals, displaying of genitals, and displaying films or pictures depicting such prohibited acts. Certain liquor license holders, and dancers performing at their premises, instituted a declaratory judgment action against the Department, the state, and various state officials in the United States District Court for the Central District of California, challenging the constitutionality of the regulations. The three-judge District Court held that the regulations unconstitutionally abridged the plaintiffs' freedom of expression guaranteed by the First and Fourteenth Amendments, since the regulations could not be justified under Supreme Court decisions either as a prohibition of obscenity or as a valid regulation of conduct having a communicative element (326 F Supp 348).

A New Jersey state assemblyman whose district included the Borough of Oradell, and three registered voters of the Borough, instituted an action for declaratory and injunctive relief in the Chancery Division of the Superior Court of Bergen County, New Jersey, challenging the constitutionality of a Borough ordinance requiring that any person, including representatives of "Borough Civic Groups and Organizations," desiring to canvass or solicit from house-to-house for a "recognized charitable cause," or for a "Federal, State, County or Municipal political campaign or cause," must "notify the Police Department, in writing, for identification only." The Superior Court held that the ordinance was invalid on several grounds, including vagueness and overbreadth, and the Appellate Division of the Superior Court affirmed. The Supreme Court of New Jersey reversed, holding that the ordinance was a proper exercise of the Borough's police power, was not unclear, and did not offend free speech interests (66 NJ 376, 331 A2d 277).

A demonstrator in front of a Rockford, Illinois, high school was convicted in the Circuit Court of Winnebago County of violating the Rockford antipicketing ordinance, which outlawed demonstrations near schools in session (except peaceful labor picketing), and the Rockford antinoise ordinance, which prohibited disturbing a school session by wilfully making a noise or diversion while on adjacent public or private grounds. The Supreme Court of Illinois affirmed (46 Ill 2d 492, 263 NE2d 866).

In an action by a railroad employee seeking recovery, under the Federal Employers' Liability Act, for injuries sustained when a rivet gun with which he was working under a railroad car discharged a metal clip which struck him in the forehead, the Circuit Court of the City of St. Louis, Missouri, entered judgment on a verdict in plaintiff's favor. The judgment was reversed by the St. Louis Court of Appeals ((Mo App) 303 SW2d 153), and the employee sought a writ of certiorari in the United States Supreme Court.

The issue presented by this case was whether the owner and operator of community antenna television (CATV) systems, which carried, as part of the programing received from the several television stations whose signals were provided to customers of the systems, copyrighted motion pictures for which the stations, but not the CATV systems, were licensed by the copyright holder, infringed the latter's exclusive performance rights under the Copyright Act of 1909 (17 USC 1 et seq.). The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled in favor of the copyright holder (255 F Supp 177), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed (377 F2d 872).

The owners of a motel and an adjacent restaurant entered into two collective bargaining agreements with a union, each agreement covering the employees of one of these establishments; these agreements contained an arbitration clause and provided that they were binding upon the employer's successors, purchasers, or lessees. Afterwards the owners sold the personal property used in these establishments, but retained ownership of the real property, which was leased to the purchaser; it was agreed that the purchaser did not assume any obligations from the labor agreements made by the seller. The purchaser then hired its own work force, among them 9 out of 53 former employees of the seller.

Defendants' petition, based on 28 USC 1443, to remove to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia criminal trespass prosecutions pending against them in the Superior Court of Fulton County, Georgia, alleged that defendants had been arrested on various dates in the spring of 1963 when they sought to obtain service at privately owned restaurants open to the general public in Atlanta, Georgia, and that their arrests were effected for the sole purpose of racial discrimination. On its own motion and without a hearing, the District Court remanded the cases to the state court. Pending defendants' appeal to the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 was enacted; this Act, as interpreted by the United States Supreme Court, prohibited trespass prosecutions of the kind involved in the instant case, even though the prosecutions were instituted prior to the passage of the Act. The Court of Appeals therefore returned the case to the District Court, with directions that defendants be given an opportunity to prove that their prosecutions had resulted from orders to leave public accommodations for racial reasons, and, upon such proof, to dismiss the prosecutions. (342 F2d 336.)

After a corporation (National) had purchased 34 percent of the voting securities of another corporation (TSC), the two corporations issued to their shareholders a joint proxy statement recommending approval of a proposal for the exchange of TSC stock for National stock. A TSC corporate shareholder brought the instant action, in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, against both corporations, seeking money damages and restitution upon its claims, among others, that in violation of the SEC Rule 14a- 9 (CFR 240.14a-9)--which prohibits proxy solicitations containing any statement which is false or misleading with respect to any material fact, or which omits to state any material fact necessary in order to make the statements therein not false or misleading--the defendants omitted from their proxy statement material facts relating to the degree of National's control, at the time of the proxy solicitation, over TSC and the favorability of the terms of the proposal to TSC shareholders. The District Court denied the plaintiff's motion for partial summary judgment on the issue of the defendants' liability (361 F Supp 108), but the Court of Appeals for Seventh Circuit reversed the denial of summary judgment to the plaintiff on its 14a-9 claims (512 F2d 324).

In 1959 the Federal Power Commission granted unconditional certificates of public convenience and necessity to numerous producers of gas in southern Louisiana. The sales contracts of the producers called for initial prices ranging from 21.4 cents to 23.8 cents per thousand cubic feet. After deliveries had commenced under these contracts, the Commission's orders were challenged by consumer interests in various federal court actions, which resulted in the Commission's being required to reconsider its previous orders. After further proceedings, the Commission imposed two conditions on the certificates which it had granted. First, it provided that the producers commence service at 18.5 cents per thousand cubic feet, plus 1.5 cents tax reimbursement where applicable, a price which it found to be "in line" with prices for Commission-certificated sales of gas from the southern Louisiana production area under generally contemporaneous contracts. Second, it provided that until just and reasonable area rates are determined for southern Louisiana, or until July 1, 1967, whichever is earlier, the producers shall not file any increased rates above 23.55 cents, the level at which rate filings might trigger increased rates by other producers under the escalation provisions of their contracts with the producers involved in the instant case. In addition, the Commission ordered the producers to refund to their customers the amounts in excess of the proper initial price which the producers had already collected under the original certificates. (30 FPC 283.) The plaintiff, a New York corporation doing business in Texas, purchased insurance agreements covering risks connected with property located in Texas from Lloyds of London, England, and the Institute of London Underwriters. Taxes on the premiums paid under these policies were exacted from the plaintiff under a Texas statute providing that if any person shall purchase from an insurer not licensed in Texas a policy of insurance covering risks within the state in a manner other than through an insurance agent licensed in Texas, such person shall pay a tax of 5 percent of the amount of the gross premiums paid by the insured. The present action was instituted by the insured in a Texas state court to recover the taxes paid under protest. Judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed by the Court of Civil Appeals of Texas (340 SW2d 339) and an application for writ of error was refused by the Supreme Court of Texas (162 Tex 8, 343 SW2d 241).

A collective bargaining agreement between a longshoremen's union and employing stevedores provided "straight time hourly rates" for work done within a prescribed 44-hour time schedule, and "overtime hourly rates" for all work outside the straight time hours, with no differential for work in excess of 40 hours, the longshoremen working a varying and irregular number of hours throughout the work week.

It has an affiliation agreement with Parkland Memorial Hospital (Hospital), which requires the Hospital to offer vacant staff physician posts to University faculty members. Respondent, a physician of Middle Eastern descent who was both a University faculty member and a Hospital staff physician, claimed that Dr. Levine, one of his supervisors at the University, was biased against him on account of his religion and ethnic heritage. He complained to Dr. Fitz, Levine's supervisor. But after he arranged to continue working at the Hospital without also being on the University's faculty, he resigned his teaching post and sent a letter to Fitz and others, stating that he was leaving because of Levine's harassment. Fitz, upset at Levine's public humiliation and wanting public exoneration for her, objected to the Hospital's job offer, which was then withdrawn. C. ¬ß2000e-2(a), which prohibits an employer from discriminating against an employee "because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, and national origin" (referred to here as status-based discrimination). Under the Commodity Exchange Act (7 USCS 1 et seq.), any person complaining of a violation of the Act by a registered commodity futures broker may apply to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) for an order directing the broker to pay reparations to the complainant and may enforce that order in a Federal District Court (7 USCS 18). Under a regulation of the CFTC, it may adjudicate counterclaims arising out of the transaction or occurrence or series of transactions or occurrences set forth in the complaint. Certain customers of a commodity futures broker filed complaints with the CFTC against the broker and one of its employees, claiming that the customers' debit balance in their account with the broker was the result of the broker's numerous violations of the Act. Meanwhile, the broker filed suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois against these customers to recover the debit balance, which suit the customers moved to dismiss on the ground that the reparations proceedings would fully resolve all the rights of the parties. The broker voluntarily dismissed the federal court action and presented its debit balance claim by way of a counterclaim in the reparations proceeding. The administrative law judge in the reparations proceeding ruled in favor of the broker on the customers' claims and the broker's counterclaims, and when the customers for the first time challenged the CFTC's statutory authority to adjudicate the broker's counterclaim, the administrative law judge rejected the challenge, and the CFTC declined to review the decision and allowed it to become final. Prior to the car's transport to the dealer, the car had been partially repainted at the distributor's vehicle preparation center at a cost of $ 601.37, which was about 1.5 percent of the car's suggested retail price. The customer drove the car for approximately 9 months without noticing any flaws in its appearance before taking the car to an independent automobile detailing shop. The proprietor of the shop detected evidence that the car had been repainted and informed the customer. Thereafter, the customer brought an action in an Alabama trial court against the distributor and alleged that the failure to disclose that the car had been repainted constituted suppression of a material fact. At trial before a jury, the customer claimed that (1) his actual damages were $ 4,000, in that the value of one of the manufacturer's repainted cars was approximately 10 percent less than the value of a new car that had not been damaged and repaired; and (2) a punitive damages award of $ 4 million would provide an appropriate penalty, using the $ 4,000 actual damages estimate, in that since 1983, the manufacturer had sold as new 983 cars which had been repainted at a cost of more than $ 300 per vehicle, including 14 in Alabama. The petitioner, an alien who had had homosexual relations about three or four times a year for over 5 years immediately preceding his entry into the United States, was ordered deported on the ground that he was, at the time of entry, an alien "afflicted with psychopathic personality" and therefore "excludable from admission into the United States" under 212(a)(4) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952. The petitioner's appeal from the finding of a Special Inquiry Officer was dismissed by the Board of Immigration Appeals, and his petition for review was dismissed by the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, one judge dissenting. The Court of Appeals held that the term "psychopathic personality" was intended to include homosexuality, and that the term as so construed was not unconstitutional on the ground of vagueness. (363 F2d 488.)

The two petitioners were found guilty of contempt for failure to testify, after grant of immunity, before a grand jury, and were sentenced to 2 years' imprisonment, with the proviso that they would be released upon answering the questions put to them. The judgments of convictions were rendered by the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York; the conviction of the petitioner in No. 412 was affirmed by the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit (345 F2d 290), and the conviction of the petitioner in No. 442 (235 F Supp 887) was also affirmed by the same Court of Appeals (346 F2d 5).

A defendant who had pleaded guilty in the United States District Court for the Western District of Washington to one count of importation of marijuana and who was sentenced to 5 years' imprisonment and a $ 15,000 fine was subsequently indicted in the Northern District of Florida for conspiring to import marijuana, conspiring to possess marijuana with intent to distribute, using a telephone to facilitate illegal drug activities, and engaging in a continuing criminal enterprise (CCE) in violation of the Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970 (21 USCS 848). At trial, evidence of the marijuana importation which was the subject of the Washington conviction was introduced. The trial court instructed the jury that in addition to the offenses charged as substantive counts in the Florida indictment, the felony offenses of possession of marijuana with intent to distribute it, distribution of marijuana, and importation of marijuana would qualify as predicate offenses to the continuing criminal enterprise count. The Washington evidence, as well as other evidence introduced in the Florida trial, tended to prove these latter three offenses. The defendant was convicted by a jury on the continuing criminal enterprise count, the two conspiracy counts, and the telephone facilitation count. His 40 years' imprisonment on the continuing criminal enterprise count was made concurrent with the prison terms on the other counts, but consecutive to the prison terms from the Washington conviction, and the continuing criminal enterprise fine of $ 100,000 was in addition to the fine on the other counts and the Washington fine. One charged with stealing cattle was convicted in a Florida state court on six counts and sentenced to serve five years' imprisonment on each count, the terms to be be served consecutively. He unsuccessfully sought relief by various post-conviction remedies, among them a petition for habeas corpus filed in 1952, in which he alleged, among other grounds for relief, that his imprisonment was in violation of his rights under the Federal Constitution, but in which he did not allege, as he had done in previous post-conviction proceedings, that his conviction was based solely upon perjured testimony. In 1955 he instituted the present proceeding by filing, without the aid of counsel, another petition for a writ of habeas corpus in the Supreme Court of Florida. In this petition he again alleged, inter alia, that he was convicted solely on the basis of perjured testimony, coupling these allegations with a claim that his imprisonment deprived him of liberty in violation of the Federal Constitution. His petition was denied, without opinion, on the ground that he failed to show probable cause to believe that he was detained in custody without lawful authority. His application for a writ of certiorari was granted by the United States Supreme Court, but the State of Florida questioned the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court on the ground that the decision below might have rested on adequate state grounds.

A state statute requiring that, as a prerequisite to having his name appear upon the ballot, every candidate for public office must file an affidavit that he is not a subversive person, as defined in the statute, which has been construed by the highest court of the state as requiring an affidavit to the effect that the affiant is not a person who is engaged in one way or another in the attempt to overthrow the government by force and violence, and that he is not knowingly a member of an organization engaged in such an attempt, does not infringe the constitutional rights of a candidate for municipal office who is denied a place on the ballot because of his refusal to comply with the requirement.

The University of Michigan's college of literature, science, and the arts used an undergraduate admissions policy under which, beginning in 1998, an applicant could be awarded a maximum of 150 points and generally was automatically admitted if awarded at least 100 points.
