In each of these cases, an employer and employee entered into a contract providing for individualized arbitration proceedings to resolve employment disputes between the parties. Each employee nonetheless sought to litigate Fair Labor Standards Act and related state law claims through class or collective actions in federal court. Although the Federal Arbitration Act generally requires courts to enforce arbitration agreements as written, the employees argued that its ‚Äúsaving clause‚Äù removes this obligation if an arbitration agreement violates some other federal law and that, by requiring individualized proceedings, the agreements here violated the National Labor Relations Act. The employers countered that the Arbitration Act protects agreements requiring arbitration from judicial interference and that neither the saving clause nor the NLRA demands a different conclusion. Until recently, courts as well as the National Labor Relations Board's general counsel agreed that such arbitration agreements are enforceable. In 2012, however, the Board ruled that the NLRA effectively nullifies the Arbitration Act in cases like these, and since then other courts have either agreed with or deferred to the Board's position.

The Education of the Handicapped Act (EHA) (20 USCS 1400 et seq.), which provides federal financial assistance to states that provide a "free appropriate public education" for all disabled children, requires that the parents or guardians of a disabled child be given an opportunity for an impartial hearing with respect to any complaints they may have concerning the child's educational placement (20 USCS 1415(b)(2)), and the right to seek administrative review of any decisions they think inappropriate (20 USCS 1415(c)). If that review proves unsatisfactory, either the parents or the local school authorities may file a civil action in any state court of competent jurisdiction or in a Federal District Court (20 USCS 1415(e)(2)). A "stay-put" provision (20 USCS 1415(e)(3)) directs that the child shall remain in his or her then current educational placement pending completion of any review proceedings unless the parents and state or local education agencies otherwise agree. In 1980, two emotionally disturbed students were suspended indefinitely from San Francisco public schools for violent and disruptive conduct related to their disabilities, pending the completion of expulsion proceedings. After unsuccessfully protesting the action against him, one of the students brought suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, seeking injunctive relief against local school officials and the state superintendent of public instruction. The other student obtained leave to intervene in the suit. The District Court (1) found that the suspensions and proposed expulsions deprived the students of their rights under the EHA, (2) permanently enjoined the school district from taking any disciplinary action other than a 2-day or 5-day suspension against any dis

Shortly after being hired as a research sociologist by a state hospital, the plaintiff was discharged because of her refusal to subscribe to the Massachusetts statutory loyalty oath requiring public employees to swear or affirm, upon the penalty of perjury, to "uphold and defend" the federal and state constitutions, and to "oppose the overthrow" of the federal or state government "by force, violence, or by any illegal or unconstitutional method." The plaintiff filed a complaint alleging the unconstitutionality of the statute and seeking an injunction and damages in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, which, sitting as a three- judge panel, granted the injunction, holding that although the "uphold and defend" clause of the oath was constitutional, nevertheless the "oppose the overthrow" clause was fatally vague and constituted a violation of First Amendment rights (300 F Supp 1321). On appeal by the Commonwealth, the United States Supreme Court remanded for consideration of whether the case was moot in light of a suggestion that the plaintiff's job had been filled in the interim (397 US 238, 25 L Ed 2d 275, 90 S Ct 1099), and the District Court, on remand, concluded that the case was not moot and reinstated its earlier judgment.

A corporation filed a request with the Federal Trade Commission for disclosure of documents concerning the investigation of a subsidiary corporation. The Commission had investigated the subsidiary in connection with a civil penalty action but the suit had been dismissed with prejudice. The Commission refused to release some documents on the basis that they were exempt from mandatory disclosure under Exemption 5 of the Freedom of Information Act (5 USCS 552(b)(5)), which exempts from disclosure interagency or intraagency memorandums or letters which would not be available by law to a party in litigation with the agency. The United States District Court for the District of Columbia held that all the requested documents were exempt from disclosure under Exemption 5. The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit held that four documents could not be withheld unless the Commission could show that litigation related to the terminated action existed or potentially existed (671 F2d 553).

A grand jury indicted a company and two company officers on two counts of conspiracy to defraud the United States and nine counts of tax fraud. The defendants each pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to defraud the government, and all other counts were dismissed. Thereafter, the government moved for disclosure of all grand jury materials to attorneys in the Justice Department's Civil Division, their paralegal and secretarial assistants, and certain Defense Department experts, for use in preparing and conducting a possible civil suit against the defendants under the False Claims Act (31 USCS 231 et seq.) The officers and company opposed the disclosure and made an allegation of grand jury misuse for civil purposes. The United States District Court for the Southern District of California granted the requested disclosure. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that Civil Division attorneys could obtain disclosure only by showing particularized need under Rule 6(e)(3)(C)(i) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure and that the District Court had not applied a correct standard of particularized need (642 F2d 1184).

In No. 11, the patentee and a licensee under a patent on a clamp for vibrating shank plows brought a patent infringement suit in the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri. The District Court found the patent valid and infringed (216 F Supp 272), but the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed. (333 F2d 529.) In Nos. 37 and 43, consolidated actions brought in the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri for judgments declaring invalid a patent on a plastic finger sprayer with a hold-down overcap, the patent was sustained by the District Court (220 F Supp 414), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed. (336 F2d 110.)

A railroad employee met an unwitnessed death at the defendant railroad's yard near cars which he was going to adjust when last seen, and with which other cars collided, after having broken loose, as the result of the breaking of a coupler, from a cut of cars that was being moved in a switching operation.

A railroad which had condemned Iowa land for railroad use, pursuant to a state statute permitting such condemnation, filed a complaint in a federal District Court, alleging diversity of citizenship, and seeking to have the assessment of damages resulting from the condemnation reduced. The railroad also filed an appeal from the assessment in a state court (the Iowa condemnation statute providing for state court review of such assessments), and then filed a petition to remove the cause to the federal District Court. The landowner moved to dismiss the railroad's original complaint, and to remand the case removed.

A seaman filed suit against a shipowner in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, based on a claim that while working on the defendant's ship, he suffered a head injury which resulted in an ear disorder, the complaint including a count for maintenance and cure. The shipowner's medical witness, whose testimony at the trial was the only medical diagnosis as to when the ear disorder became permanent and not susceptible to curative treatment, conceded that the seaman's head injury could have caused the ear disorder, but also said that the disorder was not a condition that could be cured by treatment. After the jury awarded the seaman an amount for maintenance and cure, the shipowner moved for judgment notwithstanding the verdict on the ground that the award was not within the permissible scope of maintenance and cure. The District Court denied the motion, holding that maintenance and cure, although not available for a sickness declared to be permanent, continued until such time as the incapacity was declared to be permanent. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, in an unpublished opinion (see 495 F2d 1374), reversed as to the maintenance and cure point, holding that once the seaman reached maximum medical recovery the shipowner's obligation to provide maintenance and cure ceased, and that since the record did not permit an inference other than that the seaman's condition was permanent immediately after the accident, the District Court's holding impermissibly extended the shipowner's obligation.

A corporation which proposed to lease a building for the operation of a group home for the mentally retarded filed suit in a Federal District Court, alleging that a city zoning ordinance requiring a special use permit for the operation of a group home for the mentally retarded was invalid on its face and as applied because it discriminated against the mentally retarded in violation of the equal protection clause. The District Court held the ordinance and its application constitutional. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed, holding that mental retardation is a quasi-suspect classification, that under the applicable "heightened scrutiny" standard of review, the ordinance was invalid on its face because it did not substantially further any important governmental interests, and that the ordinance was also invalid as applied (726 F2d 191).

The National Labor Relations Board adopted a finding of its trial examiner that employers committed unfair labor practices under 8(a) (2) of the amended National Labor Relations Act--the provision barring employer domination of labor organizations--when they dealt with employee committees, established by the employers to represent nonunion employees, with respect to matters, covering nearly the whole scope of the employment relationship, commonly considered and dealt with in collective bargaining. (17 NLRB 1633.) The employers petitioned the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit to review and vacate the Board's findings and order; the Board's answer sought enforcement. The Court of Appeals set aside the Board's order, finding that the employers dominated the employee committees but holding that the committees were not "labor organizations" as that term is defined in 2(5) of the amended National Labor Relations Act; the Court of Appeals held, further, that 9(a) of the Act, as amended in 1947, in effect excluded such employee committees from the statutory definition of "labor organizations." (256 F2d 281.)

Pennsylvania levied an annual property tax on the total value of freight cars owned by a Pennsylvania corporation authorized to operate a railroad only within the state, although some of its cars were run on fixed routes and regular schedules over the lines of its parent corporation in New Jersey and other cars were run regularly, habitually, and/or continuously on the lines of other railroads outside Pennsylvania, although not on fixed schedules. This application of the tax was upheld by the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania, as against contentions that it violated the commerce clause and the due process and equal protection clauses of the United States Constitution. (403 Pa 419, 169 A2d 878.)

One section of a city's licensing ordinance governing coin-operated amusement establishments required the city's chief of police to consider whether a license applicant had any "connection with criminal elements," while another section prohibited a licensee from allowing children under 17 years of age to operate the amusement devices unless accompanied by a parent or a legal guardian. After a corporation proposed to open an amusement center, the city exempted from the prohibition against operation of amusement devices by unattended children certain amusement centers,--the features of which were defined in terms of the corporation's rules--as long as children under the age of seven were accompanied by an adult. However, the corporation's application for a license was refused because the chief of police concluded that the corporation's parent corporation was connected with criminal elements. After the corporation successfully brought suit in a Texas state court challenging the ordinance and obtained an injunction requiring the city to issue it a license, the city adopted a new ordinance repealing the corporation's exemption and reinstating the 17-year age requirement, while defining the term "connected with criminal elements" in some detail. The Corporation commenced an action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, seeking an injunction against enforcement of the new ordinance. The District Court ruled that the language "connected with criminal elements," even as defined, was unconstitutionally vague, but upheld the age restriction (434 F Supp 473). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the former holding and reversed the latter (630 F2d 1029).

Under 28 USCS 2244, as amended by the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA), (1) 28 USCS 2244(d)(1) generally applies a 1-year limitation period to a federal habeas corpus application by a person in custody pursuant to the judgment of a state court, and (2) 28 USCS 2244(d)(2) provides that the time during which a properly filed application for "State post-conviction or other collateral review" with respect to the pertinent judgment or claim is pending shall not be counted toward any period of limitation under 28 USCS 2244(d). Before AEDPA's April 24, 1996, effective date, an accused's state robbery conviction became final. The accused filed a habeas corpus petition in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York. The District Court dismissed the petition without prejudice, on the basis that it was not apparent that the accused had exhausted available state remedies. On May 20, 1997, without having returned to state court, the accused filed a second federal habeas corpus petition. The District Court dismissed the accused's second petition on the basis that the accused had not filed the petition within a reasonable time from AEDPA's effective date. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed the District Court's dismissal of the petition and expressed the view that (1) the accused's first federal habeas corpus petition was an application for "other collateral review," within the meaning of 2244(d)(2), and (2) the first filing therefore tolled the limitation period and made the accused's second federal habeas corpus petition timely (208 F3d 357).

In each of these cases, an employer allegedly fired a long-time employee simply for being homosexual or transgender. Clayton County, Geor- gia, fired Gerald Bostock for conduct “unbecoming” a county employee shortly after he began participating in a gay recreational softball league. Altitude Express fired Donald Zarda days after he mentioned being gay. And R. G. & G. R. Harris Funeral Homes fired Aimee Ste- phens, who presented as a male when she was hired, after she in- formed her employer that she planned to “live and work full-time as a woman.” Each employee sued, alleging sex discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The Eleventh Circuit held that Title VII does not prohibit employers from firing employees for being gay and so Mr. Bostock’s suit could be dismissed as a matter of law. The Second and Sixth Circuits, however, allowed the claims of Mr. Zarda and Ms. Stephens, respectively, to proceed. Held: An employer who fires an individual merely for being gay or transgender violates Title VII. Pp. 4–33.

A class action was filed in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia by three individuals and a nonprofit corporation whose purpose was to make equal opportunity in housing a reality in the Richmond, Virginia metropolitan area against the owners of an apartment complex and one of its employees, alleging that the defendants engaged in "racial steering" violative of 804 of the Fair Housing Act of 1968 (42 USCS 3604) and seeking declaratory, injunctive, and monetary relief. One of the individuals was a black "renter" who, attempting to rent an apartment from the owners, inquired about the availability of an apartment at the complex and was falsely told that no apartments were available. The other two individuals were "testers"--individuals who, without an intent to rent or purchase a home or apartment, pose as renters or purchasers for the purpose of collecting evidence of unlawful steering practices--who were employed by the organization to determine whether the owners practice racial steering. One of the testers was black and on four separate occasions on which she made inquiries as to the availability of apartments was told that no apartments were available, while the other tester was white and was told that there were vacancies. The three individual plaintiffs were all residents of Richmond or the adjacent Henrico County in which the complex was located, and they averred that they had been injured by the discriminatory acts of the defendants, the renter claiming that he had been denied the right to rent real property in Henrico County, he and the two tester plaintiffs alleging that the owners' practices deprived them of the important social, professional, business and economic, political and aesthetic benefits of interacial associations tha

In a suit by the Wage-Hour Administrator to enjoin alleged violations of the overtime compensation requirement of _ 7 of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the evidence summarized in the opinion held adequate to support a finding by the district court that certain "operating engineers" who had charge of a power plant in the absence of the chief engineer, supervised the work of firemen and coal passers, received monthly salaries in excess of $ 200, and enjoyed privileges usually reserved for supervisory employees, were exempted by _ 13 (a) as employees employed in an "executive" capacity.

The petition for writ of certiorari is granted, the judgments are vacated and the case is remanded to the Supreme Court of Appeals of Virginia for reconsideration in light of Peterson v. City of Greenville, 373 U.S. 244: The petitioners, 10 Negroes, remained seated at the lunch counter of a store even though the manager, in the presence of the police, announced "that the lunch counter was being closed and would everyone leave" the area. The manager asked petitioners to leave because integrated service was not only contrary to local customs but also in violation of a city ordinance requiring separation of the races in restaurants. The petitioners were convicted in the Recorder's Court of the City of Greenville, South Carolina, for violating the state trespass statute. An appeal to the Greenville County Court was dismissed, and the Supreme Court of South Carolina affirmed. (239 SC 298, 122 SE2d 826.)

Certain Michigan taxpayers instituted an action in the United States District Court for the Western District of Michigan challenging the constitutionality, under the establishment clause of the First Amendment, of two programs adopted by a public school district under which supplementary classes for students in various nonpublic schools, primarily sectarian, were financed by the public school system, taught by teachers hired by the public school system, and conducted in classrooms in the nonpublic schools which were "leased" by the public schools and bore signs identifying them as public school classrooms while the classes were in session. Under the Shared Time program, the teachers of these classes were full-time public school employees, about 10 percent of whom had previously taught in nonpublic schools, often those in which they conducted classes under the program; while under the Community Education program, classes were conducted by part-time public school employees, practically all of whom were otherwise employed full time by the nonpublic schools involved. The District Court held that both programs violated the establishment clause (546 F Supp 1071). The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed (718 F2d 1389).

A complaint in an action brought by the government against a Chicago trade association of plastering contractors, a local labor union of plasterers, and the union's president for violation of 1 of the Sherman Anti-trust Act, which forbids combinations or conspiracies in restraint of interstate trade or commerce, states a cause of action where it is alleged in the complaint that the defendants did approximately 60 per cent of the plastering contracting business in the Chicago area, that substantial quantities of the materials used and furnished by the contractors were produced in other states and shipped into Illinois, that there was a continuous and almost uninterrupted flow of plastering materials from out-of-state origins to Illinois job sites for use there by plastering contractors, that restraint or disruption of plastering work in the Chicago area necessarily affected this interstate flow of plastering materials adversely, and that for years the defendants had acted in concert to suppress competition among local plastering contractors, to prevent out-of-state contractors from doing any business in the Chicago area, and to bar entry of new local contractors without approval by a private examining board set up by the union, and that the effect of all this was an unlawful and unreasonable restraint of the flow in interstate commerce of materials used in the Chicago plastering industry.

In the present action brought against the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act plaintiffs sought to recover for damages allegedly caused through the negligence of the Coast Guard in permitting the light of a lighthouse operated by it on an island within the boundaries of Louisiana to become extinguished and not repairing the light nor giving warning that it was not functioning. The issue was whether governmental activities of the kind involved in the present case were within the scope of the act, which provides (28 USC 2674) that the United States shall be liable "in the same manner and to the same extent as a private individual under like circumstances."

Respondent Monsanto invented and patented Roundup Ready soybean seeds, which contain a genetic alteration that allows them to survive exposure to the herbicide glyphosate. It sells the seeds subject to a licensing agreement that permits farmers to plant the purchased seed in one, and only one, growing season. Growers may consume or sell the resulting crops, but may not save any of the harvested soybeans for replanting. Petitioner Bowman purchased Roundup Ready soybean seed for his first crop of each growing season from a company associated with Monsanto and followed the terms of the licensing agreement. But to reduce costs for his riskier late-season planting, Bowman purchased soybeans intended for consumption from a grain elevator; planted them; treated the plants with glyphosate, killing all plants without the Roundup Ready trait; harvested the resulting soybeans that contained that trait; and saved some of these harvested seeds to use in his late-season planting the next season. After discovering this practice, Monsanto sued Bowman for patent infringement. Bowman raised the defense of patent exhaustion, which gives the purchaser of a patented article, or any subsequent owner, the right to use or resell that article. The District Court rejected Bowman's defense and the Federal Circuit affirmed.

In criminal proceedings in the Oklahoma courts, petitioner was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. Thereafter, he pleaded guilty to a charge of kidnaping the murder victim and was sentenced to death by the District Court of Tulsa County, Oklahoma. On appeal, the Criminal Court of Appeals of Oklahoma affirmed ((Okla Crim) 321 P2d 990).

A probationary federal employee, who had been notified that she would be discharged on a specified date, filed an administrative appeal with the Civil Service Commission after the employing agency had rejected her contention that regulations governing notice to the employee when discharge was based on pre-employment conditions were applicable and should have been followed by the employing agency. While the administrative appeal was pending, the employee instituted an action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia seeking a temporary restraining order and interim injunctive relief against her removal from employment pending determination of her administrative appeal. The District Court granted a temporary restraining order pending a hearing on the temporary injunction, and when the government refused to produce the discharging officer to testify as to the grounds for the employee's prospective discharge, continued the restraining order indefinitely, until the witness was produced. Thereupon, the government appealed to the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which affirmed the District Court's injunctive order (149 App DC 256, 462 F2d 871).

The United States Attorney General instituted an action against the Hazelwood, Missouri, School District and certain of its officials in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, alleging that the defendants had engaged in a "pattern or practice" of discrimination against Negroes in hiring teachers, in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e et seq.). The District Court entered judgment for the defendants, finding that the government's statistical evidence, showing that relatively small numbers of Negro teachers were employed by the school district, was nonprobative upon comparing the percentage of Negro teachers to the percentage of Negro pupils in the district, and ruling that the government's evidence failed to establish a pattern or practice of discrimination (392 F Supp 1276). The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed, holding that (1) the statistical comparison should have been made between the racial composition of the school district's teaching staff and the racial composition of the qualified public school teacher population in the relevant labor market, and (2) in accordance with the government's contention, the relevant labor market area included the nearby city of St. Louis as well as the county in which the defendant school district was located, notwithstanding the defendants' contention that statistical comparisons would be distorted by including St. Louis because of its special attempts to maintain a 50% Negro teaching staff--the Court of Appeals directing judgment for the government (534 F2d 805).

Canadian railroads transporting asbestos from the Province of Quebec to points in Vermont joined with American railroads, which transported the asbestos from there to other points in the United States, in the publication of joint through rates available to consignees in the northeastern United States, which were substantially lower than the combination through rates available to consignees in the southern United States. After hearings, the Interstate Commerce Commission found that the higher combination rates to complainants in the South were violative of 49 USC 1(5) and 3(1), and directed railroads engaged in transportation within the United States to cease participation in this transportation practice. (303 ICC 743.) A three-judge United States District Court for the District of Vermont set aside the Commission's order. (182 F Supp 516.)

The United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas denied a petition for habeas corpus relief by an accused who had been convicted by a Texas state court and sentenced to death for the capital murder of a peace officer. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the District Court's judgment denying habeas corpus relief (823 F2d 845). Subsequently, the accused's execution was rescheduled, and the District Court granted the accused a stay of execution, but the Court of Appeals vacated the stay of execution (842 F2d 95). The United States Supreme Court granted a stay of the accused's execution pending the Supreme Court's disposition of the accused's petition for a writ of certiorari (485 US 983, 99 L Ed 2d 494, 108 S Ct 1283). After the Supreme Court's decision in Penry v Lynaugh (1989) 492 US 302, 106 L Ed 2d 256, 109 S Ct 2934, wherein the court held that, in the absence of instructions informing a jury in a Texas state court that it could consider certain mitigating evidence in sentencing a person who had been convicted of capital murder, the imposition of a death sentence under the Texas capital sentencing procedure violated the prohibition, under the Federal Constitution's Eighth Amendment, of cruel and unusual punishment, the Supreme Court granted the accused's petition for a writ of certiorari limited to the question whether, at the time the accused was tried, there was cause for not raising a claim based upon arguments later accepted in Penry v Lynaugh, supra, and, if not, whether the application of a procedural bar to the claim would result in a fundamental miscarriage of justice (493 US 888, 107 L Ed 2d 182, 110 S Ct 231).

This case presented the question whether prejudgment interest should ordinarily be awarded in a patent infringement suit under 35 USCS 284. In an action in the United States District Court for the District of Delaware, instituted by a patent owner against an alleged infringer, the District Court ultimately entered judgment for the patent owner, holding that the owner was entitled to damages including prejudgment interest. The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed (667 F2d 347).

A road contracting company was engaged in the repair of roads, railroads, and similar facilities within the state of Pennsylvania. It also manufactured a road surfacing mixture at its plants, which was used, either by it or its customers, in repair work on roads and railroads serving interstate commerce. All the material was produced in Pennsylvania for use exclusively within that state, and none of it was shipped across state lines. It was the contention of the Wage and Hour Administrator that the company's "off-the-road" plant employees, engaged in the production of the road materials, were within 7(a) of the Fair Labor Standards Act covering employees engaged "in the production of goods for commerce."

An accused who had three prior felony convictions--a Pennsylvania state court conviction for robbery, and Maryland state court convictions for burglary and attempted burglary--was convicted in the United States District Court for the District of Maryland of possession of a firearm by a convicted felon in violation of 18 USCS 922(g)(1). The Federal Government moved, based on the state convictions, to have the accused's firearms possession sentence enhanced under the Armed Career Criminal Act (18 USCS 924(e)), which raised the penalty for possession of a firearm by a felon from a maximum of 10 years in prison to a mandatory minimum sentence of 15 years and a maximum of life in prison without parole if the accused had three previous convictions for a violent felony. The accused argued that he had received ineffective assistance of counsel in the two Maryland cases, and that therefore, the convictions in those cases could not be used for sentence enhancement. The District Court--expressing the view that (1) 924(e) provided no statutory right to challenge prior convictions relied upon by the government for sentence enhancement, and (2) the Federal Constitution barred the use of a prior conviction for sentence enhancement only when there was a complete denial of counsel in the prior proceeding--sentenced the accused to 235 months in prison (786 F Supp 533). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, expressing the view that the accused's challenges to his prior convictions were the fact-intensive type that posed a risk of unduly delaying and protracting the entire sentencing process, affirmed the District Court judgment (988 F2d 1355).

The Sixth Circuit did not apply the appropriate standard of review under AEDPA. A "fairminded jurist" could conclude that repetition of the tip did not establish that the uncontested facts it conveyed were submitted for their truth. Such a jurist might reach that conclusion by placing weight on the fact that the truth of the facts was not disputed. No precedent of this Court clearly forecloses that view. It is also not beyond the realm of possibility that a fairminded jurist could conclude that Etherton was not prejudiced when the tip and Pollie's testimony corresponded on uncontested facts. After all, Pollie himself was privy to all the information contained in the tip. A reasonable judge might accordingly regard the fact that the tip and Pollie's testimony corresponded to be unremarkable and not pertinent to Pollie's credibility. (In fact, the only point of Pollie's testimony actually reflected in the tip was that he and Etherton were traveling between Detroit and Grand Rapids.) Etherton's underlying complaint is that his appellate lawyer's ineffectiveness meant he had "no prior opportunity to cross-examine the anonymous tipster." Brief in Opposition 11. But it would not be objectively unreasonable for a fairminded judge to conclude-especially in light of the deference afforded trial counsel under Stricklandthat the failure to raise such a claim was not due to incompetence but because the facts in the tip were uncontested and in any event consistent with Etherton's defense. See Harrington, 562 U. S., at 105 ("Even under de novo review, the standard for judging counsel's representation is a most deferential one."). A fairminded jurist could similarly conclude, again deferring under Strickland, that appellate counsel was not incompetent in drawing the same conclusion. A

Under California's three strikes law, a defendant who is convicted of a felony and has previously been convicted of two or more serious or violent felonies must receive an indeterminate life imprisonment term. Such a defendant becomes eligible for parole on a date calculated by reference to a minimum term, which, in this case, is 25 years. While on parole, petitioner Ewing was convicted of felony grand theft for stealing three golf clubs, worth $ 399 apiece. As required by the three strikes law, the prosecutor formally alleged, and the trial court found, that Ewing had been convicted previously of four serious or violent felonies. In sentencing him to 25 years to life, the court refused to exercise its discretion to reduce the conviction to a misdemeanor -- under a state law that permits certain offenses, known as "wobblers," to be classified as either misdemeanors or felonies -- or to dismiss the allegations of some or all of his prior relevant convictions. The State Court of Appeal affirmed. Relying on Rummel v. Estelle, 445 U.S. 263, 63 L. Ed. 2d 382, 100 S. Ct. 1133, it rejected Ewing's claim that his sentence was grossly disproportionate under the Eighth Amendment and reasoned that enhanced sentences under the three strikes law served the State's legitimate goal of deterring and incapacitating repeat offenders. The State Supreme Court denied review.

A former state employee filed suit under 42 USCS 1983 against state officials, alleging that the officials had violated the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by discharging the employee without a formal pretermination or a prompt posttermination hearing. The United States District Court for the Northern District of Florida granted the requested relief, ultimately holding that the state officials had forfeited their qualified immunity from suit under 1983 by not following state administrative regulations in discharging the employee. The United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit affirmed (710 F2d 838).

While a railroad employee's action against his employer, alleging wrongful discharge and denial of a fair hearing, was pending in a Utah state court, the United States Supreme Court decided Andrews v Louisville & Nashville R. Co. (1972) 406 US 320, 32 L Ed 2d 95, 92 S Ct 1562, holding that a railroad employee alleging a violation of a collective bargaining agreement must submit such a dispute to the National Railroad Adjustment Board for resolution in accordance with the provisions of the Railway Labor Act (45 USCS 151-188). By stipulation of the parties, the state court action was dismissed, and the employee instituted a proceeding before the Adjustment Board. The Board dismissed the employee's action for failure to comply with the time limits prescribed by the collective bargaining agreement, holding that the agreement's time requirements were not tolled during the pendency of the state court action. The employee then instituted an action in the United States District Court for the District of Utah, seeking an order directing the Board to hear the merits of his case, but the District Court affirmed the Board's order and held that the employee had failed to establish any of the grounds for reversal of Board orders specified in the Act (45 USCS 153 First (q)) (423 F Supp 324). The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed, remanding the case to the Board (576 F2d 854).

In a suit in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee by the trustee of a union welfare and retirement fund against a coal company for failure to make royalty payments under a national agreement, the coal company filed a cross claim against the union for alleged conspiracy in violation of the antitrust laws, partly by agreeing with the larger coal companies to impose the terms of the agreement on all coal operators, regardless of their ability to pay. After a jury verdict against the union, the court overruled the union's motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict or in the alternative for a new trial. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed. (325 F2d 804.)

In Green v County School Board (1968) 391 US 430, 20 L Ed 2d 716, 88 S Ct 1689, the United States Supreme Court held that (1) the time for "deliberate speed" in eliminating de jure school segregation had run out; (2) the obligation of schools once segregated by law was to come forward with a plan that promised to work realistically "now"; and (3) student assignments, faculty, staff, transportation, extracurricular activities, and physical facilities had to be free from racial discrimination. Shortly thereafter, black schoolchildren and their parents instituted a class action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia for the desegregation of a Georgia county school system which had once been segregated by law. The school system voluntarily began working with the Federal Government to devise a comprehensive desegregation plan, and the District Court in June 1969 entered a consent order approving the proposed plan. For the next 17 years, judicial intervention into the affairs of the school system was limited and infrequent, but demographic changes occurred, including (1) an increase in the overall proportion of black students from 5.6 percent to 47 percent, and (2) a shift in residential patterns, so that the population of the northern half of the county became predominantly white, and the southern half became predominantly black. In 1986, school officials, seeking a declaration that the school system had satisfied its duty and had achieved unitary status, filed a motion for final dismissal. After a federal grand jury indicted two defendants for drug-related offenses and conspiracy, the prosecutor successfully sought a superseding indictment expanding the conspiracy charge, presenting in support of that indictment the testimony of two law enforcement agents who were sworn together and testified in tandem before the grand jury. The defendants did not learn about this joint testimony until their trial before the United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia had already begun, although they had diligently searched for error and the prosecution apparently had not deliberately concealed the event. They then moved to dismiss the indictment, contending that the simultaneous presence of the two agents had violated Rule 6(d) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure; but the District Court took the motion under advisement until after the petit jury had returned a guilty verdict, and then denied it, holding that Rule 6(d) had been violated but that the error was harmless as to all counts of the indictment. A panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed and remanded with regard to the conspiracy counts and directed that that portion of the indictment be dismissed, holding that the Rule 6(d) violation invalidated the superseding indictment, but affirmed as to the other counts which had simply been incorporated from the original indictment (735 F2d 136). This decision was upheld by the Court of Appeals after rehearing en banc (756 F2d 994).

Under California law, (1) a defendant convicted of first-degree murder was eligible for the death penalty if the jury found one of the "special circumstances" listed in a statute to be true; (2) if the jury found the existence of one of the special circumstances, then the jury was instructed to take into account another statute's separate list of sentencing factors, describing aspects of the defendant and the crime; and (3) this second list's factors included (a) the circumstances of the crime of which the defendant was convicted, and (b) the existence of any special circumstances (eligibility factors) found to be true. In a California capital trial, an accused was convicted on charges of first-degree murder of one person, attempted murder of another person, robbery, burglary, and attempted robbery. The jury (1) found four special circumstances from the first statutory list; and (2) then, in the penalty phase--at which the jury was instructed to consider the second list's factors--sentenced the accused to death.

The State of New York submitted its 1972 reapportionment plan for certain counties to the United States Attorney General under 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (42 USCS 1973c), but the Attorney General concluded that as to certain state legislature districts in Kings County, the state had failed to demonstrate under 5 that the redistricting had neither the purpose nor the effect of abridging the right to vote by reason of race or color. Thereafter, the state submitted a revised plan which did not change the number of districts with nonwhite majorities, but which changed the size of nonwhite majorities in most of such districts. Under the revised plan, a community of Hasidic Jews that had been previously located in a single assembly district with a 61% nonwhite majority and a single senate district with only 37% nonwhites, was divided between different election districts having 65% nonwhite majorities--the state having concluded that a 65% nonwhite majority was necessary to obtain the Attorney General's approval as to such districts. Shortly after the revised redistricting plan had been submitted to the Attorney General, an action on behalf of the Hasidic Jewish community was instituted in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York, the plaintiffs alleging that the state's use of racial criteria and quotas in developing the revised reapportionment plan violated the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendment rights of the members of the Jewish community. The District Court dismissed the complaint (377 F Supp 1164), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed (510 F2d 512).

A citizen brought suit against the city of Memphis, its police department, and various individuals, alleging that the constitutional rights of his deceased son had been violated when a police officer shot the youth in order to prevent his escape from the scene of a burglary, even though he did not appear to be armed. The United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee dismissed the complaint, ruling that the officer's actions were authorized by a Tennessee statute which allowed the police to use all necessary means to effect an arrest where a suspect fled or forcibly resisted after being notified of the intent to arrest, and that this statute was constitutional. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed and remanded, holding that the statute violated the Fourth Amendment (710 F2d 240).

The plaintiff, appointed a member of the War Claims Commission to serve during the life of the Commission, was removed by the President of the United States on the ground that the President regarded it as in the national interest to complete the administration of the War Claims Act with personnel of his own selection. Thereupon the plaintiff brought the present action in the United States Court of Claims for recovery of his salary as a War Claims Commissioner from the day of his removal to the last day of the Commission's existence. A divided Court of Claims dismissed the petition (135 Ct Cl 827, 142 F Supp 910).

The United States District Court for the Northern District of California dismissed, for failure to state a claim warranting relief, a complaint by 16 individuals seeking intervention on their own behalf and on behalf of all persons similarly situated in a pending employment discrimination action, which was in the process of settlement by the original parties. The District Court had not certified a class at the time of the dismissal. A notice of appeal of the dismissal was filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, but, due to a clerical error by a secretary employed by an attorney, omitted one individual's name. The Court of Appeals reversed and remanded the case to the District Court for further proceedings, in an order which also omitted the individual's name. On remand, the opposing party moved for partial summary judgment against the individual whose name had been omitted, on the ground that the District Court's prior judgment of dismissal was final as to the individual by virtue of his failure to appeal. The District Court granted the motion, but left open the question whether the individual could participate in the litigation as a member of a class, should a class be properly certified, and the Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that unless a party is named in the notice of appeal, a federal appellate court does not have jurisdiction over him, pursuant to Rule 3(c) of the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure (807 F2d 178).

The accused was sentenced by a California court in 1980 to a prison term of 15 years to life for the killing of his wife, but became eligible for parole in 1990. After a parole suitability hearing was held in 1989, the California board of prison terms determined that the accused was not suitable for parole for several reasons, including the facts that he had previously been convicted of murder and had killed his wife while on parole from his prior incarceration. Under the law in place at the time of the 1980 killing, the accused would have been entitled to subsequent suitability hearings on an annual basis. However, in 1981, the California Legislature amended the law, authorizing the deferral of subsequent suitability hearings for up to 3 years if a prisoner had been convicted of more than one offense involving the taking of life and if the board (1) found that it was not reasonable to expect that parole would be granted at a hearing during the following years, and (2) stated the bases for its finding. The board accordingly (1) found that the accused would not reasonably be expected to be granted parole in 1990 or 1991, and (2) scheduled the next hearing for 1992. The accused filed a petition for habeas corpus in the United States District Court for the Middle District of California, asserting that, as applied to him, the 1981 amendment violated the ex post facto clause of Art I, 10, cl 1 of the Federal Constitution. The District Court denied the habeas corpus petition, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the ex post facto clause was violated (16 F3d 1001).

Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio, and Tennessee define marriage as a union between one man and one woman. The petitioners, 14 same-sex couples and two men whose same-sex partners are deceased, filed suits in Federal District Courts in their home States, claiming that respondent state officials violate the Fourteenth Amendment by denying them the right to marry or to have marriages lawfully performed in another State given full recognition. Each District Court ruled in petitioners' favor, but the Sixth Circuit consolidated the cases and reversed.

The Texas Constitution provided a ceiling on the amount which the state could spend on welfare assistance grants, and because the constitutional ceiling was insufficient to bring each recipient up to his full standard of need under federally aided assistance programs, the state, while leaving Old Age Assistance (OAA) at 100 percent of the full standard of need, reduced Aid to the Blind (AB) and Aid for Permanently and Totally Disabled (APTD) by 5 percent of the full standard of need, and reduced Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) by 25 percent of the full standard of need. About 87 percent of the recipients of AFDC were Negroes and Mexican-Americans, whereas a substantially smaller percentage of the recipients of OAA, AB, and APTD were Negroes and Mexican-Americans. Under the Texas system of computing AFDC benefits, the 25 percent reduction was subtracted from the standard of need before an AFDC recipient's outside income was subtracted. This method of computation resulted in many AFDC recipients receiving smaller benefits than they would have received if their outside income were subtracted from the standard of need before subtracting the 25 percent reduction. In the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, various Texas recipients of AFDC brought class actions seeking injunctive and declaratory relief against the Texas system of computing AFDC benefits. A three-judge District Court denied relief, holding that neither the Social Security Act nor the Fourteenth Amendment was violated.

The issue in the present case concerned the validity of a regulation, issued by a Colorado stockyard company under the Packers and Stockyards Act of 1921, which prohibited any market agency engaged in business at the stockyard from soliciting business for, or diverting it to, other markets with which the agency was registered. The validity of this regulation was challenged by a market agency which was registered not only with the Colorado stockyard company but also with other stockyards. The market agency filed a complaint with the Secretary of Agriculture, but did not offer any evidence as to the unreasonableness of the regulation, and its complaint was dismissed by the Judicial Officer (15 Agr Dec 638). On the agency's petition for review, the Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed the decision of the Judicial Officer (241 F2d 192), holding that the regulation was void on its face.

And in answering that question the Court was not bound by the state court's interpretation of a similar -- or even identical -- state statute. Even by itself, the word "violent" in ¬¨√ü 924(e)(2)(B) connoted a substantial degree of force. When the adjective "violent" was attached to the noun "felony," its connotation of strong physical force was even clearer. The court declined to remand the case for consideration under the so-called "residual clause" in ¬¨√ü 924(e)(2)(B)(ii) because the Government had disclaimed at sentencing any reliance upon the residual clause.

Plaintiffs-appellees are the parents and minor children of Vermont families whose state welfare assistance was terminated, or whose applications for such assistance were rejected, pursuant to a state welfare regulation because the fathers were receiving unemployment compensation. The plaintiffs filed a class action in the United States District Court for the District of Vermont against the Commissioner of the Vermont Department of Social Services and the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare to enjoin the enforcement of (1) 407(b)(2) (C)(ii) of the Social Security Act (42 USCS 607(b)(2)(C)(ii)), under which the definition of "dependent child" as including a needy child deprived of parental support by reason of the father's unemployment is applicable if a state plan under the Act's Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) program denies aid to a dependent child so defined "with respect to any week for which such child's father receives unemployment compensation," and (2) the Vermont welfare regulation which, insofar as relevant, defines an "unemployed father" as one who is not receiving unemployment compensation during the same week as assistance is granted. A professional for-profit fundraiser sued the Maryland Secretary of State in the Circuit Court for Anne Arundel County, Maryland, alleging an unconstitutional infringement on its right to free speech and assembly under the First and Fourteenth Amendments by a Maryland statute prohibiting a charitable organization, in connection with any fundraising activity, from paying or agreeing to pay as expenses more than 25 percent of the amount raised, but authorizing a waiver of the percentage limitation where the 25 percent limitation would effectively prevent a charitable organization from raising contributions. The fundraiser alleged that it regularly charged a Maryland customer more than 25 percent of the gross raised for an event it promoted, and that the Maryland Secretary of State informed it that it would be prosecuted if it failed to comply with the statute. The Circuit Court upheld the statute on the merits and the Maryland Court of Special Appeals affirmed (48 Md App 273, 426 A2d 985), but the Maryland Court of Appeals reversed on the ground that the statute was unconstitutional (294 Md 160, 448 A2d 935).

The National Labor Relations Board petitioned the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit for enforcement of orders for reinstatement of employees allegedly discharged or laid off in violation of 8(a) (1) and (3) of the Labor Management Relations Act (29 USC 158(a) (1) and (3)). The petitions were denied. (286 F2d 16; 288 F2d 630.)

In Stone v Powell (1976) 428 US 465, 49 L Ed 2d 1067, 96 S Ct 3037, it was held that, when a state has given a full and fair chance to litigate a claim under the Federal Constitution's Fourth Amendment, federal habeas corpus review is not available to a state prisoner who alleges that his or her conviction rests on evidence obtained through an unconstitutional search and seizure. Police officers investigating a double murder in Michigan brought a suspect to a police station for questioning. When the suspect denied any involvement in the murders, an officer told him that he could either give them the truth or they would charge him and lock him up. The suspect then admitted furnishing the murder weapon to the killer, who had called the suspect after the crime and told him where the weapon and other incriminating items had been discarded. The present action was instituted by Negro school children to test the constitutionality of the Alabama School Placement Law of 1955, the material provisions of which appear in the headnote, infra. The United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama held that the act was not invalid upon its face, in view of the presumption that it would be administered in a constitutional manner by the admission of qualified pupils upon a basis of individual merit without regard to their race or color. (162 F Supp 372.)

A corporation's trustee in reorganization under Chapter X of the Bankruptcy Act brought suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York against the debtor's indenture trustee, on behalf of the debenture holders, seeking to recover the principal amount of the outstanding debentures as damages for the indenture trustee's alleged bad-faith failure to compel the debtor's compliance with the indenture terms. In the reorganization proceeding, the trustee in reorganization filed a counterclaim against the indenture trustee and an objection to the indenture trustee's claim for services rendered, and also moved to compel an accounting by the indenture trustee. The District Court dismissed the independent action and the counterclaim, and denied the motion for an accounting. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed en banc (439 F2d 118).

The exigent circumstances rule justified a warrantless search when the conduct of the police preceding the exigency was reasonable. The exigent circumstances rule applied when the police did not gain entry by means of an actual or threatened violation of the Fourth Amendment. One officer testified without contradiction that the officers banged on the door as loud as they could and announced either "Police, police, police" or "This is the police." There was no evidence they either violated the Fourth Amendment or threatened to do so prior to the point when they entered the apartment. There was no evidence of a "demand" of any sort, much less a demand that amounted to a threat to violate the Fourth Amendment. Any contradictory evidence not brought to the Supreme Court's attention was for the state court to address on remand. As the officer testified, noises inside the apartment then led the officers to believe that drug-related evidence was about to be destroyed, and, at that point they explained they were going to make entry. Given that the announcement was made after the exigency arose, it could not have created the exigency.

Finding that livestock and commodities dealers in San Antonio, Texas, who delivered in their own trucks to customers in Louisiana and bought sugar there for backhauling to Texas and resale en route or within a day or two after arrival in San Antonio, were engaged in for-hire carriage and not in transportation in furtherance of their primary business enterprise, so as not to require Interstate Commerce Commission operating authority, the Commission ordered them to cease and desist from conducting such unlawful transportation. (81 MCC 337.) A three-judge United States District Court for the Western District of Texas set aside the order. (219 F Supp 781.)

The defendant mailed a punchboard, together with a circular, an order blank, and a letter indicating how the addressee might obtain merchandise free by selling the chances on the punchboard and how certain lucky numbers would reward the purchaser with prizes. If the addressee desired to put the scheme into operation, the merchandise could be obtained by ordering it for a consideration.

A Danish seaman, while temporarily in New York, joined the crew of a ship of Danish flag and registry, owned by a Danish citizen, and signed ship's articles, written in Danish, providing that the rights of crew members would be governed by Danish law and by the employer's contract with a Danish union, of which the seaman was a member. He was negligently injured aboard the ship in the course of employment, while in Havana harbor. In his suit under the Jones Act the courts below rendered judgment in his favor, proceeding on the theory that American rather than Danish law applied.

The defendant was convicted of second degree murder upon trial in a Connecticut state court, and the conviction was affirmed by the Supreme Court of Connecticut. (155 Conn 124, 230 A2d 573.) The trial court admitted a confession and evidence as to the defendant's partial re-enactment of the crime at the request of the police, which confession and re-enactment had been made on the third day of interrogation after the defendant's arrest on a coroner's warrant, and had been preceded by two earlier confessions that the trial judge excluded from evidence as not having been voluntarily made. During the 30 to 48 hours that the defendant was held for interrogation by the police, the defendant's attorneys had made numerous unsuccessful attempts to communicate with the defendant or the officer in charge, even obtaining a writ of habeas corpus issued by a state judge, which proved fruitless when the sheriff could not locate the officer in charge or the coroner, and the defendant had been denied permission to communicate with the outside world on three separate occasions.

Upon arriving at the scene of an accident, a police officer observed the driver of one vehicle, arrested him for operating his vehicle while under the influence of intoxicating liquor, and took him to the police station where the driver was asked to take a breath analysis test, but refused to do so. The Registrar formally suspended the driver's license and advised him of his right to appeal the suspension to the Board of Appeal. Although the state law also provided for an immediate hearing before the Registrar after the driver surrendered his license, the driver took an appeal to the Board of Appeals. A New York statute dealing with obscene literature authorizes the chief executive, or legal officer, of a municipality to bring an action for an injunction to prevent the sale or distribution of obscene written and printed matter. The statute entitles the person, firm, or corporation sought to be enjoined to a trial of the issues within one day after joinder of issue and to a decision by the court within two days of the conclusion of the trial. If a final order or judgment of injunction is entered, surrender, or seizure in default of surrender, of the obscene material and its destruction are required. The statute provides, further, that every person, firm, or corporation who sells or distributes obscene written or printed matter after the service of a summons and complaint in an action brought under the statute is chargeable with knowledge of its contents. In a prosecution under the statute in the Supreme Court, Special Term, New York County, certain booklets were found to be obscene, their further distribution was enjoined, and their destruction was ordered (208 Misc 150, 142 NYS2d 735).

C. _ 1983 against the Governor, the Adjutant General of the Ohio National Guard, various other Guard officers and enlisted members, and the university president, charging that those officials, acting under color of state law, "intentionally, recklessly, willfully and wantonly" caused an unnecessary Guard deployment on the campus and ordered the Guard members to perform allegedly illegal acts resulting in the students' deaths.

In seeking the injunction, the former judge claimed that (1) he had been coerced into giving the grand jury testimony by the concerted action of an assistant attorney general of the state and members of the New Jersey Supreme Court when the members of the court had met with the former judge shortly before he appeared before the state grand jury and had interrogated him with regard to the subject matter of the grand jury investigation and the propriety of a municipal judge invoking the privilege against compulsory self-incrimination, and (2) the significant role played by members of the New Jersey Supreme Court made it impossible for the former judge to receive a fair trial in the New Jersey state court system. The Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) of the United States Department of the Interior issued a biological opinion which concluded that the long-term operation of the Klamath Project--a federal reclamation project consisting of a series of lakes, rivers, dams, and irrigation canals in northern California and southern Oregon--was likely to jeopardize the continued existence of two endangered species of fish. The biological opinion identified measures that the FWS believed would avoid jeopardy, which measures included the maintenance of minimum water levels on two lakes in the project. The Bureau of Reclamation--the federal agency administering the project--notified the FWS that the Bureau intended to operate the project in compliance with the biological opinion. Two Oregon irrigation districts that received water from the project--together with the operators of two ranches within those districts--filed an action in the United States District Court for the District of Oregon against the Secretary of the Interior and some officials of the FWS. The plaintiffs--invoking the citizen-suit provision of the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA) (16 USCS 1540(g)) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (5 USCS 701 et seq.)--contended, among other matters, that (1) the lake-level restrictions (a) would adversely affect the plaintiffs' use of water from the project, and (b) were not necessary to protect the fish; (2) the defendants, by issuing a biological opinion which made unsubstantiated findings as to the necessity of the restrictions, had violated 7 of the ESA (16 USCS 1536), which requires each federal agency to use the best scientific and commercial data available in insuring that any agency action does not jeopardize endangered species; (3) the imposition of minimum water el

A prisoner in Montana's state prison, who had been trained by the prison as an inmate law clerk, offered to give legal advice to a fellow inmate who had been charged with assaulting a prison guard. Because the prisoner was precluded by prison regulations from visiting the fellow inmate directly, the offer was made by letter. The letter was intercepted and read by prison officials who sanctioned the prisoner, on the basis of the letter's content, for violating prison rules prohibiting insolence and interfering with due process hearings. The prisoner, alleging a violation of his rights under the First Amendment of the Federal Constitution, brought suit against prison officials, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief in the United States District Court for the District of Montana. The District Court, in granting summary judgment for the prison officials, concluded that there was a valid rational connection between the prison's inmate correspondence policy and the objectives of prison order, security, and inmate rehabilitation such as to render the regulations impinging on inmates' constitutional rights valid. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, in reversing, (1) reasoned that inmates have a First Amendment right to assist other inmates with their legal claims, and (2) concluded that the prison rules, as applied to the prisoner, impermissibly infringed his First Amendment rights (195 F3d 1121).

The trial judge's instructions to the jury repeatedly emphasized that all jury determinations, including findings as to mitigating circumstances, had to be unanimous. The jury then (1) found that there was an aggravating circumstance in the case, (2) checked the spaces marked "no" after each mitigating circumstance listed on the verdict form and wrote "none" in the space for "other mitigating circumstances," and (3) returned a sentence of death. The inmate appealed his conviction and sentence, partly on the theory that the state's death penalty statute, as applied, was unconstitutionally mandatory because it required jurors to impose a death sentence if they unanimously found an aggravating circumstance but could not unanimously agree that any particular mitigating circumstance was present, even if some or all jurors believed that some mitigating circumstance was present. Shortly after oil escaping from an oil retention pit at a drilling facility in Oklahoma had run into a tributary of the Arkansas River system, the lessee of the facility notified a regional office of the Environmental Protection Agency that the discharge of oil had taken place, such notification being in accordance with 311(b)(5) of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act (33 USCS 1321(b)(5)), which imposes a duty upon "any person in charge of a vessel or of an onshore facility or an offshore facility" to report discharges of oil into navigable waters in violation of 311(b)(3) of the Act to the "appropriate agency of the United States Government" and subjects a person not making a report to a fine and possible imprisonment, while also establishing a form of "use immunity" by specifying that notification under 311(b)(5) cannot be used against the person who makes a required report "in any criminal case, except a prosecution for perjury or for giving a false statement." The lessee later submitted a full written report on the discharge of oil and it was forwarded to the Coast Guard, the agency responsible for administering 311(b)(6) of the Act (33 USCS 1321(b)(6)), which provides for the imposition of a "civil penalty" against the person in charge of a facility from which oil is discharged in violation of 311(b)(3) of the Act.
