A Border Patrol agent in the United States Immigration and Naturalization Service was indicted in the Superior Court of Pima County, Arizona on a state charge. Because the charge arose from an act committed while on duty, the agent, pursuant to 28 USCS 1442(a)(1), removed the case to the United States District Court for the District of Arizona where the case was tried before a jury, and a verdict of guilty returned. However, the District Court, acting sua sponte, determined that the agent was immune from prosecution on a state criminal charge and set aside the jury verdict (445 F Supp 1123). The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit dismissed the state's appeal on the ground that jurisdiction was lacking, reasoning, among other things, that a criminal proceeding removed to federal court under 1442(a)(1) arises under federal law and accordingly is to be controlled by that law rather than state law. The court concluded only Congress can authorize an appeal by a state in a 1442(a)(1) criminal prosecution, and that it had not done so, and it also rejected the suggestion that 28 USCS 1291, the general federal appeals statute, provided authorization for the state's appeal (608 F2d 1197).

In Rehaif v. United States, 588 U. S. ___, the Court clarified the mens rea requirement for firearms-possession offenses under 18 U. S. C. ¬ß922(g). After Rehaif, the Government in a felon-in-possession case must prove not only that the defendant knew he possessed a firearm, but also that he knew he was a felon when he possessed the firearm. See 588 U. S., at ___. Prior to Rehaif, Gregory Greer and Michael Gary were separately convicted of being felons in possession of a firearm in violation of ¬ß922(g)(1). Greer‚Äôs conviction resulted from a jury trial during which Greer did not request‚Äîand the District Court did not give‚Äîa jury instruction requiring the jury to find that Greer knew he was a felon when he possessed the firearm. Gary pled guilty to two counts of being a felon in possession of a firearm. During Gary‚Äôs plea colloquy, the District Court did not advise Gary that, if he went to trial, a jury would have to find that he knew he was a felon when he possessed the firearms. On appeal, both Greer and Gary raised new mens rea arguments based on Rehaif. Greer requested a new trial based on the District Court‚Äôs failure to instruct the jury that Greer had to know he was a felon to be found guilty. Applying plain-error review, the Eleventh Circuit rejected that argument. Gary argued that his guilty plea must be vacated because the District Court failed to advise him that, if he went to trial, a jury would have to find that he knew he was a felon. The Fourth Circuit agreed with Gary, holding that the failure to advise him of that mens rea element was a structural error that required automatic reversal even though Gary had not raised the argument in the District Court.

Petitioner Virginia Uranium, Inc., wants to mine raw uranium ore from a site near Coles Hill, Virginia, but Virginia law flatly prohibits uranium mining in the Commonwealth. The company filed suit, alleging that, under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, the Atomic Energy Act (AEA) preempts state uranium mining laws like Virginia's and ensconces the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) as the lone regulator in the field. Both the District Court and the Fourth Circuit rejected the company's argument, finding that while the AEA affords the NRC considerable authority over the nuclear fuel life cycle, it offers no hint that Congress sought to strip States of their traditional power to regulate mining on private lands within their borders.

Georgia for many years exempted retirement benefits paid by the state from state personal income taxation, but did not so exempt retirement benefits paid by the Federal Government. Following a decision of the United States Supreme Court which declared such a tax scheme to be unconstitutional, Georgia repealed its special tax exemption for state retirees, but did not offer refunds to federal retirees. A federal retiree sued Georgia in Georgia state court, seeking a refund on the basis of a Georgia statute providing for the refund of any taxes which had been illegally assessed and collected. The state court denied the refund, and the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed on the basis that the refund statute did not apply where the law under which the taxes were collected was subsequently held invalid. The retiree sought reconsideration, which the Georgia Supreme Court denied. The retiree then petitioned for certiorari, and the United States Supreme Court remanded (509 US ____, 125 L Ed 2d 717, 113 S Ct 3028) to the Georgia Supreme Court for further consideration in light of Harper v Virginia Dept. of Taxation (1993) 509 US ____, 125 L Ed 2d 74, 113 S Ct 2510, which had held that a state was free to choose which form of relief it offered--predeprivation process, postdeprivation process, or both--so long as such relief satisfied the minimum requirements of due process. On remand, the Georgia Supreme Court again denied the retiree's claim, holding that Georgia's predeprivation procedures were ample and satisfied the requirements of the due process clause of the Federal Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment (263 Ga 602, 437 SE2d 320).

The United States brought an antitrust action against the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers, an unincorporated association, and certain of its officers, based on (1) alleged restraint of trade arising out of the association's mode of dealing with outsiders, and (2) alleged restraint of competition among the association's members as between themselves. The suit was settled by a consent decree approved by the District Court for the Southern District of New York, which reserved jurisdiction and later modified the decree. Prior to the adoption of a second modification of the decree, certain members of the association, contending that the proposed modification did not go far enough toward ameliorating the position of the small publishers as against the few large publishers, moved to intervene in the action, pursuant to Rule 24(a)(2) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, which authorizes intervention as of right in an action by one whose interest is or may be inadequately represented in the action and who is or may be bound by the judgment in the action. The motions were denied.

Fourteen months after a decedent's death a California state court allowed his widow, as a statutory widow's allowance, $ 3,000 per month for 24 months from the decedent's death; the widow was paid $ 42,000 as of the date of the order, plus $ 3,000 per month for the remaining 10 months. On the federal estate tax return filed on behalf of the estate, the full $ 72,000 was claimed as a marital deduction under 812(e) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939. The deduction was disallowed, and the United States District Court for the Southern District of California granted summary judgment for the United States in a suit for refund. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed. (317 F2d 821.)

In granting an injunction against a strike called by a union against a railroad in connection with a controversy, then pending before the National Railroad Adjustment Board, resulting from orders of the railroad which, in effect, eliminated the jobs of two of five-men way-freight crews and changed the home or away-from-home terminals of the remaining crews, the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas imposed conditions requiring that the railroad either restore the situation which existed prior to the orders, or pay the employees adversely affected by the orders the wages they would have received had the orders not been issued. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit sustained the injunction but vacated the conditions, holding that the District Court had no power to attach them. (266 F2d 335.)

Petitioner Moones Mellouli, a lawful permanent resident, pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor offense under Kansas law, the possession of drug paraphernalia "to ... store [or] conceal ... a controlled substance." Kan. Stat. Ann. ¬ß21-5709(b)(2). The sole "paraphernalia" Mellouli was charged with possessing was a sock in which he had placed four unidentified orange tablets. Citing Mellouli's misdemeanor conviction, an Immigration Judge ordered him deported under 8 U. S. C. ¬ß1227(a)(2)(B)(i), which authorizes the deportation (removal) of an alien "convicted of a violation of ... any law or regulation of a State, the United States, or a foreign country relating to a controlled substance (as defined in section 802 of Title 21)." Section 802, in turn, limits the term "controlled substance" to a "drug or other substance" included in one of five federal schedules. 21 U. S. C. ¬ß802(6). Kansas defines "controlled substance" as any drug included on its own schedules, without reference to ¬ß802. Kan. Stat. Ann. ¬ß21-5701(a). At the time of Mellouli's conviction, Kansas' schedules included at least nine substances not on the federal lists. The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) affirmed Mellouli's deportation order, and the Eighth Circuit denied his petition for review.

Nonunion employees at a coal mine in Wyoming selected two labor union employees, who were not employees at the mine, to serve as miners' representatives pursuant to a provision of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Amendments Act of 1977 (Mine Act) (30 USCS 813(f)). The operator of the mine did not post information regarding the miners' representatives, as required by an administrative regulation ( 30 CFR 40.4), but complained to the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) that the designation compromised the operator's rights under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) (29 USCS 151 et seq.). After a registrant, whose local draft board had rejected his claim to classification as a conscientious objector and classified him 1-A, was ordered to report for induction, he brought an action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California seeking to have his induction enjoined and to have the rejection of his claim to conscientious objector classification declared improper on various grounds. The District Court entered a preliminary injunction preventing the registrant's induction until after a determination of his claim on the merits, and held that it had jurisdiction to hear the claim despite 10(b)(3) of the Military Selective Service Act of 1967, prohibiting judicial review of a draft board's classification except as a defense to a criminal prosecution, and that such statute, as applied to prevent preinduction review of the registrant's classification, was unconstitutional.

In an action in the District Court for Polk County, Iowa, an Illinois corporation which manufactured animal feed in Illinois and sold its products in Iowa, challenged the constitutionality of Iowa's statutory single-factor sales formula for apportioning an interstate business' income for Iowa income tax purposes. Iowa's single-factor formula is based on a comparison of an interstate corporation's gross sales within the state to the taxpayer's total gross sales, whereas Illinois (and most other states) employ a three-factor formula based on a comparison of a taxpayer's in-state property, payroll, and sales with the taxpayer's total property, payroll, and sales. The trial court held that the Iowa single-factor formula violated the commerce clause of the Federal Constitution (Art 1, 8, cl 3) and the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, but the Supreme Court of Iowa reversed (254 NW2d 737).

Respondents Maurice Davis and Andre Glover were charged with multiple counts of Hobbs Act robbery and one count of conspiracy to commit Hobbs Act robbery. They were also charged under 18 U.S.C. ¬ß 924(c), which authorizes heightened criminal penalties for using, carrying, or possessing a firearm in connection with any federal ‚Äúcrime of violence or drug trafficking crime.‚Äù ¬ß 924(c)(1)(A). ‚ÄúCrime of violence‚Äù is defined in two subparts: the elements clause, ¬ß 924(c)(3)(A), and the residual clause, ¬ß 924(c)(3)(B). The residual clause in turn defines a ‚Äúcrime of violence‚Äù as a felony ‚Äúthat by its nature, involves a substantial risk that physical force against the person or property of another may be used in the course of committing the offense.‚Äù Ibid. A jury convicted the men on most of the underlying charges and on two separate ¬ß 924(c) charges for brandishing a firearm in connection with their crimes. The Fifth Circuit initially rejected their argument that ¬ß 924(c)'s residual clause is unconstitutionally vague, but on remand in light of Sessions v. Dimaya, 584 U.S. ‚Äì‚Äì‚Äì‚Äì, 138 S.Ct. 1204, 200 L.Ed.2d 549 (2018), the court reversed course and held ¬ß 924(c)(3)(B) unconstitutional. It then held that Mr. Davis's and Mr. Glover's convictions on the ¬ß 924(c) count charging robbery as the predicate crime of violence could be sustained under the elements clause, but that the other count‚Äîwhich charged conspiracy as a predicate crime of violence‚Äîcould not be upheld because it depended on the residual clause.

One state law required tobacco shippers to utilize a delivery company which provided a recipient-identification service, and the other state law deemed a person to know that a package from a tobacco retailer contained tobacco. The association contended that the laws were preempted because they related to carrier service, but the AG argued that the laws merely protected the public health by preventing sales of tobacco products to minors. The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously held that both state laws were preempted by federal law. In regulating delivery service procedures, the recipient-verification provision focused on carrier services, thereby creating a direct connection with motor carrier services which had a significant and adverse impact on the congressional goal of precluding state regulation in lieu of competitive market forces. Similarly, the deemed-to-know provision directly related to carrier services by imposing civil liability on carriers which failed sufficiently to examine every package. Further, federal preemption provided no exception based on the State's public health concerns, and the State had other legislative alternatives for enforcing its ban on underage smoking.

Between 1990 and 1993, six freelance authors contributed articles in which they had registered copyrights to periodicals published by print publishers. Under agreements with the print publishers, but without the freelancers' consent, electronic publishers copied the articles appearing in the periodicals, including the freelancers' articles, into computer databases that contained thousands or millions of files with individual articles from thousands of collective works, either in one series or in scores of series. Users of the databases, which resided either on CD-ROMs or on the electronic publisher's central discs, could search for articles by author, subject, date, publication, headline, key term, words in text, or other criteria, or, in the case of the CD-ROMs, by means of an index. Whether written by a freelancer or periodical staff member, each article was presented to, and retrievable by, a database user in isolation, clear of the context the original print publication presented, although in one of the CD-ROM products--which was image-based rather text-based--an article appeared with the other materials published on the same page or pages, but without any material published on other pages of the original periodical. In 1993, the freelancers filed a civil action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleging that their copyrights were infringed when, as permitted and facilitated by the print publishers, the electronic publishers placed their articles in the databases. The District Court granted summary judgment for the publishers, holding that 17 USCS 201(c) shielded the database reproductions, as (1) the privilege conferred upon owners of copyrights in collective works by 201(c) was conveyed from the print publishers to the elec

A music publisher's agent placed disputed funds in an escrow account and brought an interpleader action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York following a controversy between the publisher and the heirs of the deceased author of a copyrighted song over the division of royalty income generated by sound recordings of the song. The author had originally assigned his entire interest in all renewals of the copyright to the music publisher in exchange for an advance royalty and 50 percent of all net royalties the publisher received for sound recordings. Subsequently the publisher registered a renewal copyright of the song and issued more than 400 licenses to recording companies who made and sold recordings of the song that generated the disputed royalty income. The sound recordings at issue constituted derivative works within the meaning of 17 USCS 304(c)(6)(A), which provides that a derivative work prepared under the authority of a copyright grant before termination of the grant may continue to be utilized under the terms of the grant after its termination. The author's heirs subsequently terminated the grant to the publisher and demanded that all royalties on the derivative works be remitted to them. The District Court entered judgment for the publisher (543 F Supp 844), concluding that the terms of the agreements that were in effect prior to the termination of the grant governed the record companies' obligation to pay royalties and that under those arrangements the publisher and the author's heirs were each entitled to a 50 percent share in the net royalties. A female employee of the Texas Department of Community Affairs brought an action against the Department in the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas, alleging that the Department's failure to promote her and its subsequent decision to terminate her employment had been predicated on gender discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e et seq.). After a bench trial, the District Court held that neither decision was based on gender discrimination, the court relying on testimony that the decisions were based on consultation among trusted advisors and on a nondiscriminatory evaluation of the relative qualifications of the individuals involved and that the Department thought that it could improve efficiency by terminating the employee and two others who did not work well together. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the District Court's decision that the employee was not discriminated against when she was not promoted, but reversed the District Court's finding that the Department's testimony sufficiently had rebutted the employee's prima facie case of gender discrimination in the decision to terminate her employment, the court reaffirming its previously announced views that the defendant in a Title VII case bears the burden of proving by a preoponderance of the evidence the existence of legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the employment action and that the defendant also must prove by objective evidence that those hired or promoted were better qualified than the plaintiff, and finding that the Department had not met either of these evidentiary burdens on the discharge issue (608 F2d 563).

The Secretary of the Department of Health, Education and Welfare is authorized by 204(a)(1) of the Social Security Act (42 USCS 404(a)(1)) to recoup erroneous overpayments made to a beneficiary under the old-age, survivors', or disability insurance program by decreasing future payments to which the overpaid person is entitled, but 204(b) of the Act (42 USCS 404(b)) bars recoupment from any person who is without fault if recoupment would defeat the purpose of the Act or would be against equity and good conscience. Under Department procedures, after a recipient is notified of the ex parte determination that an overpayment has been made, the recipient may file a written request either seeking reconsideration of that determination or asking the Secretary to waive recovery in accordance with 204(b), with recoupment beginning after a decision on the papers goes against the recipient, and an oral hearing being granted only if the recipient thereafter continues to object to recoupment. Several recipients of benefit payments brought suit in the United States District Court for the District of Hawaii and the United States District Court for the Western District of Washington, alleging that recoupment procedures violated 204 and the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment. The District Court in Hawaii, after certifying a class of all recipients resident in Hawaii who were or would be subject to recoupment, held that due process required that the Secretary provide an opportunity for an informal hearing before an independent decision maker prior to recoupment (371 F Supp 960). In each of two cases, an accused was convicted of various federal drug offenses and of violation of 18 USCS 924(c)(1), which requires the imposition of specified penalties on a person who uses or carries a firearm during and in relation to any crime of violence or drug trafficking crime. In the first case, (1) the police found a firearm inside a bag in the locked trunk of an automobile, after stopping the driver for a traffic offense and arresting him after finding cocaine in the driver's compartment; and (2) the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, in affirming the accused's conviction, expressed the view that the accused could be convicted of using a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime, since the jury could reasonably have inferred that the accused had used the gun in the trunk to protect his drugs and drug proceeds and to facilitate sales (995 F2d 1113). In a contempt proceeding for failure to comply with a court order to enforce a subpoena duces tecum issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission in aid of an investigation pursuant to _ 20 (a) of the Securities Act of 1933, 48 Stat. 74, a district court adjudged the defendant guilty of contempt and imposed an unconditional fine, but refused to grant any coercive relief designed to force him to produce the subpoenaed documents. He paid the fine and took no appeal. The Commission filed a notice of appeal in the district court and subsequently a statement of points challenging as error the court's action in imposing the fine instead of a remedial penalty to make him produce the documents. The circuit court of appeals held that the district court erred in imposing the fine and directed that the defendant be ordered imprisoned until he produced the documents.

Articles XIX and XXI of the Convention Respecting Double Taxation, March 4, 1942, United States-Canada (56 Stat 1405-1406, TS No. 983) oblige the United States, upon request and consistent with United States revenue laws, to obtain and convey information to Canadian authorities to assist the authorities in determining a Canadian taxpayer's income tax liability. The Canadian Department of National Revenue asked the United States Internal Revenue Service (IRS) to secure and provide pertinent bank records to help determine the Canadian income tax liability of some Canadian citizens who maintained accounts in a bank in the state of Washington. The IRS Director of Foreign Operations determined that the Canadian requests should be honored, and served the bank with administrative summonses for the records, but (1) at the citizens' request, the bank refused to honor the summonses, and (2) the citizens, petitioning the United States District Court for the Western District of Washington to quash the summonses, claimed that, under the circumstances, United States law proscribed the use of the summonses, because (a) 26 USCS 7602(c) prohibited the IRS from issuing such a summons in order to further an IRS investigation of a United States taxpayer when a United States Justice Department referral for criminal prosecution was in effect, and (b) Canada, with respect to each citizen, was in the preliminary stage of a criminal investigation. However, the United States Magistrate who held a consolidated hearing on the citizens' claims expressed the view that, even if the citizens' legal arguments were correct, the citizens had failed to carry their burden of showing that the Canadian investigation had reached a stage equivalent to a Justice Department referral for criminal prosecution. Two operators of a Georgia "numbers game," who were themselves liable for federal taxes on gambling, along with two of their clerical functionaries, who were not personally liable for such taxes, were convicted, in a prosecution in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, of conspiracy to evade and defeat the payment of the taxes. The convictions were affirmed by the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. (259 F2d 886.)

The owner of a tract of land being developed as a residential subdivision sued the County Regional Planning Commission and its members and staff in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, alleging that the application of various zoning laws and regulations to its property amounted to a "taking" of that property. At trial, the jury agreed and awarded the owner $ 350,000 as just compensation for the "taking." The court then granted judgment notwithstanding the verdict in favor of the Commission on the taking claim, reasoning in part that the owner was unable to derive economic benefit from its property on a temporary basis only, and that such a temporary deprivation, as a matter of law, cannot constitute a taking. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed, holding that application of government regulations affecting an owner's use of property may constitute a taking if the regulation denies the owner all "economically viable" use of the land, and that the evidence supported the jury's finding that the property had no economically feasible use during the time between the Commission's refusal to approve the preliminary plat and the jury's verdict. The court rejected the District Court's holding that the taking verdict could not stand as a matter of law and determined that damages were required to compensate for a temporary taking (729 F2d 402).

In a prosecution in the Fifth Judicial District Court, Iron County, Utah, in which defendant's oral confession was admitted in evidence, defendant was convicted of the murder of her husband, and the conviction was affirmed by the Supreme Court of Utah, which held that the admission of the confession did not deprive defendant of the due process of law guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment (5 Utah2d 59, 296 P2d 726).

Prior to the outbreak of the Korean hostilities, military export shipments passing through army base piers in Norfolk, Virginia, were carried by the railroads at a single rate covering both transportation and pier services, including wharfage and handling. In accordance with its tariffs, the railroads furnished, through a specified public wharfinger, these accessorial services for the government, as well as commercial shippers, at public sections of these piers without additional charge. With the outbreak of the Korean conflict, the government found it necessary to operate directly certain portions of the piers in order to facilitate the shipment of military supplies. The railroads continued to charge the same line-haul rate as before on government shipments and refused to grant the government an allowance for its performance of the accessorial services theretofore performed by the railroads without charge. A complaint in which the United States sought a determination that this refusal of the railroads constituted a violation of the Interstate Commerce Act was dismissed by the Interstate Commerce Commission (289 ICC 49).

The District Court of Dodge County, Nebraska, dismissed a habeas corpus petition by a minor who, after a hearing without a jury before a juvenile court judge, had been found to be a delinquent child and ordered committed to a boys' training school because of an act which, if committed by an adult, would have constituted forgery under state law. A divided Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed, the Nebraska Constitution requiring the concurrence of five judges to hold a legislative act unconstitutional, and only four of the seven judges being of the opinion that state statutory provisions which required that juvenile hearings be without a jury and be based on the preponderance of the evidence were unconstitutional (183 Neb 461, 161 NW2d 508).

The plaintiffs, an organization and individuals active in fostering civil rights for Negroes in Louisiana, filed a complaint in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, seeking declaratory relief and an injunction restraining defendants from prosecuting or threatening to prosecute plaintiffs for alleged violations of the Louisiana Subversive Activities and Communist Control Law and the Louisiana Communist Propaganda Control Law. The complaint alleged that the statutes were invalid on their face and that the threats to enforce them against the plaintiffs were made only to discourage them from continuing their civil rights activities. A three-judge District Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. (227 F Supp 556.)

The case at hand involved some asserted failures, by the United States Bureau of Land Management (BLM) in its stewardship of public lands in Utah, to take certain actions with respect to the use of off-road vehicles (ORVs). Several challengers filed suit in the United States District Court for the District of Utah and alleged that the District Court had the authority, under _ 706(1), to remedy the BLM's asserted failures. The challengers included three claims that (1) under the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA) (43 USCS __ 1701 et seq.), the BLM, by permitting ORV use in certain "wilderness study areas" (WSAs)--roadless lands that had been recommended as suitable for "wilderness" designation, without Congress's having acted yet on the recommendation--had violated the FLPMA's nonimpairment mandate (in 43 USCS _ 1782(c)) to continue to manage WSAs "in a manner so as not to impair the suitability of such areas for preservation as wilderness"; (2) the BLM had contravened the FLPMA's requirement (in 43 USCS _ 1732(a)) to manage public lands in accordance with land-use plans when they were available, by failing to comply with three alleged commitments involving (a) a 1991 resource-management plan for the San Rafael area, and (b) a 1990 ORV-implementation plan for the Henry Mountains area; and (3) under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) (42 USCS __ 4321 et seq.), the BLM had improperly failed to take a "hard look" at whether the BLM ought to undertake ‚àö¬∂[***138]‚àö¬∂ supplemental environmental analyses for areas in which ORV use allegedly had increased. However, the District Court entered a dismissal with respect to these three claims.

The Duval County, Florida sheriff's department prepared a report on a sexual assault. The report, which identified the victim by her full name, was placed in the department's pressroom. Although the department did not restrict access either to the pressroom or to the reports made available therein, the room contained signs to the effect that the names of rape victims were not matters of public record and were not to be published. A reporter-trainee for a weekly newspaper copied the police report verbatim, including the victim's full name, and a reporter for the newspaper prepared an article, derived entirely from the copied police report, which again included the victim's full name. The newspaper published the article in violation of its own internal policy of not publishing the names of sexual offense victims. The victim, claiming emotional distress, filed suit in the Circuit Court of Duval County against the sheriff's department and the newspaper. The victim alleged that the newspaper had violated a Florida statute that made it unlawful to publish in any instrument of mass communication the name of the victim of a sexual offense. The department reached a pretrial settlement with the victim, but following a trial, the newspaper was found negligent and the victim was awarded compensatory and punitive damages. The District Court of Appeal of Florida, First District, affirmed (499 So 2d 883), and the Supreme Court of Florida denied review.

A private golf and country club which was a nonprofit Oregon corporation derived most of its income from membership dues and other receipts from club members, and such income was exempt from federal income tax under 501(c)(7) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (26 USCS 501(c)(7)). Also, the club derived nonexempt "unrelated business taxable income"--which, for social clubs, is defined, under 512(a)(3)(A) of the Code (26 USCS 512(a)(3)(A)) as encompassing all sources of income except receipts from club members--from sales of food and drink to nonmembers, and from the return on its investments. In calculating its federal income tax liability for two fiscal years, the club offset its net losses on nonmember sales against the earnings from its investments and therefore reported no unrelated business taxable income for the two tax years. In computing the losses on nonmember sales, the club identified variable, or direct, expenses, such as the cost of the food sold to the nonmembers, and fixed, or indirect, overhead expenses, which would have been incurred regardless of whether sales had been made to nonmembers. The club allocated fixed expenses to nonmember sales using a "gross-to-gross method," based on the ratio that nonmember sales bore to total sales. For each year, the variable expenses were less than the income from nonmember sales, but the total of the fixed and variable expenses exceeded the income from nonmember sales. On audit, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, determining that the club's losses from nonmember sales could not be used to offset investment income because the club had failed to show that its nonmember sales had been undertaken with an intent to profit, determined tax deficiencies for each year reflecting the tax owed on the investment income. The assignee of territorial rights in a combination patent covering a top structure for automobile "convertibles" sued a manufacturer of replacements for the fabric components in such top structures for patent infringement, the top structures having been incorporated, without authority, in 1952-1954 Ford cars. The United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts dismissed the complaint. The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reversed on the ground that purchasers of convertible 1952-1954 model Ford cars directly infringed the patent and the manufacturer of replacement fabrics was guilty of contributory infringement by supplying such fabrics. (312 F2d 52.)

Inter partes review allows private parties to challenge previously issued patent *1351 claims in an adversarial process before the Patent Office. At the outset, a party must file a petition to institute review, 35 U.S.C. ¬ß 311(a), that identifies the challenged claims and the grounds for challenge with particularity, ¬ß 312(a)(3). The patent owner, in turn, may file a response. ¬ß 313. If the Director of the Patent Office determines ‚Äúthere is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition,‚Äù ¬ß 314(a), he decides ‚Äúwhether to institute ... review ... pursuant to [the] petition,‚Äù ¬ß 314(b). ‚ÄúIf ... review is instituted and not dismissed,‚Äù at the end of the litigation the Patent Trial and Appeal Board ‚Äúshall issue a final written decision with respect to the patentability of any patent claim challenged by the petitioner.‚Äù ¬ß 318(a). Petitioner SAS sought review of respondent ComplementSoft's software patent, alleging that all 16 of the patent's claims were unpatentable. Relying on a Patent Office regulation recognizing a power of ‚Äúpartial institution,‚Äù 37 C.F.R. ¬ß 42.108(a), the Director instituted review on some of the claims and denied review on the rest. The Board's final decision addressed only the claims on which the Director had instituted review. On appeal, the Federal Circuit rejected SAS's argument that ¬ß 318(a) required the Board to decide the patentability of every claim challenged in the petition.

A municipal official testified before a state grand jury in New Jersey after prosecutors and the official's attorneys agreed that if the official testified neither his statements nor any evidence derived from them could, under a New Jersey immunity statute, be used in subsequent state criminal proceedings, with the exception of prosecutions for perjury or false swearing. When an agreement could not be worked out to avoid the official's criminal prosecution, he was indicted for misconduct in office and extortion by a public official. After completion of the state's case in the official's state criminal trial, defense counsel requested a ruling by the trial judge as to the use of the official's previous grand jury testimony. The trial judge ruled that if the official testified and gave an answer on direct or cross-examination which was materially inconsistent with his grand jury testimony, the prosecution could use that testimony in cross-examining the official. Because of the ruling the official did not testify, and he was ultimately found guilty. The Superior Court of New Jersey, Appellate Division, reversed the conviction and remanded the case for a new trial, holding that use of the immunized grand jury testimony to impeach the official would have violated the United States Constitution (151 NJ Super 200, 376 A2d 950). Afterwards, the Supreme Court of New Jersey denied the state's petition for certification of an appeal (75 NJ 597, 384 A2d 827).

The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected all the claims of two environmental groups who were challenging standards promulgated by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to air pollution. (657 F2d 298). Notwithstanding their lack of success on the merits, the groups filed a request for attorney's fees incurred in the action, relying on 307(f) of the Clean Air Act (42 USCS 7607(f)), which permits the award of attorney's fees in certain proceedings whenever the court determines that such an award is appropriate. The Court of Appeals agreed with the groups that it was appropriate for them to receive fees where they contributed to the goals of the Act (672 F2d 33, 684 F2d 972).

Defendants appeal from a judgment which found strict union shop clauses in a railroad collective bargaining agreement void and enjoined the appellants from requiring membership in the appellant union as a condition of continued employment.

The Township of Scott, Pennsylvania, passed an ordinance requiring that ‚Äú[a]ll cemeteries ... be kept open and accessible to the general public during daylight hours.‚Äù Petitioner Rose Mary Knick, whose 90-acre rural property has a small family graveyard, was notified that she was violating the ordinance. Knick sought declaratory and injunctive relief in state court on the ground that the ordinance effected a taking of her property, but she did not bring an inverse condemnation action under state law seeking compensation. The Township responded by withdrawing the violation notice and staying enforcement of the ordinance. Without an ongoing enforcement action, the court held, Knick could not demonstrate the irreparable harm necessary for equitable relief, so it declined to rule on her request. Knick then filed an action in Federal District Court under 42 U.S.C. ¬ß 1983, alleging that the ordinance violated the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The District Court dismissed her claim under Williamson County Regional Planning Comm'n v. Hamilton Bank of Johnson City, 473 U.S. 172, 105 S.Ct. 3108, 87 L.Ed.2d 126, which held that property owners must seek just compensation under state law in state court before bringing a federal takings claim under ¬ß 1983. The Third Circuit affirmed.

Oklahoma liquor retailers brought an action under 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act, in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma, to enjoin an alleged statewide market division by all Oklahoma liquor wholesalers. The District Court, sitting without a jury, entered judgment for the wholesalers on the ground, among others, that the interstate commerce prerequisite of the Act was not satisfied. The Court of Appeals affirmed on the ground that the proof was insufficient to show that the activities complained of were in or adversely affected interstate commerce. (377 F2d 901.)

In a jurisdictional dispute between a Plasterers' local and a Tile Setters' local over an employer's work of applying mortar to receive tile, the National Joint Board for Settlement of Jurisdictional Disputes awarded the work to the Plasterers' local. When the Tile Setters' local and the employer refused to acquiesce in this decision, the Plasterers' local picketed that employer and another employer who employed Tile Setters for this work. Neither employer was bound by the Board's decision. Unfair labor practice charges were filed against the Plasterers' local under 8(b)(4)(D) of the amended National Labor Relations Act. The NLRB, in a proceeding under 10(k) of the Act to determine the dispute, awarded the work to the Tile Setters, and upon the Plasterers' refusal to abide by the NLRB's award, the NLRB issued a cease and desist order against the Plasterers' local. The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit set aside the NLRB's order on the ground that 10(k) precluded the NLRB's jurisdictional award because the competing unions had agreed on a voluntary method of adjustment (142 App DC 146, 440 F2d 174).

A California state prisoner, challenging a disciplinary action that had been imposed on him approximately 6 months previously, appealed the action pursuant to California's prisoner-grievance system. The prison's appeals coordinator rejected the grievance as time-barred under the applicable state regulations, because the grievance had not been filed within 15 working days of the action being challenged. The prisoner subsequently brought suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California under 42 U.S.C.S. _ 1983 against some California correctional officials. The District Court, in granting the officials' motion to dismiss, said that the prisoner had not fully exhausted his administrative remedies as required by a provision of the Prison Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (PLRA) (42 U.S.C.S. _ 1997e(a)), which provides that no federal action may be brought by a prisoner with respect to prison conditions "until such administrative remedies as are available are exhausted."

The Court granted certiorari in this case to decide whether, when the Government has obtained a warrant under 18 U. S. C. ¬ß2703, a U. S. provider of e-mail services must disclose to the Government electronic communica- tions within its control even if the provider stores the communications abroad. 583 U. S. ___ (2017).

Having been barred by a privately owned shopping center's security guards from handbilling in the shopping center, draft and war protesters secured an injunction in the United States District Court for the District of Oregon against interference with their noncommercial handbilling in a peaceful and orderly manner in the shopping center in public areas, when they were open to general public access (308 F Supp 128). The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed (446 F2d 545).

After election officials in Montgomery County, Maryland, announced that because certain persons lived on the grounds of the National Institutes of Health, a federal enclave located within the county, they did not meet the residency requirements for voting in Maryland elections, these persons brought suit in the United States District Court for the District of Maryland, requesting that a three-judge court be convened to enjoin as unconstitutional this application of the Maryland voter residency law. A three-judge court was convened and granted the plaintiffs injunctive relief, holding that to deny them the right to vote would violate the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment (295 F Supp 654).

A suspect in a sexual assault was transported to a Connecticut police station and three times advised of his self-incrimination rights under Miranda v Arizona (1966) 384 US 436, 16 L Ed 2d 694, 86 S Ct 1602, 10 Ohio Misc 9, 36 Ohio Ops 2d 237, 10 ALR3d 974. Each time, the suspect indicated that he would not give a written statement without an attorney present, but that he was willing to talk about the incident. The resulting oral confession was held admissible at the suspect's subsequent criminal trial, in which (1) the Connecticut court, after a suppression hearing, found that the suspect had voluntarily waived his right to counsel, and (2) the suspect took the stand in his own defense and testified that he understood his rights as they were read to him. However, the suspect's eventual conviction for sexual assault, unlawful restraint, and possession of a controlled substance was reversed by the Connecticut Supreme Court, on the ground that the confession was inadmissible. The Connecticut Supreme Court expressed the view that (1) the suspect had invoked his right to counsel under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution, where no particular form of words had ever been required to trigger an individual's protections under the Fifth Amendment; and (2) under the test of Edwards v Arizona (1981) 451 US 477, 68 L Ed 2d 378, 101 S Ct 1880, the trial court's finding of waiver was erroneous, because the state had presented no evidence that the suspect had initiated the encounters with police--subsequent to the suspect's request for counsel--which had resulted in the incriminating statements (197 Conn 50, 495 A2d 1044).

In enforcing a cease and desist order of the National Labor Relations Board, the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit deleted certain clauses. (280 F2d 441, 283 F2d 26.) Certiorari granted; judgment reversed and case remanded to the Court of Appeals to enter judgment affirming and enforcing a cease-and-desist order of the National Labor Relations Board -- without deletion of references to other employers and other persons.

After the owner and lessee of land on the island of Oahu, Hawaii, consulted with the Army Corps of Engineers regarding a plan for the development of a lagoon on their land known as Kuapa Pond, the Corps acquiesced in proposals by the lessee to dredge a channel so that the pond, which was separated from a navigable bay and the Pacific Ocean by a barrier beach, could be made into a marina joined to the bay. After the dredging operation was completed and millions of dollars had been invested in the development of a marina-style community of over 20,000 persons around the pond, a dispute arose between the developers and the Corps concerning whether authorization from the Corps had to be obtained for future construction, filling, or excavation in the marina, and whether the owner and lessee were precluded from denying the public access to the pond on the theory that the improved pond was "navigable water of the United States." The United States then brought an action against the owner and lessee in the United States District Court for the District of Hawaii regarding the dispute. The District Court ruled that although the pond was navigable water of the United States, and, as such, subject to the regulatory power of Congress under the commerce clause of the Constitution (Art 1, 8, cl 3), it was not navigable for the purpose of defining the scope of the federal navigational servitude imposed by the commerce clause, and that the government lacked the authority to open the pond to the public without payment of compensation to the owner (408 F Supp 42). In 1992, a police officer in Milwaukee approached a 1981 two-door Oldsmobile with California license plates in a motel parking lot--a car that was arguably characteristic of one typically used by drug couriers--and asked the two men inside the car whether they had any illegal drugs or contraband. The men said they did not, but they consented to a search of the car. A second officer, conducting the search without having obtained a warrant, discovered cocaine inside an interior panel. The men were arrested on drug charges. In pretrial motions to suppress the cocaine evidence, it was alleged that the officers had violated the men's rights under the Federal Constitution's Fourth Amendment by detaining the men in the parking lot and by searching inside the panel without a warrant. A United States Magistrate Judge concluded that the circumstances had given the officers reasonable suspicion to stop and question the men, but not probable cause to conduct a warrantless search. The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin--adopting the Magistrate Judge's recommendation with respect to reasonable suspicion, but not the reasoning as to probable cause--ruled that the cocaine need not be excluded, and the men were convicted. Defendants were indicted under the federal civil rights statute (18 USC 241) for a conspiracy to injure and intimidate three Negroes in the exercise of their right to patronize a restaurant under the "Public Accommodations" part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Defendants were outsiders not connected with the restaurant. The United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia granted a motion to dismiss the indictment on the ground that 207(b) of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 makes the provision for relief by injunction the exclusive remedy under the Act. (269 F Supp 706.)

After they were convicted in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York of violating 18 USC 371 and 2114, two defendants were sentenced to concurrent terms of 25 and 5 years, without being asked before the sentences were imposed whether they had anything to say in their own behalf. After the convictions were affirmed by the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, the prisoners moved the District Court to vacate their sentences and resentence them in accordance with Federal Criminal Procedure Rule 32(a), which provides that "before imposing sentence the court shall afford the defendant an opportunity to make a statement in his own behalf and to present any information in mitigation of punishment." The District Court granted the motions and ordered that the prisoners be returned to the court for resentencing. The United States filed a notice of appeal form both orders, and the resentencing was stayed upon its motion. The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed on the ground that the sentencing court's failure to comply with Rule 32(a) did not constitute a ground for collateral relief. (301 F2d 376.)

The Extradition Treaty, May 4, 1978, [1979] United States-United Mexican States (31 UST 5059, TIAS No. 9656) provides (1) in Article 22(1), that the treaty shall apply to specified offenses committed before and after the treaty entered into effect; and (2) in Article 9, that (a) neither contracting party shall be bound to deliver up its own nationals, but the executive authority of the requested party shall, if not prevented by that party's laws, have the power to deliver such nationals up, if, in the party's discretion, it is deemed proper to do so, and (b) if extradition is not granted pursuant to the prior provision, the requested party shall submit the case to the party's competent authorities for the purpose of jurisdiction, provided that the party has jurisdiction over the offense. A Mexican citizen and resident was indicted in the United States on numerous federal charges for allegedly participating in the kidnap and murder of a Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent and the agent's pilot. The accused was forcibly abducted from Mexico to the United States and was arrested in the United States by DEA officials. Section 186 of the New York Election Law imposes a general requirement that a person must enroll in a political party at least 30 days before the November general election in order to be eligible to vote in the party's primary election held during the following year. During 1971, the petitioners, New York residents, became old enough to vote, but they neither registered as voters nor attempted to enroll in a political party until December, so that their enrollment in a party was, under 186, too late to entitle them to vote in the party primary election in June, 1972. In the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York, the petitioners, seeking declaratory relief, alleged that 186 unconstitutionally deprived them of their right to vote in the 1972 primary and abridged their freedom to associate with the political party of their choice. The District Court granted the petitioners declaratory relief, but the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed, holding that 186 safeguarded a compelling state interest in discouraging "raiding," whereby voters of one party fraudulently designate themselves as voters of another party in order to influence or determine the results of the other party's primary (458 F2d 649).

Defendant, a member of Jehovah's Witnesses, conducted religious services in a public park without the license required by a city ordinance after his application (in proper form) for such license had been denied by the city council. His conviction of violating the ordinance was affirmed by the highest court of the state, which held that the ordinance was valid on its face, that defendant's remedy for any arbitrary conduct of the city council was in appropriate civil proceedings, and that a wrongful refusal of a license is not a bar to prosecution for acting without a license.

Two individuals who bought and registered cars outside of the state of Vermont before they became residents of that state, and who were required to pay the full use tax in Vermont upon registering their cars there after they became residents, filed a suit in Vermont Superior Court alleging, inter alia, that Vermont's failure to afford them credit for the out-of-state sales taxes they had paid, which credit, under a Vermont motor vehicle use tax statute, was provided in the case of vehicles acquired outside the state by Vermont residents, violated the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Superior Court dismissed the complaint, and the Vermont Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the statute was rationally related to the legitimate state interest in raising revenue to maintain and improve the highways and it rationally placed the burden on those who used them (144 Vt 649, 478 A2d 993).

An Arkansas city, in an application to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), sought a permit for the city's new sewage treatment plant under the National Pollution Discharge Elimination System (NPDES). The EPA, pursuant to 402(a)(1) of the Clean Water Act (33 USCS 1342(a)(1)), issued a permit which (1) authorized the plant to discharge up to half of its effluent into a stream whose waters ultimately entered a river which flowed into Oklahoma, but (2) imposed various conditions, including a provision that the permit would be modified if a pending study determined that more stringent limitations were necessary to insure compliance with Oklahoma's water quality standards. Oklahoma authorities, challenging the permit before the EPA, alleged that the plant's discharge violated Oklahoma standards prohibiting any degradation of water quality in the river in question. An administrative law judge (ALJ) affirmed the issuance of the permit on the ground that the discharge would not have an "undue impact" on Oklahoma waters; but the EPA's Chief Judicial Officer (CJO), remanding for application of a different standard of review, interpreted Oklahoma's ban on degradation of the river in question as allowing the permit to be upheld if the record showed by a preponderance of the evidence that the authorized discharges would not cause an actual detectable violation of Oklahoma water quality standards. On remand, the ALJ made detailed factual findings and determined that the CJO's standard had been met. The CJO sustained the issuance of the permit. The Superior Court, Elkhart County, Indiana, upheld the Indiana tax sale statute against constitutional challenge by a mortgagee who contended that it had not received constitutionally adequate notice of the pending tax sale of and the opportunity to redeem the property following the tax sale since it was not informed of the pending sale either by the county auditor or by the mortgagor, who had been informed of the sale. The auditor, following the state law, had posted a notice of the sale in the county courthouse and published a notice once each week for three consecutive weeks. The Indiana Court of Appeals affirmed (427 NE2d 686).

A union which was the certified bargaining agent of all of an employer's "production and maintenance employees," but not of its "salaried technical" employees, and which had a collective bargaining agreement with the employer requiring the arbitration of all unresolved disputes involving the "interpretation, application or claimed violation" of the agreement, filed a grievance asserting that certain employees represented by another union, which was the certified bargaining representative for the employer's "salaried, technical" employees, were performing production and maintenance work. When the employer refused to arbitrate, the first union petitioned the New York Supreme Court for an order compelling arbitration. The court refused, the Appellate Division affirmed (15 App Div 2d 7, 221 NYS2d 303), and the New York Court of Appeals affirmed on the ground that the matter was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the National Labor Relations Board because it involved a definition of bargaining units. (11 NY2d 452, 230 NYS2d 703, 184 NE2d 298.)

In 1911 a testator devised to the city of Macon, Georgia, a tract of land to be used as a park for white people only; the will provided that the park should be under the control of a board of managers, all of whom were to be white. The city kept the park segregated for some years, but in time let Negroes use it, taking the position that the park was a public facility which it could not constitutionally operate on a segregated basis. Thereupon, individual members of the board of managers brought the present suit in a Georgia state court against the city and others, asking that the city be removed as trustee and that the court appoint new trustees, to whom title to the park would be transferred. Several Negro citizens of Macon intervened, alleging that the racial limitation was contrary to the laws of the United States, and asking that the court refuse to appoint private trustees. Thereafter the city resigned as trustee. Other heirs of the testator intervened, asking for reversion of the trust property to the testator's estate in the event that the court refused to substitute new trustees for the city. The state court accepted the resignation of the city as trustee and appointed three individuals as new trustees, finding it unnecessary to pass on the other claims of the heirs. On appeal by the Negro intervenors, the Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed. (220 Ga 280, 138 SE2d 573.)

The Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York found appellant guilty of violating a New York criminal obscenity statute by hiring others to prepare obscene books, publishing such books, and possessing them with intent to sell them (26 Misc 2d 152, 207 NYS2d 390); his conviction was affirmed by the Appellate Division, First Department. (17 App Div 2d 243, 234 NYS2d 342.) The Court of Appeals affirmed without opinion. (15 NY2d 671, 255 NYS2d 881, 204 NE2d 209, remittitur amended 15 NY2d 724, 256 NYS2d 936, 205 NE2d 201.)
Petition for writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit denied. Justice Barrett took no part in the consideration or decision of this petition.

A labor dispute between the steel industry and its employees was referred by the President to the Federal Wage Stabilization Board. The Board's recommendation resulted in no settlement. When the union gave notice of a nation-wide strike, the President issued an executive order directing the Secretary of Commerce to take possession of and operate most of the steel mills throughout the country and to promulgate additional rules and regulations consistent with the policy proclaimed and needed to effectuate this policy. The order was not based upon any statutory authority. It contained a finding that the President's action was necessary to avoid a national catastrophe, since a work stoppage would immediately imperil the national defense at a time when American armed forces were fighting in Korea. The President immediately informed Congress of his action and stated his intention to abide by the legislative will.

The government instituted condemnation proceedings in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Washington to condemn a leasehold interest in certain lands owned by a railroad (the government having contracted to also acquire the railroad's fee). The lessee had erected buildings and improvements on the property during the lessee's occupancy under a series of leases from the railroad since 1919, the current lease having 7 1/2 years to run. The District Court accepted the lessee's contention that in determining the value of the leasehold interest, the lessee was entitled to the full market value of the use of the land and buildings, without limitation of such use to the remainder of the term of the lease, thus including consideration of the possibility of renewal of the lease. On appeal, the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed, accepting the government's theory that a tenant's expectancy in a lease renewal was not a compensable legal interest and could not be included in the valuation of structures erected by the tenant, which valuation was limited to salvage value and loss of use only over the remainder of the lease term (450 F2d 125).

An Interstate Commerce Commission order directed inclusion of the New York, New Haven, and Hartford Railroad Company in a merger of the New York Central and the Pennsylvania Railroad Companies, but approved the merger and authorized its consummation prior to the inclusion of the first railroad. A bondholder of the New York, New Haven, and Hartford Railroad Company petitioned the Commission to reconsider the order, but the petition was denied. The bondholder then instituted an action challenging the merger order in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, which court dismissed the complaint. (261 F Supp 386.)

Twelve days after the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois entered a final order denying his petition for naturalization, a Canadian national served notice of motions to amend certain findings of fact and to grant a new trial. Although the motions were not timely, since they were not filed within 10 days of the entry of the final order, the government did not object to the timeliness of the motions and the District Court specifically declared that the motion for new trial was made "in ample time." The motions were denied and the Canadian national appealed to the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit within 60 days of the denial of the motions but not within 60 days of the entry of the final order appealed from. The Court of Appeals dismissed the appeal on the ground that the post-trial motions did not toll the running of the 60-day time period for appeal, because the motions were untimely. (318 F2d 681.)

A Jacksonville, Florida, ordinance prohibits showing films containing nudity by a drive-in movie theater when its screen is visible from a public street or place. The manager of a drive-in theater, after having been charged with violating the ordinance, brought a declaratory action in the Circuit Court, Duval County, Florida, alleging that the ordinance violated his First Amendment rights. The trial court upheld the ordinance as a legitimate exercise of the municipality's police power. The District Court of Appeal, First District of Florida, affirmed (288 So 2d 260) and the Florida Supreme Court denied certiorari (294 So 2d 93).

In response to racial tension in a community and its schools, the Board of Education and the teachers union in Jackson, Michigan added a provision to their collective bargaining agreement under which, if it were to become necessary to lay off teachers, those with the most seniority would be retained, except that at no time would there be a greater percentage of minority teachers laid off than the percentage of minority teachers employed at the time of the layoff. This provision was designed to preserve the effects of a hiring policy whose goal had been to increase the percentage of minority teachers in the school system. When layoffs became necessary, the board adhered to the provision, with the result that certain nonminority teachers were laid off while minority teachers with less seniority were retained. The displaced nonminority teachers brought suit in United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, alleging violation of the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court dismissed the teachers' claims, holding that the racial preferences were permissible as an attempt to remedy societal discrimination by providing role models for minority schoolchildren (546 F Supp 1195). The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed on similar grounds (746 F2d 1152).

A Texas tax on the occupation of "gathering gas," measured by the entire volume of gas "taken," was upheld by the Texas Court of Civil Appeals, as applied to interstate natural gas pipeline companies which took gas from the outlet of an independent gasoline plant within Texas for the purpose of immediate interstate transmission.

In 1966, a New York state court convicted the respondent of a felony and used the respondent's 1964 Tennessee murder conviction as a predicate for sentencing the respondent as a second offender. The respondent's first Tennessee trial, in 1954, had resulted in a conviction, but the conviction was overturned in 1964 in federal habeas corpus proceedings, on the ground that the respondent had been denied the effective assistance of counsel at the 1954 trial. The respondent's second Tennessee trial, which resulted in another conviction, occurred in 1964, by which time the prosecution's principal witness at the first trial had become a resident of Sweden. The witness' son, who lived in Texas, testified at the second Tennessee trial that the witness was residing in Sweden, and a transcript of the witness' testimony at the first trial was admitted in evidence at the second trial. In habeas corpus proceedings in the United States District Court for the Western District of New York, the respondent challenged his New York sentence as a second offender, on the ground that his 1964 Tennessee conviction had been obtained in violation of his Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment right to confront the witness. The District Court denied relief, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed, holding that the 1964 Tennessee conviction had been obtained in violation of the respondent's right of confrontation and was thus an improper predicate for his New York sentence as a second offender (442 F2d 561).

In proceedings in the United States District Court for the District of Connecticut, a three-judge panel upheld the validity of a Connecticut welfare statute imposing punitive sanctions if a mother of an illegitimate child, receiving benefits under the Federal Social Security Act's Aid to Families with Dependent Children program, did not divulge to officials the name of the child's putative father or institute a paternity action. The court ruled that the Connecticut statute did not conflict with the Social Security Act, or violate due process, equal protection, or privacy rights (365 F Supp 65).

In the course of litigation involving a labor union's challenge to a United States Department of Labor (DOL) regulation which was issued pursuant to the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 (OSH Act) (29 USCS 651 et seq.), and which imposed on only manufacturers certain requirements aimed at insuring that employees were informed of potential hazards posed by chemicals found at their workplace, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit directed the DOL, under threat of contempt, to publish in the Federal Register within 60 days either a hazard communication standard applicable to all workers covered by the OSH Act, including workers in sectors other than manufacturing, or a statement of reasons why such a standard was not feasible. The DOL responded by promulgating a revised regulation which was applicable to employers in all economic sectors, and which also included three provisions--as to labeling and employee training, and as to accessible data sheets concerning health and safety information--which provisions were not contained in the regulation as originally promulgated. At the same time, the DOL submitted the revised regulation to the United States Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1980 (PRA) (44 USCS 3501 et seq.), which generally authorizes OMB review of proposed information collection requests by a federal agency. The OMB disapproved the three new provisions, based on its determination that the requirements were not necessary to protect employees. Although the DOL disagreed with the OMB's assessment, the DOL published notice that the three provisions were withdrawn. The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, in proceedings to enforce a cease and desist order of the National Labor Relations Board, deleted sua sponte certain clauses of the order. (281 F2d 797.) Certiorari granted; judgment reversed and case remanded to the Court of Appeals to enter judgment affirming and enforcing a cease-and-desist order of the National Labor Relations Board as consented to by respondent - without deletion of references to other labor organizations.

A method employed in 1969 for selecting job applicants for positions with a California county's fire department had a disparate impact on the hiring of blacks and Mexican-Americans. The county, voluntarily in 1971, developed new procedures for screening job applicants, such new procedures involving a written examination graded on a pass-fail basis, the selection of 500 of the passing applicants at random for oral interviews and physical agility tests, and the ranking of passing applicants on an eligibility list in terms of the results of the physical agility tests and oral interviews. In 1972 the written test implementing the 1971 procedures was given, but before random selections could be made, an action was brought in a California state court against the county alleging that the random selection process violated provisions of the county charter and civil service regulations. The state court enjoined the county from using the random selection method pending trial on the merits, and ultimately the county, being unable to devise a nonrandom method of screening job applicants and lacking the resources to interview all of the applicants who had passed the 1972 examination, stopped hiring. When vacancies in the fire department increased and manpower needs became critical, the county's Department of Personnel proposed to expedite the hiring of sufficient firefighters to meet immediate urgent requirements by interviewing the top 544 scorers on the 1972 written test, of whom 492 were white, 10 black, and 33 Mexican-American. After federal income tax legislation provided for the deductibility of accelerated depreciation allowances, public utilities, like other taxpayers, could elect to deduct accelerated depreciation rather than straight-line depreciation for tax purposes. However, for purposes of the Federal Power Commission's regulation of utility rates, any utility which used accelerated depreciation for tax purposes was initially required by the Commission to use "normalization," whereby the utility would compute its cost of service for ratemaking purposes as if it had been using straight-line depreciation, so as to avoid giving present customers of the utility the benefit of tax deferral attributable to accelerated depreciation. After it became apparent that through utilities' expansion and replacement of their property, accelerated depreciation was resulting in permanent tax savings rather than mere tax deferral, any utility which used accelerated depreciation for tax purposes was required by the Commission to "flow-through" any tax savings to their customers by using accelerated depreciation in calculating the cost of service for ratemaking purposes. Prior to 1969, a gas transmission company had been using this "flow-through" method of computing accelerated depreciation for ratemaking purposes. However, after the enactment of 441 of the Tax Reform Act of 1969, which dealt with public utilities' depreciation allowances, the company requested the Commission to permit, among other things, that the company change to the "normalization" method of computing accelerated depreciation for ratemaking purposes with respect to property acquired by the company prior to 1970 and with respect to replacement property acquired by the company after 1969. In the early 1980s, as a result of market, contractual, and regulatory forces, interstate natural gas pipeline companies cut back their purchases of gas extracted from the Hugoton field in Kansas. In effect, interstate pipelines used the Hugoton field for storage while they took gas for their immediate needs from elsewhere. This practice was facilitated by a regulation of the Kansas corporation commission that permitted gas producers to extract stored gas essentially at any time. Meanwhile, gas wells in the Hugoton field which were used for intrastate purchases became overproduced. The corporation commission found that the imbalance between overproduced and underproduced Hugoton wells was causing drainage between wells that posed a threat to the correlative rights of producers. In an effort to solve this problem, the corporation commission adopted a regulation providing for the permanent cancellation of producers' rights to extract assigned quantities of gas from the Hugoton field if production was delayed beyond allotted time periods. An interstate pipeline company challenged this regulation on the grounds that it infringed on the jurisdiction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) under the Natural Gas Act (NGA) (15 USCS 717 et seq.) in that the regulation, although directed to producers, affected interstate pipelines' purchasing decisions and hence price structures and required the abandonment of gas dedicated to interstate commerce. The corporation commission ultimately dismissed this challenge.
