This is a companion case to Sears, Roebuck & Co. v Stiffel Company, supra, p. 661. A manufacturer of fluorescent lighting fixtures brought suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois against another such manufacturer, alleging an infringement of its design patent on a lighting reflector and unfair competition by the manufacture and sale of similar fixtures. The District Court held that the design patent was invalid, but enjoined the second manufacturer from unfairly competing with the patentee by the sale of identical or confusingly similar reflectors. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed on the ground that there was substantial evidence to support a finding of likely confusion, and that this finding was sufficient to support a holding of unfair competition under Illinois law. (311 F2d 26.)

After an ex parte investigation, the Interstate Commerce Commission issued an order incorporating findings that certain commodities were not agricultural commodities within the meaning of the provision of the Federal Motor Carrier Act exempting motor vehicles used in carrying such commodities from, inter alia, the statutory requirement of a certificate of public convenience and necessity or a permit issued by the commission. A motor carrier who was not a party to the administrative proceedings sought to enjoin the order of the Commission and the District Court denied relief, holding that the Commission's order was not subject to judicial review.

The Texas legislature adopted a reapportionment plan for Texas' congressional districts. Under the plan, the population of the smallest district (458,581) was approximately 4.1 percent smaller than that of the largest district (477,856), and the average deviation among districts was .745 percent, or 3,421 persons. The plaintiffs challenged the plan in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, and the plaintiffs proposed alternative reapportionment plans known as Plan B and Plan C. Plan B generally followed the redistricting pattern of the legislature's plan, adjusted district lines where necessary to achieve smaller population variances among districts, and involved smaller population variances than either the legislature's plan or Plan C. Plan C substantially disregarded the configuration of districts in the legislature's plan, was based on consideration of no factors other than population, and provided for more compact and contiguous redistricting than either the legislature's plan or Plan B. A three-judge District Court was convened, held that the legislature's plan was unconstitutional, and ordered the implementation of Plan C.

Physicians who provide abortion services brought a class action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois challenging the constitutionality of an Illinois abortion law and seeking declaratory and injunctive relief. A pediatrician moved to intervene as a party defendant and to be appointed guardian ad litem for fetuses who survive abortion, based on his conscientious objection to abortions and on his status as a pediatrician and as a parent of an unemancipated minor daughter. The District Court granted the motion, without indicating whether the intervention was permissive or as of right. Ultimately, the District Court permanently enjoined the enforcement of certain provisions of the law which impose criminal liability on physicians for violating prescribed standards of care for performing abortions and the requirements for furnishing a patient with particular abortion-related information (579 F Supp 464). The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed and also permanently enjoined the enforcement of another provision (749 F2d 452). The pediatrician filed a notice of appeal to the United States Supreme Court and a jurisdictional statement. The state of Illinois did not appeal, but filed a "letter of interest" with the Supreme Court under Supreme Court Rule 10.4, stating in the letter that the state's interest was identical to that advanced by it in the lower courts and was essentially coterminous with the pediatrician's position.

The defendant, convicted in Ohio state court of burglary and sentenced to life imprisonment, sought to file a copy of an earlier notice of an appeal and of a motion for leave to appeal in the Supreme Court of Ohio. In involuntary bankruptcy proceedings against a stockbroker in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, the referee adjudicated the broker an involuntary bankrupt, holding that the appointment of a liquidator by a stock exchange when the broker, undertaking self- liquidation, availed itself of the exchange's special trust fund established to avoid bankruptcy of member firms, constituted an act of bankruptcy under the provisions of 3a(5) of the Bankruptcy Act, relating to the appointment of a "receiver or trustee." The bankruptcy court denied a petition to review the referee's order, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed, holding that the appointment of the liquidator was not an act of bankruptcy (471 F2d 178). After the United States Supreme Court had granted certiorari to review the judgment of the Court of Appeals, the bankruptcy court entered an unappealed order confirming an arrangement under Chapter XI of the Bankruptcy Act, the broker's petition for relief under Chapter XI having been filed after the referee's order was entered in the involuntary bankruptcy proceedings (471 F2d 178).

Negro employees of southern railroads brought a suit against a labor union, their exclusive bargaining representative under the Railway Labor Act, to enjoin compliance with a collective labor agreement, negotiated by the union, which discriminated against colored firemen by denominating them as "not promotable," while white firemen were "promotable" under the agreement. The suit was brought in the District of Columbia, under a statute permitting an action to be maintained if the defendant was found within the district.

Section 16's definition of a crime of violence is divided into two clauses‚Äîoften referred to as the elements clause, ¬ß 16(a), and the residual clause, ¬ß 16(b). The residual clause, the provision at issue here, defines a ‚Äúcrime of violence‚Äù as ‚Äúany other offense that is a felony and that, by its nature, involves a substantial risk that physical force against the person or property of another may be used in the course of committing the offense.‚Äù To decide whether a person's conviction falls within the scope of that clause, courts apply the categorical approach. This approach has courts ask not whether ‚Äúthe particular facts‚Äù underlying a conviction created a substantial risk, Leocal v. United States, 550 U.S. 192, 208, 127 S.Ct. 1586, 167 L.Ed.2d 532.

The petitioner, a sergeant in the United States Army, who after entering the service had acquired a bona fide domicil in Texas, instituted an original mandamus proceeding in the Supreme Court of Texas to require his local election officials to permit him to vote. The issue was whether a provision of the Texas Constitution prohibiting any member of the Armed Forces of the United States who moved his home to Texas during the course of his military duty from ever voting in any election in that state so long as he was a member of the Armed Forces deprived petitioner of a right secured by the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Supreme Court of Texas decided that it did not and refused to issue the writ, two justices dissenting. (378 SW2d 304.)

Two laborers who worked for a railroad at its Virginia terminal, where coal was loaded from railway cars to ships on navigable waters, were injured while they were engaged in cleaning spilled coal from the loading equipment, which task was one of their employment duties. In an unrelated incident at another Virginia coal loading terminal, a pier machinist who was employed by another railroad was injured while engaged in his primary job of repairing that railroad's coal loading equipment. The three employees commenced separate actions in Virginia trial courts against the railroads, seeking damages for their personal injuries under the Federal Employers' Liability Act (45 USCS 51-60). In each case, the railroad challenged the trial court's jurisdiction on the ground that the employee's exclusive remedy was provided by the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act (LHWCA) (33 USCS 901-950; later renamed). The trial courts concluded that the employees in each case were covered by the LHWCA, and dismissed the employees' suits. All three employees appealed. Reviewing the judgments against the two laborers on consolidated appeal, the Supreme Court of Virginia reversed, holding that the laborers were not covered by the LHWCA since they had been performing purely maintenance tasks, and thus that they should be treated no differently under the LHWCA than those who were excluded because they performed purely clerical tasks (235 Va 27, 365 SE2d 742). Subsequently, in an unpublished order, the Virginia Supreme Court also reversed the trial court's judgment in the pier machinist's case, relying on its decision in the laborers' case.

The defendant railroad moved assembled units of a locomotive and a substantial number of cars a substantial distance (2 miles), without stops or with a stop preceded and followed by a mile of uninterrupted travel, from its classification yard to the track of a consignee, or vice versa, for the purpose of delivering the cars. The only operable brakes were those upon the engine. The present suit for statutory penalties, instituted by the United States, charged the railroad with the operation of trains in violation of the Safety Appliance Act, which, in 1 and 9, requires every "train" moving in interstate traffic to have power brakes on not less than 50 per cent of the cars. The District Court rendered judgment for the defendant on the theory that the movements complained of were properly classified as switching movements. The Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed by a divided vote. (258 F2d 262.)

A company with an office in Minnesota had a pension plan, under which employees could receive a pension upon retirement at age 65 regardless of length of service. Furthermore, an employee's right to a pension vested prior to age 65 if certain requirements as to length of service and age were met. The company was the sole contributor to the pension fund, but the plan neither required the company to make specific contributions nor imposed any sanction for failing to contribute adequately. The company retained a virtually unrestricted right to amend the plan, and was free to terminate it and distribute the assets at any time according to a predetermined method. Minnesota enacted a statute, under which private employers of 100 or more employees providing pension benefits under qualified plans were subject to a "pension funding charge" upon termination of the plan or closing of an office within the state. The charge was assessed if pension funds were not sufficient to cover full pensions for all employees working at least 10 years. After enactment of the statute, in a move planned before its passage, the company closed its Minnesota office. Several discharged employees, who had no vested pension rights under the plan, were nonetheless pension obligees under the statute. The state notified the company that it owed a significant pension funding charge, and the company brought suit in the United States District Court for the District of Minnesota for injunctive and declaratory relief, claiming that the act unconstitutionally impaired its contractual obligation to its employees under its pension agreement. A three-judge District Court upheld the statute as applied to the company (449 F Supp 644).

Defendants arrested by state officers on a vagrancy charge while sitting in a parked automobile were convicted in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky of conspiring to rob a federally insured bank, largely on evidence obtained by the state officers' search of the car after the defendants had been arrested, searched, and taken to police headquarters, and the car had been removed to a garage. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed, rejecting the defendants' contention, timely made in the courts below, that the search and seizure violated the Fourth Amendment.

During a criminal trial in a Pennsylvania state court in 1966, the three defendants committed various disrespectful and disruptive acts, and after a verdict of guilty was returned, the trial judge sentenced them on contempt charges, the two defendants in the case at bar having been sentenced to terms totaling 11 to 22 years and 6 to 12 years, respectively. In 1971, the United States Supreme Court, in Mayberry v Pennsylvania, 400 US 455, 27 L Ed 2d 532, 91 S Ct 499, vacated the third defendant's contempt conviction and remanded for a retrial of the contempt charges before a different judge, and the defendants in the instant case were also retried in separate proceedings before another judge, who denied requests for jury trials and found the defendants guilty of the various contempt charges, sentencing them to no more than 6 months on any single count, but ordering that the sentences were to be served consecutively, thus resulting in an aggregate sentence for one defendant of 3 years and 3 months, and an aggregate sentence for the other defendant of 2 years and 8 months. The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania affirmed (453 Pa 619, 306 A2d 294).

The defendant Negro, charged in an Alabama state court with murder of a white man, failed to raise before trial, as required by state law, the issue of systematic exclusion of Negroes from jury service. However, the issue was raised after conviction in his motion for a new trial. The trial judge sustained objections to all questions concerning systematic discrimination and denied the motion. The Supreme Court of Alabama affirmed the conviction, finding that the defendant's claim of jury discrimination was not supported by any evidence. (276 Ala 513, 164 So 2d 704.)

A New Jersey prisoner (1) who had been convicted in a state trial of sexual assault and unlawful possession of a weapon, and (2) whose direct state appeals had been unsuccessful, filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus in the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey. Finding that the prisoner's constitutional rights had been violated at his state trial, the District Court in effect ordered that the prisoner be released unless within 30 days the state afforded the prisoner a new trial (629 F Supp 511). Subsequently, the District Court denied a motion for a stay of the release order, pending a state appeal of the decision, and the District Court expressed the view that (1) under Federal Court of Appeals precedent, such a stay could be granted only if it was demonstrated that there was a risk that the prisoner would not appear for subsequent proceedings, and (2) no such showing had been made. In turn, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit--although willing to consider a state appeal of the District Court's decision--summarily denied a motion for a stay, pending consideration of the appeal, of the District Court's release order.

A portion of the citizen suit provision ( 6972(b)(1)) states that except under certain circumstances, no action may be commenced against an alleged violator prior to 60 days after the plaintiff has given notice of the alleged violation to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the state in which the alleged violation occurred, and the alleged violator. One who was convicted in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts of 75 counts of making false claims against the government was committed to the Attorney General pursuant to 18 USC 4208(b) pending a study to be used "as a basis for determining the sentence to be imposed," and more than three months after the commitment order the court suspended sentence and placed the defendant on probation. The defendant's appeal within 10 days from the order placing him on probation was dismissed as untimely by the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, on the ground that the time for appeal expired 10 days after entry of the commitment order. (307 F2d 839.)

After passing a competitive civil service examination, the plaintiffs, honorably discharged veterans, had been appointed attorneys in the Department of Agriculture under wartime civil service regulations which provided that a person so appointed shall not acquire a classified civil service status. Because of a reduction in force they were separated from service, although nonveteran attorneys with classified civil service status were retained under the pertinent regulations. Subsequently the plaintiffs were denied reemployment, although the Department rehired some nonveteran attorneys, who had been released with the plaintiffs, with a lower reduction-in-force priority under these regulations than the plaintiffs. Upon these facts the plaintiffs charged infringement of both their retention preference and reemployment preference, in violation of the provisions of the Veterans Preference Act.

A defendant and his codefendant were indicted in a Maine Superior Court on several counts of theft by receiving stolen goods, and the defendant who was represented by a retained counsel pleaded not guilty to the charges. Without the knowledge of the defendant, his codefendant, accompanied by his lawyer, met with police officers and gave full confessions of his participation with the defendant in committing the crimes for which they had been indicted. The codefendant also accepted the deal offered by the police officers that no further charges would be brought against him if he would testify against the defendant and otherwise co-operate in the prosecution of the defendant on the pending charges. Subsequently, the police arranged to have the codefendant wear a body recorder/transmitter at a meeting between the defendant and his codefendant for the purpose of planning a defense strategy for their upcoming trial. The defendant did in fact make incriminating statements during that meeting. The defendant filed a pretrial motion to suppress the recorded incriminating statements he made to his codefendant as having been obtained in violation of his right to the assistance of counsel under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments, but the trial court denied this motion on the ground that the recordings were made in order to gather information concerning the anonymous threats which the codefendant had been receiving and to protect the codefendant, and also to gather information concerning the defendant's plan to kill a prosecution's witness. The defendant was convicted of some of the charges after some of his recorded incriminating statements made at the meeting with his codefendant were admitted in evidence. The Supreme Judicial Court of Maine reversed and remanded for a new trial,

A competitor of a Japanese corporation, which manufactured electric razors in Japan and sold them to American distributors, filed patent infringement and unfair competition claims in an action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida against the Japanese corporation and one of its American distributors. The distributor counterclaimed against the competitor for alleged antitrust violations. The District Court (1) entered judgment for the competitor on its patent infringement claim, and neither defendant appealed such judgment; (2) entered judgment for the competitor on the antitrust counterclaim; and (3) ordered a new trial on the unfair competition claim. On interlocutory appeal by the distributor, the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit reversed the judgment on the antitrust counterclaim and remanded the case for a new trial. The Japanese corporation took no further part in the litigation for some time. In a second trial, the District Court entered judgments for the distributor on both the unfair competition claim and the antitrust counterclaim. The competitor appealed both judgments to the Court of Appeals. While the appeal was pending, the competitor and the distributor entered into a settlement agreement in which they agreed jointly to request that the Court of Appeals vacate the District Court's judgments. After the competitor and the distributor filed their joint motion to vacate, the Japanese corporation filed a motion to intervene for purposes of opposing vacatur. The Court of Appeals (1) denied the motion to intervene; and (2) granted the vacatur motion because the settlement motion included all the parties to the appeal (971 F2d 728). The United States Supreme Court granted the Japanese corporation's petition

However, in 104(b)(2) and 106(c) of the NGPA (15 USCS 3314(b)(2), 3316(c)), the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC)--the successor agency to the FPC--was authorized to prescribe a maximum lawful ceiling price for "any" sale of old gas "or category thereof, as determined by" the FERC, so long as such price was (1) higher than the maximum lawful price which would otherwise be applicable under the NGPA, and (2) "just and reasonable" within the meaning of the Natural Gas Act of 1938 (15 USCS 717 et seq.). The plaintiff, while a resident of Illinois, purchased from a British company licensed to do business in Illinois, Florida, and other states, a contract of insurance providing world-wide coverage against "all risks" of loss or damage to the property covered. Some months thereafter the plaintiff, having moved to Florida, instituted the present diversity of citizenship action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida to recover losses sustained in Florida and caused by deliberate acts of plaintiff's wife. The litigation presented three issues: (1) whether the "all risks" coverage of the policy included losses resulting from wilful injury to or appropriation of the injured property by the insured's spouse; (2) whether, as a matter of Florida law, a Florida statute invalidating contract provisions fixing the period of time for bringing suit under the contract was applicable to the insurance contract involved, the suit not having been brought within 12 months of the discovery of the loss, as required by the insurance policy; and (3) whether, as a matter of federal constitutional law, the Florida statute mentioned above could be applied to the insurance policy purchased in a sister state under the circumstances described above. The District Court entered judgment upon a verdict for the plaintiff and denied a motion for judgment non obstante veredicto. On appeal, the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed, sustaining the defense based upon the suit clause of the insurance contract on the ground that Florida could not apply its statute to the Illinois-made contract consistently with the requirement of due process. (265 F2d 522.)

The defendants, officers, directors, and employees of a nationwide corporation, also a defendant, were indicted in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia for having used the mails "for the purpose of executing" a fraudulent scheme in violation of 18 USC 1341 and for conspiring to so use the mails. The indictment alleged that the defendants, pursuant to a preconceived scheme, pretending to be able to help businessmen to obtain loans or sell out their businesses, obtained from their victims applications for the corporate defendant's services and advance payments, and thereafter mailed to the victims the accepted application and a form letter for the purpose of lulling them into a feeling of security. The District Court dismissed 34 of 43 substantive counts on the ground that these counts did not charge a federal offense, since the money had already been obtained by the defendants before the acceptances were mailed, and hence these mailings could not have been "for the purpose of executing" the scheme.

The petitioner sought habeas corpus relief in the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri, claiming that he was denied counsel on an appeal taken by him to the Supreme Court of Missouri from his conviction of robbery in a Missouri state court. In the Missouri proceedings the petitioner's trial counsel withdrew from the case after filing a motion for a new trial and notice for appeal. The Missouri Supreme Court required preparation of the transcript for appeal, and considered the questions raised by the motion for new trial without appointing counsel for the indigent petitioner. The United States District Court denied relief, but the Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit vacated the judgment of the District Court, holding that the Missouri practice then in force was invalid. (363 F.2d 154.)

The Western Union Telegraph Company, a New York corporation with its principal place of business in that state and offices in all the other states, in the District of Columbia, and in foreign countries, held a substantial amount of undisbursed money arising out of money orders bought in Pennsylvania offices to be transmitted to payees chiefly in other states. As against the company's objection that Pennsylvania had no right to take ownership of these intangibles for itself, the Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas for Dauphin County declared the unclaimed obligations escheated. (73 Dauph Co 160, 74 Dauph Co 49.) The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania affirmed. (400 Pa 337, 162 A2d 617.)

In a class action on behalf of all federal employees, a three-judge United States District Court for the District of Columbia declared unconstitutional and enjoined enforcement of those provisions of the Hatch Act enacted into positive law in 5 USCS 7324(a)(2), which forbids federal employees to "take an active part in political management or in political campaigns" (346 F Supp 578).

An ice peddlers' union sought to break down the resistance of nonmember peddlers to efforts to get them to join the union, with the ultimate objective of obtaining better wages and working conditions, by inducing wholesale distributors to agree not to sell ice to nonunion peddlers. Such an agreement was illegal under a state statute declaring combinations in restraint of trade to be unlawful. A distributor having refused so to agree, the union resorted to peaceful picketing, the effect of which, in consequence of refusal of union members to cross the picket line, was to reduce its business by 85%. In a suit to enjoin the picketing, the union asserted that they were merely exercising their constitutional right to publicize the existence of a labor dispute and the fact that the distributor was selling ice to nonmembers of the union.

The defendants, in operating iron mills on the banks of a navigable river, discharged industrial solids in the river, thereby reducing the depth of its channel. The United States brought suit for injunctive relief in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. The District Court granted an injunction. (155 F Supp 442.) On appeal, the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed the decree appealed from and remanded the cause with directions to dismiss the complaint. (264 F2d 289.) This decision was rested on the grounds that (1) the deposits in question did not constitute an "obstruction" within the meaning of 10 of the Rivers and Harbors Act of 1899, prohibiting the creation of any obstruction, not affirmatively authorized by Congress, to the navigable capacity of any of the waters of the United States; (2) defendants' activities did not constitute a violation of 13 of the act, forbidding the discharge of any refuse matter into any navigable water, by reason of the exception contained in 13 of refuse "flowing from streets and sewers and passing therefrom in a liquid state"; and (3) that even if violations of the act were shown, no relief by injunction was permitted.

The employer had its managers rate the employees based on performance, flexibility, and critical skills, with the statistically improbable result that 30 of the 31 employees who were laid off were at least 40 years of age. The employees asserted a disparate-impact claim under the under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), 29 U.S.C.S. _ 621 et seq., and the employer contended that any disparate impact based on age was excepted from liability under 29 U.S.C.S. _ 623(f)(1) based on the employer's reliance on reasonable factors other than age (RFOA). The U.S. Supreme Court held that the burden was improperly placed on the employees to show that the employer's criteria were unreasonable, since RFOA was an affirmative defense for which the employer bore both the burden of production and the burden of persuasion. The ADEA set out liability exemptions, including RFOA, in provisions separate from the age discrimination prohibitions and, while the employees were required to identify the challenged layoff factors, the employer that sought to benefit from the RFOA exemption was required to prove that the exemption applied.

The Court has held that "the Second Amendment extends, prima facie, to all instruments that constitute bearable arms, even those that were not in existence at the time of the founding," District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U. 5. 570, 582 (2008), and that this "Second Amendment right is fully applicable to the States," McDonald v. Chicago, 561 U. 5. 742, 750 (2010). In this case, the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts upheld a Massachusetts law prohibiting the possession of stun guns after examining "whether a stun gun is the type of weapon contemplated by Congress in 1789 as being protected by the Second Amendment." The judgment of the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts is vacated, and the case is remanded for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion.

Without disclosing his knowledge about the prospective takeover bids, the employee purchased stock in the target companies and then sold his purchased shares for a profit immediately after the takeover attempts were made public. Following an investigation of the employee's stock trading activities by the Securities and Exchange Commission, the employee entered into a consent decree in which he agreed to return the profits he had made as a result of his activities, and thereafter he was also indicted and convicted at a jury trial in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York under 32(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 USCS 78ff(a)), making it a crime to willfully violate the Act, for his having violated 10(b) of the Act (15 USCS 78j(b)), which prohibits the use "in connection with the purchase or sale of any security ... While serving as a volunteer teacher at a "Freedom School" for Negro children in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, a white woman from New York entered a store restaurant with six of her students for the purpose of eating lunch. A waitress took the students' orders, but refused to serve the teacher because she was a white person in the company of Negroes. Upon her departure from the store, the teacher was arrested by the Hattiesburg police on a charge of vagrancy. She brought suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York against the store to recover damages under 42 USC 1983, which provides a civil action for the deprivation of civil rights "under color of any statute, ordinance, regulation, custom or usage, of any State or Territory." The first count of the complaint alleged that the store's refusal to serve the teacher violated her right under the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment not to be discriminated against on the basis of race, since the refusal had been pursuant to a custom of the community to segregate races in public eating places. Because the teacher was unable to prove at the trial that there were other instances in Hattiesburg of a white person having been refused service while in the company of Negroes, the District Court directed a verdict in favor of the store. The second count of the complaint, alleging that both the refusal of service and the subsequent arrest had been the product of a conspiracy between the store and the police to violate the teacher's right to equal protection of the laws, was dismissed before trial on a motion for summary judgment for failure "to allege any facts from which a conspiracy might be inferred." The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed as to both counts

As an aid to the construction of the railroad, every alternate section of public land on each side of the road was also granted in 3, which further provided that "all mineral lands shall be excepted from the operation of this act." The issue was whether, as claimed by the United States, the grant of "the right of way" included mineral rights.

A retailer of burial monuments and bronze grave markers brought an action in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia for damages and injunctive relief under 4 and 16 of the Clayton Act, alleging that five cemetery operators and a manufacturer of bronze grave markers had violated 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act by conspiring to monopolize and monopolizing the manufacture and sale of such markers. Specifically, the defendants were charged with having jointly adopted various restrictive devices to prevent, restrict, and discourage sales of markers by the plaintiff for installation in the cemeteries. After extensive pretrial discovery, the District Court granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment, concluding that there was no material issue of fact and no evidence of conspiracy. (290 F Supp 1.) The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed. (404 F2d 1008.)

After an economic strike in August, 1964, during which the employer cut back its production schedule, six strikers applied for reinstatement on August 20 and on a number of other occasions. The employer rejected their applications because no jobs were available at the time, but between October 8 and 16 it hired six new employees for jobs which the strikers were qualified to fill. It reinstated the strikers during the period from November 2 through December 14. The National Labor Relations Board concluded that the employer had been guilty of an unfair labor practice in discriminating against the strikers (153 NLRB 425), but the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit denied enforcement of the Board's order, reasoning that the strikers' right of reinstatement must be judged as of August 20, when in fact there were no jobs available. (366 F2d 126.)

Actions charging organized professional baseball clubs with violations of the Sherman Anti-trust Act were dismissed by the District Courts and the dismissals affirmed by the Courts of Appeals on the ground that the business of providing public baseball games for profit between clubs of professional baseball players was not within the scope of the federal antitrust laws.

A city ordinance in Newport, Kentucky prohibited the performance of nude or nearly nude activity on the premises of a business establishment licensed to sell liquor for consumption on the premises. Proprietors of Newport liquor establishments that offered nude or nearly nude entertainment sought declaratory and injunctive relief under 42 USCS 1983 against the enforcement of the ordinance, claiming that it deprived them of their rights under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. The trial court upheld the constitutionality of the ordinance based on the United States Supreme Court's decision in New York State Liquor Authority v Bellanca (1981) 425 US 714, 69 L Ed 2d 357, 101 S Ct 2599, in which a state law imposing an almost identical prohibition was upheld as being within the state's broad power under the Federal Constitution's Twenty-first Amendment to regulate the sale of liquor within its boundaries. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed and remanded, finding the decision in Bellanca inapplicable because Kentucky's constitution authorizes local voters, rather than the city or the state, to determine whether alcohol may be sold; and the Court of Appeals ruled that the city could not exercise in part a power it did not hold in full (785 F2d 1354).

In the United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi, a Choctaw Indian was indicted by a federal grand jury for assault with intent to kill, in violation of the Major Crimes Act of 1885 (18 USCS 1153) and 18 USCS 113(a), and was convicted of the lesser included offense of simple assault. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed, holding that the District Court was without jurisdiction over the case because the lands designated as a reservation for the Choctaw Indians residing in Mississippi, and on which the offense took place, were not "Indian country," and that, therefore, 1153 did not provide a basis for federal criminal prosecution (560 F2d 1202). After the conviction in the District Court, but before the reversal of the conviction, the Choctaw was convicted in the Circuit Court of Leake County, Mississippi, of aggravated assault in violation of state law, on the basis of an indictment relating to the same incident which was the basis of the federal conviction. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Mississippi affirmed, holding that the Federal District Court had been without jurisdiction to prosecute the defendant, and that, therefore, his arguments against state jurisdiction were without merit (347 So 2d 959).

The State of Maryland, joined by other states, instituted an action in the United States District Court for the District of Maryland, attacking the validity of amendments to the Fair Labor Standards Act which extended minimum wage and maximum hours coverage to schools and hospitals including those operated by the states or their subdivisions, and which adopted the "enterprise concept," expanding coverage to protect every employee employed in an enterprise engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, and defining such an enterprise as one which, with other qualifications, has employees engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce. The District Court concluded that the amendments did not exceed the power of Congress under the commerce clause. (269 F Supp 826.)

One week after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States, Congress passed the Authorization for Use of Military Force resolution (AUMF) (115 Stat 224, note following 50 U.S.C.S. _ 1541), which included authorization for the President to use "all necessary and appropriate force" against "nations, organizations, or persons" associated with the September 11 attacks. In May 2002, an individual, who was a United States citizen, was apprehended within the United States by federal agents supposedly executing a material-witness warrant issued by the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, in connection with a grand jury investigation into the September 11 attacks. The individual, through his appointed counsel, moved to vacate the warrant. This motion was still pending on June 9, 2002, when the President issued to the Secretary of Defense an order that (1) designated the individual as an "enemy combatant"; (2) directed the Secretary to detain the individual in military custody; (3) invoked the AUMF and the President's authority (under the Federal Constitution's Art II, _ 2, cl 1) as "Commander in Chief"; and (4) asserted that the individual was closely associated with an international terrorist organization with which the United States was at war. Meanwhile, the Federal Government (1) notified the District Court ex parte concerning these developments, and (2) asked the court to vacate the material-witness warrant (which the court did).

An autonomous government instrumentality in Puerto Rico was responsible for providing water and sewer service to the inhabitants of Puerto Rico. The instrumentality was sued by a private engineering firm in a diversity action in the United States District Court for the District of Puerto Rico. The engineering firm, which was incorporated in Delaware, alleged (1) breach of contract, and (2) damage to the firm's business reputation. The instrumentality, alleging that it was an "arm" of the state and that the action was therefore prohibited by the Federal Constitution's Eleventh Amendment, moved to dismiss the action. The District Court--finding that, because the instrumentality's ability to raise funds for payment of its contractual obligations would not affect Puerto Rico's funds, the instrumentality did not qualify for immunity under the Eleventh Amendment--denied the motion to dismiss. The instrumentality appealed such denial to the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. The Court of Appeals, noting that Puerto Rico was to be treated as a state for Eleventh Amendment purposes, dismissed the appeal for want of appellate jurisdiction and expressed the view that states and their agencies were barred from taking an immediate appeal from a District Court's denial of a motion to dismiss based on a claim of Eleventh Amendment immunity (945 F2d 10).

A dispute arose between a stock-trade-clearing firm and a husband and wife as to whether the couple was personally liable to the firm for a debt to the firm of an investment company which was wholly owned by the husband. The firm sought arbitration, by a panel of a stock exchange, of this dispute and some related disputes. The investment company, which had signed a document containing an arbitration clause, accepted arbitration, but the couple (1) had not personally signed that document; (2) denied that the couple's dispute was arbitrable; and (3) filed written objections to that effect with the arbitration panel. However, the arbitrators (1) decided that they had the power to rule on the merits of the parties' dispute; and (2) did so in the firm's favor. Under the Arbitration Act (9 USCS 1 et seq.), the couple asked the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania to vacate the arbitration award, while the firm requested the award's confirmation. The District Court confirmed the award. On appeal, however, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, in reversing in pertinent part, agreed with the couple that the couple's dispute with the firm was not arbitrable (19 F3d 1503).

An individual who, at the time, was a member of Congress was indicted for conspiracy to violate, and for substantive counts of violating, 18 USCS 201, which forbids a public official from accepting a bribe in return for being influenced in the performance of official acts. The individual moved to dismiss the indictment in the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey, arguing, among other things, that the indictment violated the speech or debate clause of the Federal Constitution (Art I, 6) because the grand jury had heard evidence concerning legislative acts, the basis for the indictment being the individual's introduction of certain private bills in the House of Representatives. The District Court held that the speech or debate clause did not require dismissal of the indictment. Subsequently, the individual petitioned the United States Court of Appeals to the Third Circuit for a writ of mandamus to compel the District Court to dismiss the indictment. The Court of Appeals declined to issue the writ (576 F2d 511).

Appellants brought an action in the District Court for the District of Vermont challenging the constitutionality of various provisions of the customs laws and seeking other relief including damages. A three-judge court was convened, and it held that it had jurisdiction under the Tucker Act (28 USCS 1346(a)(2)), rejected appellants constitutional claims, enjoined appellees from applying the customs laws except as construed by the court, declined to remit appellants' fines and returned the question of damages to the single-judge District Court (370 F Supp 312).

The defendant, a Negro, was indicted for murder of a white woman by an all-white grand jury in the Parish of Orleans, Louisiana. His motion to quash the indictment on the ground that Negroes had been systematically excluded from grand juries in the parish, including the grand jury which returned the indictment against him, was overruled, and he was tried, convicted, and sentenced to death. The Supreme Court of Louisiana affirmed (232 La 289, 94 So2d 262), holding that the record disclosed no discriminatory exclusion of Negroes from his grand jury.

Spouses effected a settlement of their respective property rights for the purposes of a divorce, providing that the agreement should be submitted to the divorce court for its approval and making it conditional upon the entry of the decree. It was also provided that the agreement should survive the divorce decree, and the decree so ordered. The pertinent state law instructed the divorce court to decree an equitable disposition of the properties of the parties.

A New Jersey municipal ordinance which forbids carrying on the business of storing goods for hire without payment of an annual license tax does not violate the Commerce Clause of the Constitution when applied (in the circumstances of this case) to a warehouse in which coal shipped from another state is stored within the municipality under a "transit" privilege, pending a decision by the owner whether to ship it to another state or to another point in the same state -- even though most of the coal actually is shipped to other states.

The defendant, an indigent, had no funds to pay for a transcript of trial proceedings in the Municipal Court of Oklahoma City required to prepare the "case-made" needed to perfect his appeal to the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals from his conviction for drunken driving, but the trial court refused, in the absence of statutory authority, to order that a copy of the transcript be provided at public expense, and the Court of Criminal Appeals, in an original proceeding brought by the defendant, also refused to order that he be provided a copy at public expense, agreeing with the trial court that no statute or ordinance authorized such an order, and holding further that the Fourteenth Amendment did not mandate that an indigent person convicted of a violation of a city ordinance, quasi-criminal in nature and often referred to as a petty offense, is entitled to a case-made or transcript at city expense in order to perfect an appeal from the conviction (439 P2d 965).

At the defendant's jury trial in the Supreme Court of Bronx County, New York, confessions which police officers had obtained from the defendant were found voluntary and were admitted in evidence. The defendant was convicted of murder, and the Appellate Division affirmed without opinion (27 App Div 2d 904, 280 NYS2d 520). On appeal to the New York Court of Appeals, the defendant for the first time raised a Fourth Amendment issue, contending that his confessions were the inadmissible fruits of his illegal detention by the police, but the Court of Appeals rejected this contention, holding that the conduct of the police in detaining the defendant was reasonable (22 NY2d 55, 290 NYS2d 898, 238 NE2d 307).

Prior to trial in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia on a charge of attempted federal income tax evasion, the defendant moved to suppress statements which he had made to special agents of the Internal Revenue Service at a noncustodial interview that had been conducted in a private home. At such interview, the government agents informed the defendant that they were investigating his federal income tax liability for certain years, and although full Miranda warnings as to the defendant's constitutional rights were not given, the agents read a printed card to the defendant, informing him that one of the agents' functions was to investigate the possibility of criminal violations of the Internal Revenue laws and related offenses, that under the Fifth Amendment, the agents could not compel the defendant to answer any questions or to submit any information which might tend to incriminate him, that anything which the defendant said and any information which he submitted might be used against him in any criminal proceeding, and that the defendant might, if he wished, seek the assistance of an attorney before responding. After the motion to suppress was denied, the defendant was convicted, and the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed the judgment of conviction (166 App DC 361, 510 F2d 741).

A deceased serviceman's father, who was named as beneficiary in his son's policy under the National Service Life Insurance Act, died without having received any part of the policy's proceeds. His second wife, who was the insured's stepmother, and his former wife, who was the insured's natural mother, filed claims to the proceeds. During the pendency of an action for determination of the proper taker, the stepmother also died. The issue in the present case concerns the distribution of the proceeds under the act of 1940, prior to its 1946 amendment. The District Court awarded to the father's estate the instalments which had matured during his lifetime. The court found that both the stepmother and the natural mother were parents who "last bore that relationship" and thus qualified to take the remaining proceeds by devolution under 602(h) (3) (C) of the act. The instalments which had matured during the stepmother's lifetime were divided equally between her estate and the natural mother; instalments thereafter maturing were awarded to the natural mother alone. The Court of Appeals agreed.

An employee of a railroad, to which the Consolidated Rail Corporation (Conrail) became successor in interest, filed suit for violation of rights conferred by 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (29 USCS 794), which prohibits discrimination against the handicapped by recipients of federal financial assistance. The administratrix of the employee's estate was substituted as a party upon his death. The District Court granted Conrail's motion for summary judgment on the ground that the employee did not have standing to bring a private action under 504 because Conrail had not received federal financial assistance the primary objective of which was to provide employment. The Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed and remanded, with all three judges of the panel agreeing that the cause of action for employment discrimination under 504 was not properly limited to situations where a primary objective of the federal assistance was to provide employment (687 F2d 767).

The president of a closely held corporation, which employed the president's son-in-law as executive vice president, owned 44 percent of the corporation's outstanding stock, for which he originally invested $ 38,900. The corporate president made loans to the corporation, guaranteed loans made to the corporation by banks, and signed a blanket agreement with the corporation's surety agreeing to indemnify the surety for any loss it suffered as the corporation's surety. The corporation defaulted in its performance of two contracts, the surety made good the corporation's default, and the corporate president indemnified the surety to the extent of $ 162,104.57. The corporate president claimed the indemnification loss as a business bad debt on his 1962 federal income tax return. The Internal Revenue Service disallowed the claim and levied assessments against the corporate president. The corporate president paid the assessments and filed refund claims in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana. At a jury trial, the corporate president testified that although his annual income was $ 40,000, he signed the indemnity agreement to protect his $ 12,000-per-year job with the corporation, and never once gave a thought to his investment in the corporation. By special interrogatory, the jury was asked to determine whether the president's signing the indemnity agreement was proximately related to his trade or business of being an employee of the corporation. The trial court charged the jury that significant motivation satisfied the requirement of a proximate relationship, and refused the government's request for an instruction that dominant motivation was the applicable standard. An independent producer of natural gas, having no interstate transmission facilities, sold the gas to interstate pipeline transmission companies which transported it and resold it to consumers and local distributing companies in fourteen states. Under the Natural Gas Act (15 USC 717 et seq.) the Federal Power Commission is authorized to regulate the rates charged by any natural gas company in connection with the transportation or sale of natural gas subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission; a natural gas company is defined by the act as a person engaged in the transportation of natural gas in interstate commerce, or the sale in interstate commerce of such gas for resale; the act excepts from the Commission's jurisdiction the production or gathering of natural gas. The Federal Power Commission ruled that the independent producer was not a natural gas company within the meaning of the Natural Gas Act, and therefore was not within the Commission's jurisdiction over rates.

The State of Idaho, acting as authorized by federal law, requested that a tract of some 27,400 acres of land within its borders be withdrawn from the public domain pending the submission of a proposed development plan as required by the Carey Act (43 USCS 641)--which authorizes the United States Secretary of the Interior, upon proper application, to donate, grant, and patent desert lands to public-land states, such as Idaho, up to certain limited amounts of acreage (in Idaho's case, 3 million acres) so that public-land states may reclaim the land--but the Idaho State Office of the Bureau of Land Management rejected the application, in part, because some of the land requested had already been withdrawn for stock-driveway purposes. The state then appealed to the Interior Board of Land Appeals as to the lands previously withdrawn for stock-driveway purposes, and it also petitioned the Board for reclassification of the stock-driveway lands as being suitable for use under the Carey Act. Prior to the time the Board affirmed the rejection of the state's Carey Act application and returned the case to the Bureau of Lands Management for initial action on the petition for reclassification of the stock-driveway lands and for further action on the remaining lands covered by the application for temporary withdrawal, the state, through its appropriate officials, brought an action in the United States District Court for the District of Idaho against the Secretary of the Interior, seeking to obtain a declaration of its rights under the Carey Act. Four railroads published tariff schedules proposing to reduce substantially their rates for transportation of grain from certain Mississippi and Ohio River ports to various points in the Southeastern United States. Pursuant to 49 USC 15(7), which authorizes the Interstate Commerce Commission to suspend the operation of proposed rates for 7 months, but provides that if an order is not made within the period of suspension the proposed rate "shall go into effect at the end of such period," the Commission suspended the operation of the proposed rates for 7 months. When the Commission did not reach a decision within 7 months, or during 5 succeeding months, the railroads announced that the reduced rates would be put into effect. A barge line competing with the railroads for grain carriage, and three shippers, brought suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama to enjoin the railroads from reducing rates pending the Commission's decision. The District Court denied relief, holding that 15(7) vests exclusive power in the Commission to suspend proposed rate changes, and the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed on the same ground. (308 F2d 181.)

Provisions of the California Elections Code (1) forbade the official governing bodies of political parties from endorsing candidates in party primaries, (2) restricted the organization and composition of such official governing bodies, (3) limited the term of office for a party's state central committee chair, and (4) required that the chair rotate between residents of northern and southern California. Various county central committees of the Democratic and Republican parties, and other groups and individuals active in partisan politics in California, brought an action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California against state officials responsible for enforcing the Code. The plaintiffs contended that the provisions in question deprived political parties and their members of the rights of free speech and free association guaranteed by the Federal Constitution's First and Fourteenth Amendments. The District Court granted summary judgment for the plaintiffs as to the provisions in question, and the United States Court of Appeals affirmed (792 F2d 802). On appeal, the United States Supreme Court vacated and remanded (479 US 1024, 93 L Ed 2d 820, 107 S Ct 864) for further consideration in light of its decision in Tashjian v Republican Party of Connecticut (1986) 479 US 208, 93 L Ed 2d 514, 107 S Ct 544. After supplemental briefing, the Court of Appeals concluded that its previous decision was supported by the Tashjian decision, supra, and accordingly reinstated its judgment affirming the District Court's decision (826 F2d 814).

Upon remand ordered by the Supreme Court of the United States in Sims v Georgia, 385 US 538, 17 L ed 2d 593, 87 S Ct 639, the judge who had presided at defendant's original trial in a Georgia state court, determined, on the basis of the printed record alone, that defendant's confession had been voluntary, and denied a new trial. The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed. (223 Ga 465, 156 SE2d 65.)

Pursuant to statutes of both states, the Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corporation (PATH), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Port Authority that operates an interstate railway system and other facilities, was (1) entitled to all of the immunities of the Port Authority, and (2) subject to suit to the same extent as the Port Authority. Two employees of PATH filed separate complaints in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York against PATH, in which complaints the employees asserted claims under several federal statutes for injuries allegedly suffered during the course of their employment. Defendant was stopped by police officers who suspected he was driving with a suspended license. After they confirmed his license was suspended, they arrested him for the misdemeanor even though under Va. Code Ann. _ 19.2-74, they should have only issued him a summons. A search subsequent to arrest revealed he was carrying crack cocaine. The Court noted that its decisions counseled against changing the calculus that the arrest was constitutionally reasonable because there was probable cause to believe defendant committed the minor crime in the officer's presence. The Court had treated additional protections exclusively as matters of state law. Virginia chose to protect individual privacy and dignity more than the Fourth Amendment required, but it also chose not to attach to violations of its arrest rules the potent remedies that federal courts had applied to Fourth Amendment violations. Linking Fourth Amendment protections to state law would have meant losing a bright-line constitutional standard as well as causing those protection to vary from place to place and from time to time. Because the arrest was constitutional, the search incident to the arrest was also constitutional.

Certain employees were discharged from a private school which specializes in dealing with troubled high school students referred to it by public school officials or by a state drug rehabilitation agency. Public funds account for at least 90 percent of the school's operating budget. The school has contracts with public school committees and with the state agency, and is subject to both state and local regulations. One of the discharged employees filed suit under 42 USCS 1983 in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, alleging that she had been discharged in violation of her constitutional rights. The District Court granted the school's motion for summary judgment, holding that the action of the school in discharging the employee could not be considered state action for purposes of 1983. Five other discharged employees brought a separate suit under 1983. In that suit a different judge of the same District Court held that the school had acted under color of state law, denied a motion to dismiss, and certified its order as immediately appealable pursuant to 28 USCS 1292(b). The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, consolidating the two actions, held that the District Court, in the action brought by the five employees, had erred in concluding that the school had acted under color of state law. The Court of Appeals affirmed the District Court's dismissal of the first employee's action, rejecting her claim that she was discharged under color of state law (641 F2d 14).

The district court's order, that had not resolved a demand for an injunction, was not final, thus, the governor's appeal was timely. For _ 1973cpurposes, the invalidated law never gained "force or effect." Thus, the reversion to the prior practice of gubernatorial appointment of a county commission vacancy was not a "change" requiring preclearance. Since the invalidated state law was never "in force or effect," the baseline practice for filling vacancies was the prior gubernatorial appointment practice. Reinstating that practice thus did not constitute a change requiring preclearance. The invalidated state law was a temporary misapplication of state law, on the books for just over three years and applied once. It was challenged in state court at first opportunity and ultimately invalidated and thus properly regarded as null and void ab initio, incapable of effecting any change for _ 1973c purposes. Practically, the district court's decision gave controlling effect to the erroneous trial court decision and rendered the Alabama Supreme Court's corrections inoperative. Nothing inherent in gubernatorial appointments violated theFifteenth Amendment or the Voting Rights Act.

A criminal defendant pleaded guilty to one count of mail fraud in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California pursuant to a plea bargain whereby the government agreed to recommend probation on condition that restitution be made. The District Court disregarded the recommendation and sentenced the defendant to 6 years of treatment and supervision under the Youth Correction Act (18 USCS 5010(b)). After being released on parole and retaken into custody because of a parole violation, the defendant filed a motion under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 32(d) and 28 USCS 2255 to withdraw his guilty plea or, in the alternative, to have his sentence vacated and be resentenced to the time already served, claiming that the government had failed to comply with its part of the plea bargain upon which his guilty plea was based. The District Court denied the motion and the United States Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that the government had breached the plea bargain agreement because the government attorney, while concurring with defense counsel's statement at sentencing that the government recommended probation with restitution, made no effort to explain the reasons for agreeing to recommend a lenient sentence, instead leaving an impression of less-than-enthusiastic support for leniency. The Court of Appeals held that when the government undertakes to recommend a sentence pursuant to a plea bargain, it has the duty to state its recommendation clearly to the sentencing judge and to express the justification for it (738 F2d 1001).

An individual filed a class action against the Secretary of Health and Human Services in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California challenging the constitutionality of 211(a)(5)(A) of the Social Security Act (42 USCS 411(a)(5)(A)), which established a gender-based presumption regarding the allocation of income from family businesses in community property states. Although the Secretary conceded the unconstitutionality of the statutory presumption, the District Court rejected the Secretary's claim of mootness, held the statute unconstitutional, granted the class's motion for summary judgment, and ordered relief. The Secretary filed a notice of appeal to the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, challenging only the District Court's remedy. The Court of Appeals granted the class's motion to dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction under 28 USCS 1291, because direct review could be had in the Supreme Court pursuant to 28 USCS 1252.

After protracted school desegregation litigation instituted in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia as a class action by Negro parents and guardians against the School Board of Richmond, Virginia, the plaintiffs, on March 10, 1970 filed, in addition to a motion for further relief, an application for the award of attorney's fees; this application was renewed on July 2, 1970. After having approved, on April 5, 1971, a noninterim plan for achievement of a unitary school system in Richmond, the District Court, on May 26, 1971, awarded plaintiffs, in exercise of its equity powers, counsel fees in the amount of $ 43,355 for services rendered from March 10, 1970 to January 29, 1971 (53 FRD 28). While the school board's appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit was pending, 718 of the Emergency School Aid Act (20 USCS 1617) became law; this statute grants authority to a federal court to award the prevailing party in a school desegregation case, upon the entry of a final order, a reasonable attorney's fee when appropriate. The Court of Appeals, sitting en banc, reversed, with one of the judges dissenting, on the grounds that (1) in the absence of a statute authorizing the award of attorneys' fees in a school desegregation case, the award was not justified under the circumstances of the instant case, and (2) 718 was not applicable because there were no orders pending or appealable on either May 26, 1971, when the District Court made its fee award, or on July 1, 1972, when 718 became effective (472 F2d 318).

Claiming that Mountain-Pacific railroads were receiving too large a share from the existing divisions of joint rates from through freight service, Midwestern railroads requested that the Interstate Commerce Commission grant them a greater share of the joint rates. The Commission, making various findings as to such matters as the railroads' costs, rates of return, and revenue needs, used a special divisional scale and issued an order giving the Midwestern railroads a greater share of the joint rates. (321 ICC 17, 322 ICC 491.) The District Court for the Southern District of California set aside the Commission's order on the grounds that certain of the Commission's findings were deficient. (238 F Supp 528.)

In January 1983, a woman lost control of her car as she traveled down a Missouri road. The car overturned, and a state trooper discovered the woman, lying face down in a ditch, without detectable respiratory or cardiac function. Paramedics who arrived at the accident scene were able to restore the woman's breathing and heartbeat, and the woman was then transported to a hospital in an unconscious state. An attending neurosurgeon diagnosed the woman as having sustained probable cerebral contusions compounded by significant oxygen deprivation, or anoxia. The estimated length of the period of her anoxia was 12 to 14 minutes; permanent brain damage generally results, the trial court later found, after 6 minutes in an anoxic state. The woman remained in a coma for approximately 3 weeks, and then progressed to an unconscious state in which she was able to orally ingest some nutrition. In order to ease feeding and further the woman's recovery, surgeons implanted a gastrostomy feeding and hydration tube with the consent of her then husband. In October 1983, the woman was admitted to a state hospital. Subsequent rehabilitative efforts proved unavailing. After it became apparent that the woman had virtually no chance of regaining her mental faculties, her parents--who had been appointed as her coguardians--asked employees of the state hospital to terminate the artificial nutrition and hydration procedures. The employees refused to honor the request without court approval. A state college professor's sex discrimination suit under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e et seq.), instituted in the United States District Court for the District of New Hampshire, resulted in a judgment for the plaintiff. The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit affirmed, stating in one portion of its opinion that with regard to an employer's burden in rebutting a prima facie case of discrimination, under the United States Supreme Court's decision in McDonnell Douglas Corp. v Green (1973) 411 US 792, 36 L Ed 2d 668, 93 S Ct 1817, the employer was required to "prove" the absence of discriminatory motive for its actions (569 F2d 169).

A female former employee of the Pennsylvania state police--alleging that some of her supervisors had subjected her to sexual harassment of such severity that she had been forced to resign--brought suit in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania against the state police under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS __ 2000e et seq.). The District Court, in granting the state police's motion for summary judgment, concluded that (1) the employee's testimony sufficed to permit a trier of fact to conclude that the supervisors had created a hostile work environment; but (2) the employer was not vicariously liable for the supervisors' conduct, as the employee had unreasonably failed to avail herself of the state police's internal procedures for reporting any harassment.

Without being advised of his right to obtain counsel or having counsel offered to him, one was sentenced to life imprisonment as a fourth offender under a state habitual criminal act. The imposition of such sentence was in the discretion of the court.

Appellant is a producer of gas in an Oklahoma natural gas field, but does not purchase from other producers in that field. The gas which it produces is transported through its own facilities to Texas, where it processes the gas, utilizes or sells the by-products, and sells the residue of natural gas to pipe-line companies.

A union had not met the noncommunist affidavit requirements of 9(h) of the amended National Labor Relations Act when it filed with the National Labor Relations Board a charge of unfair labor practices against an employer, based upon its violations of 8(a) (1) and (3) of the act. However, those requirements were met before the Board issued its complaint. A cease and desist order of the Board was challenged by the employer on the ground that the Board could not issue a valid complaint based on a charge by a union which was not in compliance with 9(h).

A county sheriff's office received an anonymous tip that marijuana was being grown on the accused's property. An investigating officer discovered that he could not see from the road the contents of a greenhouse located behind the accused's mobile home, but the officer, while circling twice over the accused's property in a helicopter at an altitude of 400 feet, was able to see with his naked eye what he thought was marijuana growing in the greenhouse, of which the roof and sides were partially open. After a search, pursuant to a warrant based on the officer's observations, revealed marijuana growing in the greenhouse, the accused was charged in a Florida state court with possession of marijuana. The trial court granted the accused's motion to suppress the evidence, and the Florida Court of Appeals, Second District, reversed, but certified to the Florida Supreme Court the question whether the helicopter surveillance constituted a "search" for which a warrant was required under the Federal Constitution's Fourth Amendment. The Florida Supreme Court (1) held that because the accused had a reasonable expectation that his activities inside the greenhouse would remain private and out of the view of aerial observers, the helicopter surveillance constitued a "search" under the Fourth Amendment, (2) quashed the decision of the Court of Appeals, and (3) ordered the trial court's suppression order reinstated (511 So 2d 282).

Respondent Village of Stratton (Village) promulgated an ordinance that, inter alia, prohibits "canvassers" from "going in and upon" private residential property to promote any "cause" without first obtaining a permit from the mayor's office by completing and signing a registration form. Petitioners, a society and a congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses that publish and distribute religious materials, brought this action for injunctive relief, alleging that the ordinance violates their First Amendment rights to the free exercise of religion, free speech, and freedom of the press. The District Court upheld most provisions of the ordinance as valid, content-neutral regulations, although it did require the Village to accept narrowing constructions of several provisions. The Sixth Circuit affirmed. Among its rulings, that court held that the ordinance was content neutral and of general applicability and therefore subject to intermediate scrutiny; rejected petitioners' argument that the ordinance is overbroad because it impairs the right to distribute pamphlets anonymously that was recognized in McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Comm'n, 514 U.S. 334, 131 L. Ed. 2d 426, 115 S. Under 29 USCS 1132(a), a participant in an employee benefit plan is allowed to bring an action to enforce the substantive provisions of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) (29 USCS 1001 et seq.). A "participant" is defined in 29 USCS 1002(7) as any employee or former employee who is or may become eligible to receive a benefit from an employee benefit plan," and an "employee" is defined in 3(6) of ERISA (29 USCS 1002(6)) as "any individual employed by an employer." Petitioner Jose Santos Sanchez is a citizen of El Salvador who challenges the denial of his application to become a lawful permanent resident (LPR) of the United States. Sanchez entered the United States unlawfully in 1997. In 2001, the Government granted him Temporary Protected Status (TPS). Section 1255 provides a way for a ‚Äúnonimmigrant‚Äù‚Äîa foreign national lawfully present in this country on a temporary basis‚Äîto obtain an ‚Äú[a]djustment of status‚Äù to LPR. 8 U. S. C. ¬ß1255. Petitioners brought suits against the Collector of Internal Revenue for refunds of social security taxes. In one of the suits several band leaders were permitted to intervene as defendants. Judgments for the petitioners in the District Court were reversed by the Circuit Court of Appeals.

State departments of motor vehicles (DMVs) required drivers and automobile owners to provide personal information--which may have included a person's name, address, telephone number, vehicle description, Social Security number, medical information, and photograph--as a condition of obtaining a driver's license or registering an automobile. Congress, finding that many states, in turn, sold this personal information to individuals and businesses, enacted the Driver's Privacy Protection Act (DPPA) (18 USCS 2721-2725), which (1) generally prohibited any state DMV, or officer, employee, or contractor thereof, from knowingly disclosing or otherwise making available to any person or entity personal information about any individual obtained by the department in connection with a motor vehicle record; (2) provided that (a) the ban on disclosure of personal information did not apply if drivers had consented to the release of their data, and (b) the prohibition of nonconsensual disclosures was subject to a number of statutory exceptions; (3) regulated the resale and redisclosure of drivers' personal information by private persons who obtained that information from a state DMV; and (4) established several penalties to be imposed on states and private actors that failed to comply with the DPPA's requirements. After a judge of the Court of Common Pleas of Hamilton County, Ohio, had summarily denied the request of out-of-state lawyers, not admitted to practice in Ohio, to appear pro hac vice to represent the defendants in a criminal prosecution, the lawyers commenced a mandamus action in the Supreme Court of Ohio, seeking to overturn the denial of admission and to remove the trial judge from the case. The Supreme Court of Ohio dismissed the mandamus action but removed the trial judge. Thereafter, the new trial judge ruled that the Ohio Supreme Court's dismissal of the mandamus action bound him to deny permission to the lawyers to represent the criminal defendants, although he did allow the lawyers to work with local counsel in preparing the case. The out-of-state lawyers then filed the instant action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio to enjoin further prosecution of the criminal case until the state trial court held a hearing on the pro hac vice application. The District Court held that the lawyers' interest in representing the criminal defendants was a constitutionally protected property right which the state courts had infringed without according the lawyers procedural due process (434 F Supp 481), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed (574 F2d 874).

He alleged that Facebook violated the TCPA by maintaining a database that stored phone numbers and programming its equipment to send automated text messages. An alien lawfully admitted to the United States for permanent residence on February 20, 1950, was called for the draft and passed his preinduction medical examination on October 11, 1950. On November 14, 1950, he requested an exemption from military service on the ground of alienage. Effective June 19, 1951, Congress withdrew such exemptions from permanent resident aliens. The alien was again called for the draft but was found to be physically unfit. Several years later his petition for naturalization was denied by the United States District Court for the Northern District of California on the ground that he was debarred from citizenship, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed (432 F2d 438).

The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (5 USCS 552) generally permits disclosure of federal agency records, but 552(b)(3) provides an exception for materials specifically exempted from disclosure by other statutes of a type described in 552(b)(3).
