An employer was charged, in thirty-two counts of an information, with violations of the minimum wage ( 6) and overtime provisions ( 7) and of the requirements for record-keeping ( 11) of the Fair Labor Standards Act. Proceeding on the theory that it is a course of conduct rather than the separate items in such course that constitute the punishable offense, the District Court ordered consolidation of the separate acts set forth in the information into three counts, charging one violation each of 6, 7, and 11.

An untenured school teacher, who had been involved in several disruptive incidents, such as arguments with another teacher and with school employees, and making an obscene gesture to female students, communicated the substance of the school principal's memorandum on teacher dress and appearance to a local radio station which used his communication in a newscast. Approximately one month later, the school board refused to renew the teacher's contract, citing his lack of tact in handling professional matters and specifically mentioning the radio station and obscene gesture incidents. The teacher instituted an action for reinstatement and damages in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio, claiming that the board's refusal to rehire him violated his First and Fourteenth Amendment rights. The District Court held that the teacher was entitled to reinstatement with back pay, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed (529 F2d 524).

Waterfront terminal facilities in Manila owned by the plaintiffs were destroyed by the United States Army to prevent them from falling into enemy hands. After the war the plaintiffs demanded compensation under the Fifth Amendment.

Prior to its amendment on July 1, 1952, 1708 of the Revised Criminal Code imposed a lesser penalty upon theft of mail or any article or thing contained therein, "if the value or face value of any such article or thing does not exceed $ 100." The lower federal courts were divided as to whether the lesser penalty was limited to thefts from mail as opposed to thefts of mail for which the maximum punishment might be imposed.

In an action brought in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania prior to the effective date of the Pennsylvania Abortion Control Act, the District Court held unconstitutional certain provisions of the Act, among others, the viability determination and standard of care provisions of 5(a) of the Act, requiring, upon pain of penal sanction for its violation, that every person performing or inducing an abortion (1) make a determination "based on his experience, judgment, or professional competence that the fetus is not viable," and (2) upon determining that a fetus "is viable or ... may be viable" to "exercise that degree of professional skill, care and diligence to preserve the life and health of the fetus which such person would be required to exercise in order to preserve the life and health of any fetus intended to be born and not aborted" and to adopt that abortion technique "which would provide the best opportunity for the fetus to be aborted alive so long as a different technique would not be necessary in order to preserve the life or health of the mother" (401 F Supp 554). On direct appeal to the United States Supreme Court from the decision of the three-judge District Court, the Supreme Court vacated part of the District Court's judgment and remanded the case (49 L Ed 2d 1204). Among other things, the three-judge District Court, on remand, adhered to its original view regarding 5(a)'s unconstitutionality, and declared 5(a)'s provisions invalid on vagueness and overbreadth grounds.

The defendant's robbery conviction by the United States District Court for the District of Columbia was affirmed by the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia (125 App DC 231, 370 F2d 477), both courts rejecting the defendant's contention that the robbery victim's automobile registration card had been found in the defendant's car through an unlawful search and was inadmissible in evidence.

The surety litigated language in the debtor's plan to provide for indemnification of the surety in the event the debtor defaulted on its workers' compensation obligations, and the parties' indemnity agreements provided that the debtor was responsible for the surety's attorney fees in litigating surety's rights in connection with the bonds issued to the debtor. The surety filed an amended claim to recover its fees, but the claim was disallowed on the ground that recovery of fees was precluded because the litigated issues involved federal bankruptcy law rather than contractual issues related to the bonds. The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously held that federal bankruptcy law did not disallow the surety's contract-based claims for attorney's fees based solely on the fact that the fees were incurred litigating bankruptcy law issues. 11 U.S.C.S. ¬¨√ü 502(b) provided that the surety's claim was allowed in the absence of a statutory exception to allowance, no such express exception was identified to warrant disallowance of the surety's claim, and the fact that the surety's entitlement to fees was contractual presented no obstacle to enforcing such entitlement in the debtor's bankruptcy.

The Federal Sentencing Guidelines first enter the sentencing process when the United States Probation Office prepares a presentence report containing, as relevant here, an advisory Guidelines range based on the seriousness of a defendant's offense and the extent of his criminal history. A district court may depart from the Guidelines, but it "must consult [them] and take them into account when sentencing." United States v. Booker, 543 U. 5. 220, 264. Given the Guidelines' complexity, a District Court's use of an incorrect Guidelines range may go unnoticed. That error can be remedied on appeal pursuant to Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 52(b), provided that (1) there is an error that was not intentionaly relinquished or abandoned, United States v. Olano, 507 U. 5. 725, 732-733; (2) the error is plain, i.e., clear or obvious, id., at 734; and (3) the error affected the defendant's substantial rights, ibid., which in the ordinary case means he or she must "show a reasonable probability that, but for the error," the outcome of the proceeding would have been different, United States v. Dominguez Benitez, 542 U. 5. 74, 82. Once these three conditions have been met, the court of appeals should exercise its discretion to correct the forfeited error if the error "'seriously affects the fairness, integrity or public reputation of judicial proceedings."' Olano, 507 U. S., at 736 (brackets omitted). A railroad brakeman claiming to have sustained personal injuries through the negligence of his employer executed a release for a consideration of $ 250. Later he brought an action in which he claimed that the release was executed in the belief that his injuries were temporary, when in fact they were not, and that it was accordingly invalid. The employer contested the issue of permanency of the injuries, and also sought to explain the small consideration for the release upon the ground that upon the evidence in its hands at the time, no liability was indicated.

The Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act of 1984 (Hatch-Waxman Act or Act) creates special procedures for identifying and resolving patent disputes between brand-name and generic drug manufacturers, one of which requires a prospective generic manufacturer to assure the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) that it will not infringe the brand-name's patents. One way to provide such assurance (the "paragraph IV" route) is by certifying that any listed, relevant patent "is invalid or will not be infringed by the manufacture, use, or sale" of the generic drug. 21 U. S. C. ¬ß3550)(2)(A)(vii)(IV). Respondent Solvay Pharmaceuticals obtained a patent for its approved brand-name drug AndroGel. Subsequently, respondents Actavis and Paddock filed applications for generic drugs modeled after AndroGel and certified under paragraph IV that Solvay's patent was invalid and that their drugs did not infringe it. Solvay sued Actavis and Paddock, claiming patent infringement. See 35 U. S. C. ¬ß271(e)(2)(A). The FDA eventually approved Actavis' generic product, but instead of bringing its drug to market, Actavis entered into a "reverse payment" settlement agreement with Solvay, agreeing not to bring its generic to market for a specified number of years and agreeing to promote AndroGel to doctors in exchange for millions of dollars. Paddock made a similar agreement with Solvay, as did respondent Par, another manufacturer aligned in the patent litigation with Paddock. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) filed suit, alleging that respondents violated ¬ß5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act by unlawfully agreeing to abandon their patent challenges, to refrain from launching their low-cost generic drugs, and to share in Solvay's monopoly profits. At defendant's third trial in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia upon a murder charge, in which the chief defense was insanity, the defendant testified for the first time, and was asked on cross- examination, "This is the first time you have gone on the stand, isn't it?" The defense moved for a mistrial, which was denied, and subsequently the defendant was found guilty. The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia affirmed. (107 App DC 159, 275 F2d 617.)

Under the doctrine of Feres v United States (1950) 340 US 135, 95 L Ed 152, 71 S Ct 153, the Federal Government is not liable under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) (28 USCS 1346, 2671-2680) for injuries to a service member where the injuries arise out of or in the course of activity incident to the member's military service. A United States Coast Guard officer--a helicopter pilot--was dispatched on a rescue mission. After the officer requested radar assistance from civilian air traffic controllers of the Federal Aviation Administration, and the controllers assumed radar control of the officer's helicopter, the helicopter crashed into a mountain in Hawaii, killing the officer and the rest of the crew. The officer's widow filed a wrongful death action under the FTCA in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, and alleged that the controllers' negligence caused her husband's death. The District Court, however, relying on the Feres doctrine, dismissed the action, on the ground that the officer had been killed in the course of his military duties. On appeal, a panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit reversed, and expressed the view that the Feres doctrine did not bar an FTCA suit on behalf of a service member, where the alleged federal tortfeasors--the air traffic controllers--were not (1) members of the Armed Forces, or (2) civilian employees engaged in activities usually associated with the Armed Forces (749 F2d 1530).
